    Module 8 · Machine learning

    Machine learning, from a straight line to a neural network

    Machine learning carried 15 marks in 2024, 12 in 2025 and 14 in 2026: about one mark in six of the subject paper. The questions are friendlier than they look: fit a line, count a model’s parameters, find the support vectors, compute an information gain, run one round of k-means. This module starts from what “learning from data” even means, builds each method from a small Data Premier League example, and then works through every DA machine-learning question asked so far.

    You need: vectors, dot products and eigenvalues from linear algebra, Bayes’ theorem from probability, mean and variance from statistics, and derivatives from calculus. Each chapter recalls the exact piece it uses.

    The route

      What does it mean for a computer to “learn”? This part starts from zero: the words every machine-learning question uses (feature, label, training set, loss), how to judge a classifier with a confusion matrix, and then the first real method, linear regression, which fits a straight line by making the squared errors as small as possible. Both chapters carry a past GATE DA question, and every later chapter of this module builds on them.

      You need: nothing from this module. Mean and covariance from statistics, derivatives from calculus and solving a small linear system from linear algebra help in Chapter 1.2; each is recalled where it is used.

      What machine learning is: learning a rule from examples

      Machine learning is a way of building a prediction rule from examples: instead of writing the rule by hand, you show the computer many past cases with their answers and let it find a rule that fits them.

      Every machine-learning question in GATE DA (about one mark in six of the subject paper) uses this chapter’s vocabulary, and 2026 Q47 asked directly for accuracy, precision and recall from a classifier’s mistakes.

      It’s like how a new team analyst learns to read a pitch: nobody hands them a rulebook; they watch hundreds of matches, note what the pitch looked like and what happened, and slowly form their own rule.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      The words (feature, label, supervised, training and test set) appear in every machine-learning question; the evaluation measures are asked directly.

      2026 Q47 · accuracy, precision, recall2026 Q12 · test set and LOOCV splits2024 Q18 · kinds of model (PCA, naive Bayes, logistic)
      Heat: every year as vocabulary; metrics asked in 2026

      A problem with no obvious rule

      The Hyderabad Hyperplanes’ physio wants to know, before each match, which players are likely to pick up an injury. Nobody can write down an exact rule for that. Too many things matter: how many overs a bowler sent down last week, how much they slept on the flight, their age, the heat.

      What the physio does have is a record of past seasons: for every player before every match, those numbers, and whether the player was actually injured. Machine learning turns that record into a rule.

      The difference from ordinary programming is the direction of travel. In ordinary programming a person writes the rule and the computer applies it to data. In machine learning the computer is given data together with the answers, and produces the rule.

      The words, one at a time

      Here is a slice of the physio’s record. Each row is one player before one match.

      Overs bowled last weekHours of sleepAgeInjured?
      226.031yes
      88.024no
      157.527no
      255.534yes
      Vocabulary
      example
      One row: one case the model can learn from (here, one player before one match). Also called a data point or an instance. The number of examples is written $n$.
      feature
      One measured input column, such as “hours of sleep”. The features of one example form a vector $\x = (x_1, \ldots, x_d)$ with $d$ entries; for the first row, $\x = (22, 6.0, 31)$ and $d = 3$.
      label
      The answer we want to predict, written $y$. Here $y$ is “injured?”, and for the first row $y = $ yes.
      dataset
      The collection of examples with their labels: $(\x_1, y_1), \ldots, (\x_n, y_n)$.
      model
      The rule being learned: a function $f$ that takes a feature vector and returns a prediction $\hat y = f(\x)$ (read “y-hat”).
      parameter
      A number inside the model that learning adjusts. In the rule "flag a player if $0.1 \times \text{overs} - 0.5 \times \text{sleep} \gt 0$", the 0.1 and the 0.5 are parameters.
      training
      Choosing the parameters so that the model’s predictions match the known labels as well as possible.

      Supervised learning: every training example comes with its label, and the model learns to predict the label from the features. Two kinds, by what the label is:

      • Regression: the label is a number (a team’s final total, a player’s auction price).
      • Classification: the label is one of a few categories, called classes (injured or not; which of the five teams wins).

      Unsupervised learning: there are no labels at all, only features. The goal is to find structure, for example groups of similar fans (clustering, Part 6) or the few directions along which the data varies most (PCA, Part 6).

      Training data and test data

      Suppose a model simply memorised the record: “player 7 before match 12: injured”. It would be perfect on the record and useless next season, because next season’s cases are new. What we care about is performance on examples the model has not seen. That ability is called generalisation.

      So before training, the data is split in two. The training set is used to choose the parameters. The test set is locked away and used only once, at the end, to estimate how the model will do on new cases. A student who has seen the exact exam paper in advance can score full marks without understanding anything; the test set is the paper they have not seen.

      Part 2 builds on this: why a model can fit its training data too well (overfitting) and how cross-validation chooses settings without touching the test set.

      Loss: a number for “how wrong”

      To train, the computer needs a single number that says how bad a prediction is. That number is the loss. Training means choosing the parameters that make the average loss over the training set as small as possible.

      A loss function $\ell(y, \hat y)$ measures the cost of predicting $\hat y$ when the truth is $y$. Two common ones:

      • Squared loss (regression): $\ell(y, \hat y) = (y - \hat y)^2$. Predicting a total of 170 when the team made 180 costs $10^2 = 100$.
      • 0–1 loss (classification): $\ell = 0$ if $\hat y = y$ and $1$ otherwise. It simply counts mistakes.

      The training error is the average loss over the training set, $\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(y_i, f(\x_i))$. The same average over the test set is the test error.

      Judging a classifier: the confusion matrix

      Say the physio’s model flags players as “at risk” (the positive class) or “fine” (the negative class). Each prediction lands in one of four boxes, and counting them gives the confusion matrix.

      Predicted positivePredicted negative
      Actually positiveTP true positive: injured, and flaggedFN false negative: injured, but missed
      Actually negativeFP false positive: fine, but flaggedTN true negative: fine, not flagged

      $$\text{accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + FP + FN + TN},\qquad \text{precision} = \frac{TP}{TP + FP},\qquad \text{recall} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}.$$

      • Accuracy: what fraction of all predictions were right.
      • Precision: of the players we flagged, what fraction were really injured? (Read along the “predicted positive” column.)
      • Recall: of the players who were really injured, what fraction did we flag? (Read along the “actually positive” row.) Also called sensitivity or true positive rate.

      With more than one class of interest, each class gets its own precision and recall: treat that class as “positive” and every other class as “negative”.

      Careful: accuracy can flatter a useless model. If only 2% of matches are rain-delayed, a “model” that always answers “no delay” is 98% accurate and never catches a single delay: its recall is 0. When one class is rare, look at precision and recall.
      Try it

      The model gives each of 20 Hyderabad Hyperplanes players an injury-risk score, and flags everyone whose score is at or above the threshold. Move the threshold and watch the four counts change. Notice that lowering it raises recall (fewer injured players missed) but lets in more false alarms. Then switch to “rare injuries” and find a threshold with high accuracy but poor recall.

      GATE DA 2026 · Q47 · MSQ · 2 marks

      Consider that 20 stories of Author X and 10 stories of Author Y were kept together without mentioning the names of the authors. A classifier was then asked to predict the author (X or Y) of each of these stories. Let, out of X’s stories, 6 were classified as that of Y. On the other hand, out of Y’s stories, 2 were classified as that of X.

      Considering X and Y as two classes, which of the following statements is/are true?

      1. Accuracy of the classifier is 11/15.
      2. Precision of Class X is higher than the Precision of Class Y.
      3. Recall of Class X is higher than the Recall of Class Y.
      4. Accuracy of the classifier is 14/15.

      1. Fill the confusion matrix. X’s 20 stories: 6 called Y, so 14 called X. Y’s 10 stories: 2 called X, so 8 called Y.

        Every question about these measures starts with the four counts. Rows are the truth, columns the prediction.

      2. Accuracy $= \dfrac{14 + 8}{30} = \dfrac{22}{30} = \dfrac{11}{15}$. So (A) is true and (D) is false.

        The correct predictions are the diagonal: X called X, and Y called Y.

      3. Precision of X: the classifier said “X” $14 + 2 = 16$ times and was right 14 times, so $\tfrac{14}{16} = 0.875$. Precision of Y: it said “Y” $8 + 6 = 14$ times and was right 8 times, so $\tfrac{8}{14} \approx 0.571$. (B) is true.

        Precision divides by how often a class was predicted, so read down the column.

      4. Recall of X $= \tfrac{14}{20} = 0.7$; recall of Y $= \tfrac{8}{10} = 0.8$. X’s recall is lower, so (C) is false. Answer: (A) and (B).

        Recall divides by how many truly belong to the class, so read along the row. Official key: A; B.

      The Hyderabad Hyperplanes’ injury model is checked on 100 player-matches: 12 true positives, 8 false positives, 4 false negatives and 76 true negatives. Find its precision and its recall.

      Precision divides TP by everything that was flagged; recall divides TP by everything that was really injured.

      Precision $= \frac{12}{12 + 8} = 0.6$. Recall $= \frac{12}{12 + 4} = 0.75$. (Accuracy would be $\frac{12 + 76}{100} = 0.88$, which sounds better than either.)

      Which of these is an unsupervised learning task?

      1. Predicting a team’s final total from its score after 10 overs, using last season’s matches.
      2. Splitting ticket buyers into groups with similar buying habits, with no group names given in advance.
      3. Deciding whether a delivery was a no-ball, from clips that umpires have already marked.
      4. Predicting a player’s auction price from past auctions.

      Ask of each task: does the training data come with the answer we want to predict?

      (B) has no labels: nobody says which group a buyer belongs to, so the method must discover the groups (clustering). (A) and (D) are supervised regression (the label is a number); (C) is supervised classification (the umpires supplied the labels).

      Of 1000 DPL matches, 20 were rain-delayed. A lazy model predicts “no delay” for every match. Taking “delayed” as the positive class, find its accuracy and its recall.

      It gets every non-delayed match right and every delayed match wrong. How many delays does it catch?

      Correct predictions: the 980 non-delayed matches, so accuracy $= 980/1000 = 0.98$. It flags nothing, so TP = 0 and recall $= 0/20 = 0$. High accuracy, no use at all.

      Which statements about training and test sets are true? (Select all that apply.)

      1. The test set should not be used to choose the model’s parameters.
      2. A training error of zero guarantees a small test error.
      3. The test error estimates how the model will do on new, unseen examples.
      4. The training and test examples should come from the same kind of data (for example, the same league and era).

      Think of the student who memorised last year’s paper.

      (A) If the test set helps choose parameters, it is no longer unseen and its error becomes optimistic. (C) That is its whole purpose. (D) A test on a different kind of data says little about the cases you care about. (B) is false: a model can memorise its training set (zero training error) and still do badly on new examples; that is overfitting, Part 2.

      A model predicts upsets (the weaker team winning) in 200 DPL matches; 50 of them were actual upsets. On these matches its recall for “upset” is 0.8 and its precision is 0.5. What is its accuracy?

      Recall gives TP. Precision then tells you how many matches were flagged in total, hence FP. The rest of the 150 non-upsets are TN.

      Recall $= TP/50 = 0.8$, so $TP = 40$ and $FN = 10$.

      Precision $= TP/(TP + FP) = 0.5$, so $40$ is half of everything flagged: 80 flagged, $FP = 40$.

      Non-upsets: $150$, of which 40 were wrongly flagged, so $TN = 110$.

      Accuracy $= \frac{40 + 110}{200} =$ 0.75.

      A tempting slip is to average precision and recall (0.65), or to take $TP/200 = 0.2$; neither is accuracy, which counts every correct prediction, including true negatives.

      A classifier gives each example a score and predicts “positive” when the score is at least a threshold $t$. Which statements are always true? (Select all that apply.)

      1. Lowering $t$ can never decrease recall.
      2. Lowering $t$ can never increase precision.
      3. Setting $t$ below every score gives recall 1.
      4. If 1% of examples are positive, any classifier with 99% accuracy has recall at least 0.5.

      Recall’s denominator (actual positives) never changes with $t$. For precision, try three examples whose scores, from highest to lowest, are negative, positive, positive.

      (A) True. Lowering $t$ only adds flagged examples, so TP can only stay the same or grow, while TP + FN (the number of actual positives) is fixed.

      (C) True. Every example is flagged, so FN = 0 and recall $= TP/TP = 1$.

      (B) False. With scores ordered negative, positive, positive (highest first), a high $t$ flags only the negative: precision 0. Lowering $t$ to include the next one gives precision $\tfrac12$. Precision can go either way.

      (D) False. Predicting “negative” for everything is 99% accurate with recall 0.

      A batter’s scores in four innings are 2, 3, 4 and 11. You must predict every innings with one constant $c$. Which pair gives, in order, the $c$ that minimises the total squared loss $\sum (y_i - c)^2$ and a $c$ that minimises the total absolute loss $\sum |y_i - c|$?

      1. 5 and 5
      2. 5 and 3.5
      3. 3.5 and 5
      4. 4 and 4

      Differentiate $\sum (y_i - c)^2$ and set it to zero. For the absolute loss, ask what happens to the total when $c$ moves a little to the right: how many points get nearer, and how many get farther?

      Squared loss: $\frac{d}{dc}\sum (y_i - c)^2 = -2\sum (y_i - c) = 0$ gives $c = \bar y = \frac{20}{4} = 5$, the mean. Total loss $9 + 4 + 1 + 36 = 50$.

      Absolute loss: moving $c$ right by a small step lowers the loss by that step for each point above $c$ and raises it for each point below. The total stops falling once half the points are on each side, so any $c$ between the two middle values 3 and 4 is best (total 10). That is the median; 3.5 is one such value. Answer (B).

      (A) assumes both losses share a minimiser; the outlier 11 drags the mean but not the median. (C) swaps them. (D) has a valid absolute-loss minimiser (4), but under squared loss 4 costs $4 + 1 + 0 + 49 = 54 \gt 50$.

      • Name the positive class before computing precision or recall.
      • Write the four counts (TP, FP, FN, TN) first; every measure is a ratio of them.
      • Keep the test set untouched until the very end.
      • Swapping precision and recall: precision divides by what was predicted positive, recall by what is positive.
      • Trusting accuracy when one class is rare.
      • Calling a task “unsupervised” just because the labels are numbers. Numeric labels mean regression, which is still supervised.
      1. Supervised learning learns a model ŷ = f(x) from examples with labels (regression for numbers, classification for categories); unsupervised learning has no labels.
      2. Train on the training set by minimising average loss; judge on an unseen test set.
      3. Accuracy = (TP + TN)/all, precision = TP/(TP + FP), recall = TP/(TP + FN).

      A model predicts rain delays and is right on 95% of matches. Only 5% of matches are actually delayed. Is it a good model?

      Yes: 95% is excellent
      What would a model that never predicts a delay score here?
      Can’t tell yet: always saying “no delay” also scores 95%
      With a rare class, accuracy alone hides whether the model catches any delays. Check its recall and precision.
      No: 95% accuracy always means poor recall
      It might catch every delay. Accuracy alone can’t say either way.
      Yes, as long as the test set was used for training
      Training on the test set makes the 95% less trustworthy, not more.

      A dataset of past matches has columns “toss won”, “home ground”, “score at 10 overs” and “won the match”. A model predicts the result before the match ends. Which column is the label?

      score at 10 overs
      That’s something the model is given, so it’s a feature.
      home ground
      Known before the match: a feature.
      won the match
      It’s the answer the model learns to predict. The other three are features.
      All four together
      The label is the one thing being predicted.

      Recall answers which question?

      Of everything the model flagged, how much was really positive?
      That one divides by what was predicted positive. Which measure is that?
      Of all predictions, how many were right?
      That counts both classes’ correct predictions.
      Of the real negatives, how many were left unflagged?
      That is about negatives. Recall is about positives.
      Of the real positives, how many did the model catch?
      Recall $= TP/(TP + FN)$: the denominator is every actual positive.

      Linear regression: the best straight line

      Linear regression predicts a number as a weighted sum of the features, and chooses the weights that make the sum of squared prediction errors on the training data as small as possible.

      GATE DA 2025 Q34 asked for the least-squares slope of a line through the origin, and the closed form $\mathbf{w} = (X\T X)^{-1}X\T\y$ met here is the starting point of ridge regression (2026 Q37 and Q55, Part 2).

      It’s like a stiff rod held by springs, one hanging from each data point: the rod settles where the springs’ total pull balances, and with springs whose energy grows with the square of their stretch, that resting place is the least-squares line.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      A direct computation (the slope of a fitted line), and the base that ridge regression changes.

      2025 Q34 · y = wx by least squares2026 Q37 · ridge regression (Part 2)2026 Q55 · ridge weights (Part 2)Sample Q12 · ridge (Part 2)
      Heat: most years, directly or through ridge

      The question

      The Bengaluru Backprops’ analyst wants to predict how many runs a batter will score from how many balls they face. Four innings from last season:

      Balls faced $x$10203040
      Runs $y$18244252

      Plot them and they lie roughly along a line. No single line passes through all four, so we need a way to say which line is best.

      A line is $\hat y = wx + b$: $w$ is the slope (extra runs per extra ball faced) and $b$ is the intercept (the prediction at $x = 0$). In machine-learning language, $w$ is a weight and $b$ a bias; both are the model’s parameters.

      For each innings, the gap between what happened and what the line predicts, $y_i - \hat y_i$, is the residual. Some residuals are positive, some negative. Squaring them makes every gap count as a cost and punishes big misses heavily. The least-squares line is the one with the smallest total of squared residuals.

      Given data $(x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_n, y_n)$, choose $w$ and $b$ to minimise the sum of squared errors $$\text{SSE}(w, b) = \sum_{i=1}^n \big(y_i - (wx_i + b)\big)^2.$$ This is the squared loss of Chapter 1.1, added up over the training set. Dividing by $n$ gives the mean squared error (MSE); the same $w, b$ minimise both.

      Try it

      Move the slope and intercept sliders to make the total of squared residuals (the vertical gaps, drawn dashed) as small as you can, then press “Best fit” to see how close you came. Drag a point (or select the plot and use the arrow keys; keys 1–4 pick a point) and watch the best line follow it. Switch to “through the origin” to see what forcing $b = 0$ costs.

      Finding the best line with calculus

      SSE is a smooth bowl-shaped function of $w$ and $b$, so its lowest point is where both partial derivatives are zero (recall from Calculus 2.2 that an interior minimum has zero gradient).

      Setting $\partial\,\text{SSE}/\partial b = -2\sum (y_i - wx_i - b) = 0$ gives $\sum y_i = w\sum x_i + nb$, that is, $\bar y = w\bar x + b$. So the best line always passes through the point of means $(\bar x, \bar y)$.

      Setting $\partial\,\text{SSE}/\partial w = -2\sum x_i (y_i - wx_i - b) = 0$ and substituting $b = \bar y - w\bar x$ gives the slope below.

      $$w = \frac{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y)}{\sum_i (x_i - \bar x)^2} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x, y)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)},\qquad b = \bar y - w\,\bar x.$$ (The sample covariance and variance from Statistics; their $\tfrac1{n-1}$ factors cancel.)

      Through the origin. If the model is forced to be $\hat y = wx$ (no intercept), only $\frac{d}{dw}\sum (y_i - wx_i)^2 = -2\sum x_i(y_i - wx_i) = 0$ remains, so $$w = \frac{\sum_i x_i y_i}{\sum_i x_i^2}.$$

      Fit $\hat y = wx + b$ to the four Backprops innings above, then fit $\hat y = wx$ through the origin, and compare the two SSEs.

      1. Means: $\bar x = 25$, $\bar y = \frac{18 + 24 + 42 + 52}{4} = 34$. Deviations: $x_i - \bar x = -15, -5, 5, 15$ and $y_i - \bar y = -16, -10, 8, 18$.

        Centring first keeps the numbers small and is exactly what the slope formula asks for.

      2. $\sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) = 240 + 50 + 40 + 270 = 600$ and $\sum (x_i - \bar x)^2 = 225 + 25 + 25 + 225 = 500$. So $w = \frac{600}{500} = 1.2$.

        Each extra ball faced is worth 1.2 runs on this line: a strike rate of 120.

      3. $b = \bar y - w\bar x = 34 - 1.2 \times 25 = 4$. The line is $\hat y = 1.2x + 4$, with predictions 16, 28, 40, 52 and residuals $2, -4, 2, 0$. SSE $= 4 + 16 + 4 + 0 = 24$.

        The residuals add to zero, as they must when the fit has an intercept (that was the $\partial/\partial b = 0$ equation).

      4. Through the origin: $\sum x_i y_i = 180 + 480 + 1260 + 2080 = 4000$ and $\sum x_i^2 = 100 + 400 + 900 + 1600 = 3000$, so $w = \frac{4000}{3000} \approx 1.333$. Its SSE is about 34.67, larger than 24.

        Removing $b$ removes a parameter, so the best fit can only get worse (or stay equal). The slope steepens to make up for the missing intercept.

      GATE DA 2025 · Q34 · NAT · 1 mark

      Given data $\{(-1, 1), (2, -5), (3, 5)\}$ of the form $(x, y)$, we fit a model $y = wx$ using linear least-squares regression. The optimal value of $w$ is ______ (Round off to three decimal places)

      1. The model has no intercept, so use $w = \dfrac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2}$.

        "$y = wx$" is the signal: a line forced through the origin. The centred formula would be wrong here, because it fits an intercept too.

      2. $\sum x_i y_i = (-1)(1) + (2)(-5) + (3)(5) = -1 - 10 + 15 = 4$. $\sum x_i^2 = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14$.

        Watch the signs: two of the three products are negative.

      3. $w = \frac{4}{14} = \frac27 \approx$ 0.286.

        Official key: 0.285 to 0.287.

      More than one feature

      Runs probably depend on more than balls faced: the batting position, the pitch, the opposition. With $d$ features the model becomes $$\hat y = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \cdots + w_dx_d + b = \mathbf{w}\T\x + b.$$ This is multiple linear regression. With two features it fits a flat plane to points in 3-D; with more, a flat “hyperplane” (the higher-dimensional version of a plane).

      To write all $n$ predictions at once, stack the examples as rows of a matrix. Put a column of ones first so that the intercept becomes just another weight: $$X = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & x_{11} & \cdots & x_{1d}\\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots\\ 1 & x_{n1} & \cdots & x_{nd}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \mathbf{w} = \begin{pmatrix} b\\ w_1\\ \vdots\\ w_d\end{pmatrix},\qquad \hat\y = X\mathbf{w}.$$ $X$ is the design matrix: $n$ rows (examples) and $d + 1$ columns. The SSE is $\norm{\y - X\mathbf{w}}^2$.

      The weights that minimise $\norm{\y - X\mathbf{w}}^2$ satisfy $$X\T X\,\mathbf{w} = X\T\y.$$ If the columns of $X$ are linearly independent, $X\T X$ is invertible and $$\mathbf{w} = (X\T X)^{-1}X\T\y.$$ For a model with no intercept, simply leave out the column of ones.

      Why. The gradient of $\norm{\y - X\mathbf{w}}^2$ with respect to $\mathbf{w}$ is $-2X\T(\y - X\mathbf{w})$; setting it to zero gives the normal equations. Read geometrically: the residual vector $\y - X\mathbf{w}$ is perpendicular to every column of $X$. The fitted values $X\mathbf{w}$ are the projection of $\y$ onto the column space of $X$ (recall projections from Linear algebra 3.2). The column of ones being perpendicular to the residuals is the statement “residuals add to zero”.

      With one feature and an intercept, the normal equations reduce to the formulas above. For the Backprops data: $X\T X = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 100\\ 100 & 3000\end{pmatrix}$ and $X\T\y = \begin{pmatrix}136\\ 4000\end{pmatrix}$. Solving gives $b = 4$, $w = 1.2$, the same line.

      When the columns are dependent (a feature repeated, a feature that is a fixed multiple of another, or fewer examples than weights), $X\T X$ is singular and infinitely many weight vectors fit equally well. Ridge regression (Part 2) fixes this by adding $\lambda I$.

      "Fit $y = wx$" (no intercept): $w = \sum xy / \sum x^2$. "Fit $y = wx + b$": $w = \sum (x - \bar x)(y - \bar y) / \sum (x - \bar x)^2$ and $b = \bar y - w\bar x$. With several features, write $X\T X$ and $X\T\y$ and solve the small system; for a $2\times2$ system, $\begin{pmatrix}a & b\\ c & d\end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix}d & -b\\ -c & a\end{pmatrix}$.

      Fit the least-squares line $\hat y = wx + b$ to the points $(1, 3)$, $(2, 5)$, $(3, 4)$, $(4, 8)$.

      $\bar x = 2.5$ and $\bar y = 5$. Multiply the deviations pairwise and add.

      Deviations: $x - \bar x = -1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5$ and $y - \bar y = -2, 0, -1, 3$.

      $\sum (x - \bar x)(y - \bar y) = 3 + 0 - 0.5 + 4.5 = 7$ and $\sum (x - \bar x)^2 = 2.25 + 0.25 + 0.25 + 2.25 = 5$, so $w = 1.4$.

      $b = 5 - 1.4 \times 2.5 = 1.5$.

      The Backprops’ fitted line is $\hat y = 1.2x + 4$ (runs from balls faced). Predict the runs for a batter who faces 35 balls, and find the residual for an innings of 42 runs off 30 balls.

      A residual is actual minus predicted.

      Prediction: $1.2 \times 35 + 4 = 46$. For 30 balls the line predicts $1.2 \times 30 + 4 = 40$, so the residual is $42 - 40 = 2$.

      A multiple linear regression with an intercept uses 3 features and is trained on 50 matches. What is the size of $X\T X$ in the normal equations?

      1. $3\times3$
      2. $4\times4$
      3. $50\times50$
      4. $50\times4$

      First find the size of $X$ itself, remembering the column of ones.

      $X$ is $50\times4$ (one row per match; a column of ones plus 3 feature columns). Then $X\T X$ is $(4\times50)(50\times4) = 4\times4$: one row and column per weight. (A) forgets the intercept; (C) is $XX\T$; (D) is $X$ itself.

      A least-squares line $\hat y = wx + b$ (with intercept) is fitted to $n \ge 3$ points whose $x$ values are not all equal. Which statements are always true? (Select all that apply.)

      1. The residuals add up to zero.
      2. The line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$.
      3. At least one residual is zero.
      4. Fitting $x$ from $y$ instead gives slope exactly $1/w$.

      (A) and (B) both come from setting $\partial\,\text{SSE}/\partial b = 0$. For (C) and (D), test the four Backprops points or a small example.

      (A) and (B) are the equation $\sum (y_i - wx_i - b) = 0$, written two ways.

      (C) is false: for $(1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 8)$ the line $1.4x + 1.5$ predicts 2.9, 4.3, 5.7, 7.1, and no residual is zero. (The Backprops fit had one zero residual by chance.)

      (D) is false: the two slopes are $\frac{\text{Cov}}{\text{Var}(x)}$ and $\frac{\text{Cov}}{\text{Var}(y)}$, whose product is $r^2$ (the squared correlation), which equals 1 only if the points lie exactly on a line.

      A model with two features and no intercept, $\hat y = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2$, is fitted by least squares to four examples: $(x_1, x_2; y) = (1, 0; 1)$, $(0, 1; 2)$, $(1, 1; 3)$, $(1, 2; 6)$. Find $w_2$ and the SSE of the fitted model. (Round off to two decimal places.)

      Build $X$ ($4\times2$, no column of ones), then $X\T X$ and $X\T\y$, and solve the $2\times2$ system.

      $X\T X = \begin{pmatrix}1+0+1+1 & 0+0+1+2\\ 3 & 0+1+1+4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 3\\ 3 & 6\end{pmatrix}$ and $X\T\y = \begin{pmatrix}1 + 3 + 6\\ 2 + 3 + 12\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}10\\ 17\end{pmatrix}$.

      Determinant $18 - 9 = 9$. So $w_1 = \frac{6\cdot10 - 3\cdot17}{9} = 1$ and $w_2 = \frac{3\cdot17 - 3\cdot10}{9} = \frac{21}{9} = \frac73 \approx$ 2.33.

      Predictions: $1$, $\tfrac73$, $\tfrac{10}{3}$, $\tfrac{17}{3}$. Residuals: $0$, $-\tfrac13$, $-\tfrac13$, $\tfrac13$. SSE $= 3\times\tfrac19 = \tfrac13 \approx$ 0.33.

      Check: the residual vector $(0, -\tfrac13, -\tfrac13, \tfrac13)$ is perpendicular to both columns of $X$, $(1, 0, 1, 1)$ and $(0, 1, 1, 2)$, as the normal equations promise. The residuals do not add to zero, because there is no intercept column.

      The Backprops’ line $\hat y = 1.2x + 4$ was fitted with $x$ in balls faced. The analyst now measures $x$ in overs ($x' = x/6$) and, because of a scoring-rule change, adds 10 to every $y$. Refitting by least squares on the converted data gives $\hat y = w'x' + b'$ with

      1. $w' = 0.2$, $b' = 14$
      2. $w' = 7.2$, $b' = 14$
      3. $w' = 7.2$, $b' = 4$
      4. $w' = 1.2$, $b' = 14$

      Rewrite the old fitted line in terms of $x'$. Is the result still the best line for the new data? Look at the slope formula: what do dividing every $x$ by 6 and adding 10 to every $y$ do to the deviations?

      Dividing $x$ by 6 divides every $x - \bar x$ by 6, so $\text{Cov}$ is divided by 6 and $\text{Var}(x)$ by 36: the slope is multiplied by 6, $w' = 7.2$ (runs per over, not per ball).

      Adding 10 to every $y$ leaves the deviations $y - \bar y$ unchanged (so the slope is unaffected) and raises $\bar y$ by 10. With $\bar x' = 25/6$: $b' = (34 + 10) - 7.2 \times \frac{25}{6} = 44 - 30 = 14$. Answer (B).

      Equivalently, $1.2x + 4 + 10 = 1.2(6x') + 14 = 7.2x' + 14$, and since the converted data are just a relabelling, the best line is relabelled the same way.

      (A) divides the slope by 6 instead of multiplying; (C) forgets the shift in $y$; (D) ignores the change of units.

      For a linear regression with an intercept (design matrix $X$ with a column of ones), in which situations is $X\T X$ certainly singular, so that $(X\T X)^{-1}X\T\y$ cannot be used? (Select all that apply.)

      1. Two feature columns are identical (the same statistic entered twice).
      2. There are 5 features and only 4 training examples.
      3. One feature takes the same value in every example.
      4. The features are measured in very different units (balls and seconds).

      $X\T X$ is invertible exactly when the columns of $X$ are linearly independent. For each option, find a column that is a combination of others, or show why none need be.

      $X\T X$ is invertible exactly when $X$ has independent columns (rank equal to the number of columns; see Linear algebra 2.2).

      (A) Two equal columns are dependent. (B) $X$ is $4\times6$, so its rank is at most 4, less than 6 columns. (C) A constant column is a multiple of the column of ones. All three make $X\T X$ singular.

      (D) Units rescale columns but do not make them dependent, so $X\T X$ can still be invertible (rescaling can make it badly conditioned numerically, which is a different issue).

      • Check whether the model has an intercept before choosing a formula.
      • Centre the data ($x - \bar x$, $y - \bar y$) when computing a slope by hand.
      • Sanity-check: with an intercept, residuals add to zero and the line passes through the means.
      • Using $\sum xy/\sum x^2$ when the model has an intercept, or the centred formula for "$y = wx$".
      • Measuring residuals perpendicular to the line; least squares uses vertical gaps.
      • Forgetting the column of ones in $X$, which drops the intercept from the normal equations.
      1. Least squares picks the weights that minimise the sum of squared residuals Σ(yᵢ − ŷᵢ)².
      2. One feature: w = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ)/Σ(x − x̄)², b = ȳ − w x̄; through the origin, w = Σxy/Σx².
      3. Many features: solve the normal equations XᵀX w = Xᵀy, so w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy when the columns of X are independent.

      Three points: $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$ and $(2, 5)$. Without computing, how steep is the least-squares line $\hat y = wx + b$?

      Slope less than 1
      The last point sits far above the trend of the first two. Which way does it pull the line?
      Slope exactly 1, through the first two points
      That line misses $(2, 5)$ by 3, and squared errors punish that heavily.
      Slope well above 1
      The point $(2, 5)$ pulls the right end up. Computing: $\bar x = 1$, $\bar y = 2$, slope $= \frac{5}{2} = 2.5$.
      Slope 0, because the residuals must add to zero
      Residuals adding to zero fixes the line’s height at the means, not its slope.

      For the model $y = wx$ (no intercept), least squares gives $w = $

      $\sum x_iy_i / \sum x_i^2$
      From $\frac{d}{dw}\sum (y_i - wx_i)^2 = 0$.
      $\bar y / \bar x$
      Only right in special cases. Differentiate the SSE with respect to $w$.
      $\sum (x_i - \bar x)(y_i - \bar y) / \sum (x_i - \bar x)^2$
      That is the slope when an intercept is also fitted.
      $\sum y_i / \sum x_i$
      Try it on $(1, 1), (2, 5)$: does it minimise the SSE?

      The formula $\mathbf{w} = (X\T X)^{-1}X\T\y$ can be used exactly when

      $X$ is square
      $X$ is $n\times(d+1)$ and is usually tall, not square.
      every residual is zero
      The formula gives the best fit even when residuals are not zero.
      $\y$ has no zero entries
      The entries of $\y$ don’t affect whether the inverse exists.
      the columns of $X$ are linearly independent
      Then $X\T X$ is invertible. If they are dependent, many weight vectors fit equally well.

      A classifier flags 40 players as at risk; 30 of them really were injured. Overall, 50 players were injured. Its precision and recall are

      0.6 and 0.75
      Precision divides by what was flagged; recall by what was really injured. Which number goes with which?
      0.75 and 0.6
      Precision $= 30/40$; recall $= 30/50$.
      0.75 and 0.75
      Recall’s denominator is the 50 injured players.
      0.3 and 0.5
      These aren’t ratios of the counts given.

      Fit $y = wx$ by least squares to $(1, 2)$ and $(2, 3)$. Then $w = $

      1.5
      That fits only the second point (3/2). Least squares balances both.
      1
      That’s the slope of the line through both points, which has an intercept.
      2
      That fits only the first point.
      1.6
      $\sum xy/\sum x^2 = (2 + 6)/(1 + 4) = 8/5$.

      Predicting tomorrow’s attendance at a DPL ground from past attendance records is

      supervised regression
      Past records give the answer (a number) for each example.
      supervised classification
      Is attendance a category or a number?
      unsupervised learning
      The past records include the answer we want to predict.
      not machine learning
      Learning a rule from past examples with answers is exactly machine learning.

      A least-squares line with intercept is fitted to data with $\bar x = 10$, $\bar y = 50$ and slope $w = 3$. The intercept is

      50
      That is $\bar y$. The line passes through $(\bar x, \bar y)$, not $(0, \bar y)$.
      20
      $b = \bar y - w\bar x = 50 - 30$.
      80
      Subtract $w\bar x$, don’t add it.
      Can’t tell without the data
      The means and the slope are enough.

      Least squares makes the training SSE as small as possible. To report how well the line will predict next season, you should give

      the training SSE, since it was minimised
      It was minimised on those very points, so it tends to look better than reality.
      the slope $w$
      The slope describes the line, not how well it predicts.
      the error on a held-out test set
      Unseen examples estimate performance on new cases.
      the number of residuals that are zero
      A few exact hits say little about typical error.

      A model is only useful if it works on data it has never seen. This part is about that gap between the training data and the real world: why a model that fits its training data perfectly can still predict badly (overfitting, and the bias–variance trade-off), how a penalty on large weights fixes it (ridge regression), and how to choose settings such as the penalty strength honestly (cross-validation). GATE DA has asked about each of these: ridge in 2026 and the sample paper, cross-validation in 2026 and the sample paper.

      You need: Part 1 (features, labels, training and test sets, squared-error loss, least-squares linear regression and the normal equations). Mean and variance from Statistics; matrix inverse from Linear algebra.

      Overfitting and the bias–variance trade-off

      A model overfits when it learns the noise in its training data along with the pattern, so it scores brilliantly on the data it has seen and badly on new data; the bias–variance trade-off explains why there is a “just right” level of complexity in between.

      GATE asks this as reasoning, not arithmetic: what happens to bias and variance when you regularise (sample paper Q12, 2026 Q37), and which model is over- or underfitting. It is also the reason ridge regression and cross-validation exist, the next two chapters.

      It’s like a student preparing for an exam by memorising last year’s answer key word for word: full marks on last year’s paper, lost on this year’s. A student who only learns “the answer is usually B” does badly on both. The one who learns the method does well on both.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      Conceptual MCQs about bias, variance and regularisation; also behind every “which model generalises better” option.

      Sample Q12 · bias and variance as λ grows2026 Q37 · what ridge’s regulariser does2026 Q12 · model selection by LOOCV
      Heat: most years, usually 1–2 marks, often folded into a ridge question

      Recall from Part 1: a feature is an input we measure (say, the stage of the innings), a label is the value we want to predict (runs scored in that over), the training set is the labelled data the model learns from, and the test set is held back to see how the model does on data it never saw. The loss we use here is squared error, and its average over a data set is the mean squared error (MSE).

      The Kalinga Kernels’ analyst wants to predict runs per over from how far into the innings the over is. Plot twelve past overs and the pattern is a dip in the middle overs and a surge at the death. They now have to choose how flexible the prediction curve should be.

      • A straight line (a degree-1 polynomial, 2 parameters) can’t bend, so it misses the dip and the surge. It is wrong on the training data and wrong on new data in the same systematic way. That is underfitting.
      • A degree-11 polynomial (12 parameters for 12 points) can pass through every training point exactly: training error zero. But to do that it swings wildly between the points, chasing the random ups and downs of those particular twelve overs. On next season’s overs it is far off. That is overfitting.
      • Somewhere between, a degree-3 or degree-4 curve follows the real shape and ignores the noise.

      A parameter is a number the model learns from data (a polynomial’s coefficients). A model’s complexity or capacity is, roughly, how many different shapes it can take; more parameters usually means more capacity. The polynomial’s degree is a hyperparameter: a setting we choose before training, not something least squares learns.

      The training error is the average loss on the training set; the test error (or generalisation error) is the expected loss on new data from the same source, estimated by the average loss on a held-out test set. A model generalises well when its test error is low. The difference, test error minus training error, is the generalisation gap.

      • Underfitting: training error high, test error high, small gap. The model is too simple.
      • Overfitting: training error low, test error much higher, large gap. The model is too flexible for the amount of data.

      Two facts about least-squares polynomials are worth knowing exactly. First, raising the degree can never increase the training error, because the degree-$d$ curves include every degree-$(d-1)$ curve (set the top coefficient to 0), and least squares picks the best one available. Second, with $n$ training points at distinct $x$ values, degree $n-1$ interpolates them: training error exactly 0. The test error does not behave like this. It first falls and then rises, a U shape.

      Try it

      Twelve overs (black dots) come from the dashed green curve plus random noise. Slide the degree from 0 to 11 and watch the small chart: training error (blue) only ever goes down, test error (red, measured on 200 fresh overs) falls and then shoots up. Then switch to “30 training sets”: each faint blue curve is the same degree fitted to a different random sample of twelve overs, and the red curve is their average. At low degree the curves agree with each other but miss the green curve (bias); at high degree their average is close to green but individual curves scatter wildly (variance).

      Bias and variance, in plain words

      Imagine training the same kind of model many times, each time on a fresh random training set of the same size, and then asking every one of those models for its prediction at the same input $x$.

      • The bias is how far the average of those predictions is from the truth. It measures systematic error: the model is too rigid to represent the real pattern, so it is wrong in the same direction whatever data it sees.
      • The variance is how much the predictions spread around their own average. It measures instability: the model is so flexible that a different sample of data gives a noticeably different curve.
      • The noise is the randomness in the labels themselves (two overs at the same stage don’t score the same). No model can remove it, so it is called irreducible error.
      Picture it: four archers. Tight group in the bull’s-eye: low bias, low variance. Tight group off to one side: high bias, low variance (a sight that’s misaligned). Arrows scattered all round the bull’s-eye: low bias, high variance (a shaky hand). Scattered and off to one side: both high.

      Let the label be $y = f(x) + \eps$, with $f$ the true function and $\eps$ noise of mean 0 and variance $\sigma^2$. Let $\hat f(x)$ be the prediction of a model trained on a random training set $D$. Then the expected squared error at $x$, averaging over both the training set and the noise, is $$E\big[(y - \hat f(x))^2\big] = \underbrace{\big(E[\hat f(x)] - f(x)\big)^2}_{\text{bias}^2} + \underbrace{E\Big[\big(\hat f(x) - E[\hat f(x)]\big)^2\Big]}_{\text{variance}} + \underbrace{\sigma^2}_{\text{noise}}.$$

      As complexity grows, bias² usually falls and variance usually rises, so their sum has a minimum in between: the bias–variance trade-off.

      Change you makeBiasVariance
      More flexible model (higher degree, more features, deeper tree, smaller k in k-NN)downup
      Stronger regularisation (larger λ in ridge, next chapter)updown
      More training data, same modelunchangeddown
      Less noisy labelsunchangeddown (and the noise term falls)

      Training error high → high bias (underfitting): use a more flexible model or better features; more data alone won’t help. Training error low but test error much higher → high variance (overfitting): get more data, simplify, or regularise. Regularisation always moves you towards “bias up, variance down”.

      The Haryana Heuristics’ analyst trains the same model on four independent training sets and asks each version to predict runs for one particular over, whose true expected value is $f(x) = 5$. The four predictions are 6, 7, 8 and 7. The label noise has variance $\sigma^2 = 1$. Find the bias², the variance and the expected squared error at this $x$.

      1. Average prediction: $E[\hat f(x)] = \frac{6 + 7 + 8 + 7}{4} = 7$.

        Bias is about the average over training sets, so average first.

      2. Bias² $= (7 - 5)^2 = 4$.

        The model is, on average, 2 runs too high: a systematic error.

      3. Variance $= \frac{(6-7)^2 + (7-7)^2 + (8-7)^2 + (7-7)^2}{4} = \frac{2}{4} = 0.5$.

        Spread of the predictions around their own average, not around the truth. (We divide by 4 because these four are treated as the whole population of training sets.)

      4. Expected squared error $= 4 + 0.5 + 1 =$ 5.5.

        The decomposition adds the three parts. Here bias dominates, so this model underfits: a more flexible model would help more than extra data.

      At a fixed input the truth is $f(x) = 10$ and the noise variance is $\sigma^2 = 3$. Five models trained on five independent training sets predict 9, 11, 13, 7 and 15. Find the bias², the variance (divide by 5) and the expected squared error.

      Average the predictions first. Variance is the spread around that average, not around 10.

      Mean prediction $= 55/5 = 11$, so bias² $= (11 - 10)^2 = 1$.

      Deviations from 11: $-2, 0, 2, -4, 4$; squares $4, 0, 4, 16, 16$, sum 40, so variance $= 40/5 = 8$.

      Expected error $= 1 + 8 + 3 = 12$.

      A model has training MSE 0.02 and test MSE 4.7. Which single change is most likely to reduce the test error?

      1. Add more polynomial features
      2. Add a ridge penalty, or collect more training data
      3. Train for longer to push the training MSE to 0
      4. Report the training MSE instead

      A tiny training error with a large test error is the signature of one of the two failure modes. Which one, and which way should complexity move?

      Low training error, high test error: overfitting, which is high variance. Regularisation and more data both reduce variance, so (B). (A) and (C) make the model fit the training data even more closely, which increases variance. (D) hides the problem instead of fixing it.

      A least-squares polynomial is fitted to 8 training points with distinct $x$ values. What is the smallest degree that is guaranteed to give zero training error, and how many parameters does that polynomial have?

      Through any 2 points with different $x$ there is a line; through any 3, a parabola.

      Through $n$ points with distinct $x$ there is exactly one polynomial of degree $n - 1$, so degree 7, with $7 + 1 =$ 8 coefficients: as many parameters as data points, which is the extreme of overfitting.

      Which changes typically reduce the variance of a regression model? (Select all that apply.)

      (A) Training on more data   (B) Raising the polynomial degree   (C) Increasing the ridge penalty λ   (D) Adding many extra irrelevant features

      Variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample. What makes a fitted curve less jumpy from sample to sample?

      (A) More data averages out the noise, so different samples give more similar fits. (C) A larger penalty pulls weights towards 0, making the model stiffer. (B) and (D) add flexibility, which increases variance. Answer: A and C.

      The Bengaluru Backprops want to estimate their true average runs per over, $\mu = 2$ (in suitable units; the analyst doesn’t know it). They have $n = 4$ independent overs, each with variance $\sigma^2 = 4$, and consider the “shrunk” estimator $c\,\bar y$, where $\bar y$ is the sample mean and $0 \le c \le 1$. Using MSE $= \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance}$, find the value of $c$ that minimises the MSE, and that minimum MSE.

      $E[c\bar y] = c\mu$ and $\operatorname{Var}(c\bar y) = c^2\sigma^2/n$. Write MSE as a quadratic in $c$ and set its derivative to 0.

      Bias $= c\mu - \mu = (c-1)\mu$, so bias² $= (1-c)^2\mu^2 = 4(1-c)^2$. Variance $= c^2\sigma^2/n = c^2 \cdot 4/4 = c^2$.

      MSE$(c) = 4(1-c)^2 + c^2$. Derivative: $-8(1-c) + 2c = 0 \Rightarrow 10c = 8 \Rightarrow c =$ 0.8. In general $c^* = \dfrac{\mu^2}{\mu^2 + \sigma^2/n}$.

      MSE$(0.8) = 4(0.04) + 0.64 =$ 0.8, against MSE$(1) = 1$ for the unbiased sample mean.

      The tempting answer is $c = 1$ because it has zero bias. Accepting a little bias (0.16) buys a larger cut in variance (from 1 to 0.64). That is exactly what ridge regression does to the weights of a linear model.

      The Nagpur Neural Nets’ analyst fits a linear model on larger and larger training sets. The training MSE rises from 2.1 to 6.0 and the test MSE falls from 9.0 to 6.3; both settle near 6, while the noise variance is known to be about 1. Which plan is most likely to lower the test error?

      1. Collect ten times more data with the same model
      2. Increase the ridge penalty
      3. Use a more flexible model, for example add squared and interaction features
      4. Remove features to make the model simpler

      Both curves have already met, far above the noise floor. Is the remaining error variance or bias?

      When training and test errors converge, the variance (the gap) has nearly vanished. The common level, about 6, is far above the irreducible noise of about 1, so the remaining error is mostly bias²: the model is too simple. The remedy is more capacity: (C).

      (A) is the tempting answer, but more data only shrinks variance, and the curves are already flat. (B) and (D) make the model stiffer, increasing bias further.

      Least-squares polynomials of degree $0, 1, \dots, 9$ are fitted to the same 10 training points with distinct $x$ values. Which statements are true? (Select all that apply.)

      (A) The training MSE never increases as the degree increases.
      (B) The test MSE never increases as the degree increases.
      (C) The degree-9 fit has training MSE exactly 0.
      (D) Over repeated training samples, the spread of the fitted value at a fixed $x$ typically grows with the degree.

      For (A), ask whether a degree-$d$ polynomial can imitate a degree-$(d-1)$ one. For (B), think of the U shape.

      (A) True: the degree-$d$ family contains the degree-$(d-1)$ family, and least squares picks the best member, so the minimum can only go down or stay put.

      (B) False: test error is U-shaped; beyond the sweet spot it rises.

      (C) True: 10 distinct points determine a unique degree-9 interpolating polynomial.

      (D) True: that spread is the variance, which grows with flexibility.

      Answer: A, C, D. The trap is (B): it confuses fitting the training data with predicting new data.

      • Judge a model by its error on data it didn’t train on.
      • Diagnose before fixing: high training error means bias; a large train–test gap means variance.
      • Remember the noise floor: no model’s expected test error goes below σ².
      • Choosing the degree (or any hyperparameter) that minimises training error: that always picks the most complex model.
      • Thinking more data cures underfitting. It cures variance, not bias.
      • Computing variance around the true value instead of around the average prediction.
      1. Training error falls as complexity grows; test error is U-shaped. Overfitting = low training error, high test error.
      2. Expected test error = bias² + variance + noise σ². Bias is systematic miss; variance is sensitivity to the training sample.
      3. More flexibility: bias down, variance up. More regularisation: bias up, variance down. More data: variance down.

      A model scores 99% accuracy on its training data but 60% on new data. What is most likely going on?

      Underfitting: the model is too simple
      An underfit model does badly on the training data too. Look at the training score.
      The test data must be mislabelled
      Possible, but the large gap between the two scores has a much more common explanation.
      Overfitting: it has memorised the training data, noise included
      Excellent on seen data, poor on unseen data: a big generalisation gap, the sign of high variance.
      The model needs to be trained for longer
      It already fits the training data almost perfectly; more training would widen the gap.

      In the decomposition $E[(y-\hat f)^2] = \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} + \sigma^2$, which term can no model reduce?

      $\sigma^2$, the noise
      It is randomness in the labels themselves, present whatever model you use.
      bias²
      A more flexible model can reduce bias.
      variance
      More data or regularisation reduce variance.
      none of them can be reduced
      Bias and variance respond to the choice of model and data. One term doesn’t.

      As the polynomial degree increases from 1 to 15 on a fixed training set of 16 points, the training error

      first falls, then rises
      That is the test error’s shape. Can a higher degree ever fit the training points worse?
      rises steadily
      A higher-degree family includes all lower-degree curves.
      stays constant
      Extra coefficients give least squares more freedom to fit.
      never increases, reaching 0 at degree 15
      Nested models: the minimum can only go down, and 16 distinct points are interpolated exactly at degree 15.

      Ridge regression: least squares with a brake on the weights

      Ridge regression is least squares plus a penalty $\lambda\norm{\w}^2$ on the size of the weights, which shrinks them towards zero and trades a little bias for a big drop in variance.

      Three GATE questions so far: 2026 Q37 (what the regulariser does, 2 marks), 2026 Q55 (compute a regularised loss, 2 marks) and sample Q12 (bias and variance as λ grows). The closed form $(X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top \y$ is fair game for a NAT.

      It’s like a coach who lets a batter adjust their technique only at a cost: small, well-justified changes get made, but wild swings to suit one bad session don’t.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      A conceptual MCQ and a one-instance loss computation, both in 2026; the sample paper’s bias–variance question.

      2026 Q37 · statements about ridge2026 Q55 · regularised loss for one instanceSample Q12 · bias and variance as λ grows
      Heat: rising, 2 questions in 2026

      Recall from Part 1: linear regression predicts $\hat y = \w^\top \x$ (a weighted sum of the features, often with an intercept) and least squares chooses $\w$ to minimise the sum of squared errors $\norm{\y - X\w}^2$, giving the normal equations $\w = (X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top \y$. Here $X$ is the data matrix, one row per training example and one column per feature.

      The Hyderabad Hyperplanes’ analyst has 12 matches and 9 features (powers of the innings stage, as in the last chapter). Least squares fits those 12 matches very closely, but look at the weights: values in the hundreds, of opposite signs, cancelling each other. Huge weights are the fingerprint of overfitting: a tiny change in one input makes the prediction swing a lot. Worse, when there are more features than examples (or two features are nearly copies of each other), $X^\top X$ is singular, its inverse doesn’t exist, and least squares has no unique answer at all.

      The fix is to charge the model for large weights. Minimise “error + λ × size of the weights”. Now a weight is allowed to be large only if it reduces the error by enough to pay for itself.

      For a penalty strength $\lambda \ge 0$ (the regularisation coefficient, a hyperparameter), ridge regression chooses $$\hat\w_\lambda = \argmin_{\w}\ \underbrace{\norm{\y - X\w}^2}_{\text{fit to data}} + \underbrace{\lambda\norm{\w}^2}_{\text{penalty}}, \qquad \norm{\w}^2 = w_1^2 + \dots + w_d^2.$$ $\norm{\w}$ is the L2 norm (ordinary length) of the weight vector, so the penalty is the squared L2 norm. The penalty is also called the regulariser; adding one is called regularisation. The intercept is normally left out of the penalty.

      Setting the gradient $-2X^\top(\y - X\w) + 2\lambda\w$ to $\0$ gives $(X^\top X + \lambda I)\w = X^\top\y$, so $$\hat\w_\lambda = (X^\top X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^\top \y.$$ For every $\lambda \gt 0$ the matrix $X^\top X + \lambda I$ is invertible (its eigenvalues are those of $X^\top X$, which are $\ge 0$, plus $\lambda$), even when there are more features than examples. With one feature and no intercept this is $\hat w = \dfrac{\sum x_i y_i}{\sum x_i^2 + \lambda}$: the least-squares slope with a bigger denominator.

      Recall from Linear algebra that adding $\lambda I$ to a symmetric matrix adds $\lambda$ to every eigenvalue: that is why the ridge matrix can always be inverted. And when the features are orthonormal ($X^\top X = I$), the formula collapses to $\hat\w_\lambda = \dfrac{1}{1+\lambda}\,\hat\w_{\text{LS}}$: every least-squares weight is shrunk by the same factor. That is why ridge is called a shrinkage method.

      What λ does

      • $\lambda = 0$: ordinary least squares. Lowest training error, highest variance.
      • λ larger: weights pulled towards 0, curve smoother; training error goes up (never down), variance goes down, bias goes up.
      • $\lambda \to \infty$: all penalised weights go to 0 and the model predicts a constant (the mean of $y$, if the intercept is unpenalised). Maximum bias, zero variance.

      So λ slides you along the bias–variance curve of the last chapter, and the best λ is somewhere in the middle. Choosing it is the job of cross-validation (next chapter), never of the test set.

      Try it

      The same twelve overs as before, now fitted with a degree-9 polynomial (10 weights). With λ near 0 the curve wiggles through the points and the bars (the nine non-intercept weights) are enormous. Drag λ up and watch the bars collapse and the curve calm down. Keep an eye on the two errors: training MSE only rises, while test MSE first falls and then rises again once λ is so large that the curve goes flat.

      Ridge = L2 penalty $\lambda\sum w_j^2$: shrinks all weights smoothly, rarely makes any exactly 0, has a closed form. Lasso = L1 penalty $\lambda\sum |w_j|$: can set weights exactly to 0 (feature selection), no closed form in general. Both: bias up, variance down as λ grows. Neither cares about the sign of a weight, only its size.

      Careful: the penalty depends on the units of each feature. Measure a feature in centimetres instead of metres and its weight becomes 100 times smaller, so it is penalised far less. Standardise features (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) before using ridge.
      GATE DA 2026 · Q55 · NAT · 2 marks

      Consider that Linear Ridge Regression is being used to learn a prediction function $y_{pred} = w^T x$, where $w, x \in \R^2$ and Mean Absolute Error (MAE) is used to measure the prediction error. A weight of 0.20 is associated with the regularizer.

      At an intermediate step of the training process, assume that the parameter $w = [-3.00,\ 4.00]^T$. In the next step, for the input $x = [1.00,\ 2.00]^T$, the predicted value of $y$ is noted. Let the relation between $x = [x_1,\ x_2]^T$ and the true value of $y$ be $y_{true} = x_1 + x_2$.

      The value of the overall regularized loss function for this instance is _______ . (Rounded off to two decimal places)

      1. Prediction: $y_{pred} = w^\top x = (-3)(1) + (4)(2) = 5$.

        A linear model is a dot product of weights and features.

      2. Truth: $y_{true} = 1 + 2 = 3$.

        Read straight from the given relation.

      3. Data loss (MAE for one instance): $|5 - 3| = 2$.

        The question says the prediction error is measured by mean absolute error; for a single instance the mean is just that one absolute error. The data term need not be squared error: “ridge” refers to the penalty.

      4. Ridge penalty: $\lambda\norm{w}^2 = 0.20 \times \big((-3)^2 + 4^2\big) = 0.20 \times 25 = 5$.

        Ridge uses the squared L2 norm. Using the unsquared norm, $0.2 \times 5 = 1$, gives 3, outside the key; using L1, $0.2 \times 7$, is lasso.

      5. Total: $2 + 5 =$ 7.00. Official key: 6.90 to 7.10.

        Regularised loss = data loss + penalty. The penalty here is larger than the error itself, a sign these weights are big.

      The Kalinga Kernels fit runs ($y$) against one standardised feature ($x$), with no intercept, on three overs: $x = (1, 2, 3)$, $y = (2, 3, 5)$. Compare the least-squares slope with the ridge slope for $\lambda = 1$.

      1. $\sum x_i y_i = 2 + 6 + 15 = 23$ and $\sum x_i^2 = 1 + 4 + 9 = 14$.

        With one feature, $X^\top X$ and $X^\top \y$ are just these two sums.

      2. Least squares: $\hat w = 23/14 \approx 1.643$.

        The normal equation from Part 1 with a 1×1 matrix.

      3. Ridge: $\hat w = \dfrac{23}{14 + 1} = \dfrac{23}{15} \approx$ 1.533.

        $\lambda$ is added to the denominator, so the slope moves towards 0. A larger λ shrinks it more; it never flips its sign.

      With no intercept, data matrix $X = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 1\\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ and labels $\y = (3, 1)$, compute the ridge solution for $\lambda = 2$.

      Compute $X^\top X$ first; it is a multiple of $I$, so adding $\lambda I$ and inverting is easy.

      $X^\top X = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 0\\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$ and $X^\top\y = (3 + 1,\ 3 - 1) = (4, 2)$.

      $X^\top X + 2I = 4I$, so $\hat\w = \tfrac14(4, 2) = (1, 0.5)$.

      Least squares would give $\tfrac12(4, 2) = (2, 1)$: ridge halved both weights, because $X^\top X$ is diagonal and the shrink factor is $\frac{2}{2 + \lambda} = \frac12$.

      One feature, no intercept: $\sum x_i^2 = 30$ and $\sum x_i y_i = 120$. The ridge slope with penalty λ is half of the least-squares slope. Find λ, then give the ridge slope when λ is doubled. (Round off to two decimal places.)

      Least squares gives $120/30$. Ridge gives $120/(30 + \lambda)$.

      Least squares: $120/30 = 4$. Half of it is 2, so $120/(30 + \lambda) = 2$ and $\lambda = 30$.

      So λ = 30. Doubling λ to 60: $\hat w = 120/90 \approx$ 1.33. Note that doubling λ did not halve the slope again: the shrink factor is $\frac{30}{30 + \lambda}$, not linear in λ.

      GATE DA 2024 sample paper · Q12 · MCQ · 1 mark

      Increasing the regularisation coefficient value in ridge regression will typically

      i) Increase the bias of the resulting model.
      ii) Decrease the bias of the resulting model.
      iii) Increase the variance of the resulting model.
      iv) Decrease the variance of the resulting model.

      Which of the following statements are correct?

      1. i and iii only
      2. i and iv only
      3. ii and iii only
      4. ii and iv only

      A larger λ pushes the weights towards 0. Is that model more rigid or more flexible?

      A larger coefficient shrinks the weights harder, making the model stiffer: it can follow the true pattern less well (bias up, i) and reacts less to the particular sample (variance down, iv). Answer (B). (Sample paper, no official key; this is our answer.)

      GATE DA 2026 · Q37 · MCQ · 2 marks

      Which of the following statements is true for Ridge Regression?

      1. The regularizer in the objective function of Ridge Regression is used to guard against scenarios where the model works well for the test data, but poorly for the training data.
      2. The regularizer of Ridge Regression uses $L1$ norm.
      3. Ridge Regression aims to reduce the number of parameters that have negative values.
      4. The regularizer of Ridge Regression may increase the bias of the model, but it helps in reducing the variance in predictions.

      Check each option against the definition: which norm, which failure mode (good on training, poor on test, or the reverse?), and does the sign of a weight matter?

      (A) has the failure mode backwards: regularisation guards against working well on training data but poorly on test data (overfitting). (B) Ridge uses the squared L2 norm; L1 is lasso. (C) The penalty $w_j^2$ is the same for $w_j$ and $-w_j$, so signs are irrelevant. (D) is the bias–variance trade-off: correct. Official key: D.

      No intercept. Training data: $\x_1 = (1, 0)$, $y_1 = 1$; $\x_2 = (0, 1)$, $y_2 = 1$; $\x_3 = (1, 1)$, $y_3 = 2$. With $\lambda = 1$, find the ridge weight $w_1$ and the value of the ridge objective $J(\w) = \norm{\y - X\w}^2 + \lambda\norm{\w}^2$ at the solution.

      Build $X^\top X$ and $X^\top \y$, add $\lambda I$, and solve the 2×2 system. Symmetry suggests $w_1 = w_2$.

      $X^\top X = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$, $X^\top \y = (1 + 2,\ 1 + 2) = (3, 3)$.

      $(X^\top X + I)\w = \begin{bmatrix}3 & 1\\ 1 & 3\end{bmatrix}\w = (3, 3)$. By symmetry $w_1 = w_2 = w$ with $4w = 3$, so $w_1 =$ 0.75.

      Predictions: 0.75, 0.75, 1.5; residuals 0.25, 0.25, 0.5; squared error $0.0625 + 0.0625 + 0.25 = 0.375$. Penalty $1 \times (0.75^2 + 0.75^2) = 1.125$. So $J =$ 1.5.

      Least squares gives $\w = (1, 1)$, a perfect fit, but under the ridge objective it scores $0 + 1\times(1 + 1) = 2$; ridge finds a lower total, 1.5, by accepting some error. A common slip is forgetting $\lambda I$ and getting $w_1 = 1$.

      A ridge model with an unpenalised intercept is trained on the Bengaluru Backprops’ data, whose labels have mean 160. As $\lambda \to \infty$, the model’s prediction for any input tends to

      1. 160, the mean of the training labels
      2. 0
      3. the least-squares prediction
      4. it does not converge, because the weights blow up

      Which parameters feel the penalty? Once they are forced to 0, what is the best constant prediction under squared error?

      An infinite penalty drives every penalised weight to 0, leaving $\hat y = b$ for every input. The intercept $b$ is free, so least squares chooses the constant that minimises $\sum (y_i - b)^2$, which is the mean: (A).

      (B) would be right only if the intercept were penalised too (or the labels centred at 0). (C) is the $\lambda = 0$ end. (D) reverses the effect of the penalty.

      Which statements about ridge regression with $\lambda \gt 0$ are true? (Select all that apply.)

      (A) $X^\top X + \lambda I$ is invertible even when there are more features than training examples.
      (B) For a large enough λ, ridge sets some weights exactly to 0 while keeping others non-zero.
      (C) Multiplying one feature’s values by 10 (and refitting) can change the model’s predictions.
      (D) As λ increases, the training error never decreases.

      (A): eigenvalues. (B): that’s the other penalty. (C): what happens to that feature’s weight, and to its penalty? (D): ridge at a smaller λ is free to choose any weights.

      (A) True: $X^\top X$ has eigenvalues $\ge 0$; adding $\lambda I$ makes them all $\ge \lambda \gt 0$.

      (B) False: ridge shrinks smoothly; exact zeros (sparsity) are a feature of the L1 penalty (lasso).

      (C) True: least squares would simply divide that weight by 10, giving the same predictions, but ridge penalises the smaller weight less, so the balance shifts and predictions change. Hence “standardise first”.

      (D) True: a larger λ puts more weight on the penalty, so the optimum trades away training fit; the training error is non-decreasing in λ.

      Answer: A, C, D.

      • Standardise features before ridge, and leave the intercept unpenalised.
      • Remember the penalty is $\lambda\sum w_j^2$, squared L2, and it ignores signs.
      • Choose λ by cross-validation on the training data.
      • Saying ridge “reduces bias”: it increases bias and reduces variance.
      • Mixing up ridge (L2, shrinks) with lasso (L1, zeros out weights).
      • Forgetting to add $\lambda I$ (not $\lambda$ to every entry) to $X^\top X$.
      1. Ridge minimises ‖y − Xw‖² + λ‖w‖²; closed form w = (XᵀX + λI)⁻¹Xᵀy, invertible for any λ > 0.
      2. λ shrinks the weights towards 0: training error up, bias up, variance down. λ = 0 is least squares; λ → ∞ predicts a constant.
      3. Regularised loss = data loss + λ × (sum of squared weights). Ridge is L2; lasso is L1 and can zero out weights.

      A model’s weights are all in the hundreds and of alternating signs, and it predicts new data badly. Adding a penalty on the sum of squared weights will most likely

      make the weights even larger
      The penalty charges for large weights. Which way will the optimiser push them?
      shrink the weights and improve predictions on new data
      Huge cancelling weights are a sign of overfitting; shrinking them cuts variance.
      set exactly half of the weights to zero
      The squared penalty shrinks smoothly; exact zeros come from an L1 penalty.
      lower the training error
      The penalty competes with the fit, so training error can only stay the same or rise.

      With $X^\top X = \begin{bmatrix}4 & 0\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ and $\lambda = 1$, the ridge weights equal the least-squares weights multiplied by

      $\tfrac12$ for both
      The shrink factor depends on each diagonal entry: $\frac{s}{s+\lambda}$.
      $\tfrac15$ and $\tfrac12$
      Close: the factor is $\frac{s}{s+\lambda}$, not $\frac{1}{s+\lambda}$.
      1 for both
      That would be $\lambda = 0$.
      $\tfrac45$ and $\tfrac12$
      With diagonal $X^\top X$, $w_j^{\text{ridge}} = \frac{s_j}{s_j + \lambda} w_j^{\text{LS}}$: $\frac{4}{5}$ and $\frac{1}{2}$. Directions with little data are shrunk most.

      Which is the ridge penalty for $\w = (2, -1, 0)$ with $\lambda = 0.5$?

      0.5
      That is λ times the sum of the weights, which lets signs cancel.
      1.5
      That is the L1 (lasso) penalty, $0.5 \times 3$.
      2.5
      $0.5 \times (4 + 1 + 0) = 2.5$.
      1.118
      That uses the unsquared norm $\sqrt5$.

      Cross-validation: choosing settings without peeking at the test set

      Cross-validation estimates how well a model will do on new data by repeatedly hiding part of the training data, training on the rest, and testing on the hidden part.

      GATE asks you to count the splits (2026 Q12: LOOCV on 900 samples) and to pick the right design for imbalanced data (sample Q11: stratified CV with area under the ROC curve). It is also how λ in ridge and the degree in polynomial regression are chosen.

      It’s like a coach picking a batting order by trying each candidate order in practice matches against different sets of their own bowlers, rather than testing it in the final and then claiming they knew all along.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      Counting folds and training-set sizes; matching the evaluation design to the data.

      2026 Q12 · number of LOOCV splitsSample Q11 · imbalanced data: stratified CV and AUC
      Heat: most years, 1 mark

      Last chapter left a problem. Ridge needs a value of λ; polynomial regression needs a degree. These are hyperparameters: settings fixed before training, which least squares does not learn. How do we choose them?

      • Not by training error: it always prefers the most flexible setting (λ = 0, highest degree).
      • Not by test error either. The test set is our one honest estimate of performance on new data. If we try twenty values of λ and keep the one with the lowest test error, that test error is now optimistic, because we picked it for being low. The test set has quietly become part of training. This is called data leakage.

      The answer is to carve a validation set out of the training data: train on the rest, measure error on the validation part, and choose the hyperparameter with the lowest validation error. The test set stays locked away until the very end.

      • Hold-out validation: split the training data once, for example 80% train / 20% validation. Cheap, but the estimate depends on which points happened to land in the validation part, and 20% of the data is never used for training.
      • k-fold cross-validation: split the training data into $k$ roughly equal parts called folds. For each $i = 1, \dots, k$: train on the other $k - 1$ folds, compute the error on fold $i$. The CV estimate is the average of the $k$ errors. Every point is used for validation exactly once and for training $k - 1$ times. Each model trains on about $\frac{k-1}{k}n$ points; common choices are $k = 5$ or $10$.
      • Leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV): $k$-fold with $k = n$. Each fold is a single point, so there are $n$ splits, $n$ models, each trained on $n - 1$ points.
      • Stratified k-fold: the folds are formed so that each has (roughly) the same class proportions as the whole data set. Essential when one class is rare.
      1. Set the test set aside. Split the remaining training data into $k$ folds.
      2. For each candidate value (each λ, or each degree): train $k$ times, each time leaving one fold out, and average the $k$ validation errors.
      3. Pick the candidate with the lowest average CV error.
      4. Retrain with that value on all the training data.
      5. Evaluate once on the test set and report that number.

      Cost: (number of candidates) × $k$ training runs, plus one final refit.

      Try it

      Twenty training samples, four of them positive (dots). Each row is one round of cross-validation: the red squares are that round’s validation fold, the blue ones are used for training. With plain k-fold, press “Reshuffle data” a few times and look at the readout: some folds can end up with no positive example at all, so recall on that fold is undefined. Switch to “Stratified k-fold” and every fold gets its share of positives. “Leave-one-out” makes 20 rounds of one sample each.

      Try it

      Thirty overs, polynomials of degree 0 to 9. The red curve is the k-fold CV error for each degree, computed from the training data only; the green curve is the true error on 200 fresh overs, which a real analyst wouldn’t have. Notice that the degree with the lowest CV error (circled) usually lands at or near the degree that is truly best, while training error (dashed) would always pick degree 9. Compare k = 2 with LOOCV: with k = 2 each model trains on only 15 points, so the CV errors run higher.

      Choosing k

      Small $k$ (say 2) is cheap, but each model trains on only half the data, so it is weaker than the final model and the CV error overestimates the true error (pessimistic bias). Large $k$ (up to LOOCV) trains on almost all the data, so that bias is small, but it costs $n$ fits, and the $n$ training sets overlap almost completely, which makes the estimate noisy. $k = 5$ or $10$ is the usual compromise. LOOCV has one more property: it involves no random split, so running it twice gives the same answer.

      Imbalanced classes

      Suppose only 5% of a data set is positive (say, matches decided by a super over). A classifier that always says “negative” scores 95% accuracy while being useless. Two fixes, which together answer sample Q11: stratify the folds so each one has about 5% positives, and use a measure that isn’t fooled by the majority class, such as the area under the ROC curve (AUC). The ROC curve plots the true-positive rate against the false-positive rate as the classifier’s threshold varies; AUC is the probability that a random positive is scored above a random negative, so always-negative scores only 0.5.

      With $n$ samples available for training/validation: $k$-fold makes $k$ splits, each training on $n - n/k$ points and validating on $n/k$. LOOCV makes $n$ splits, training on $n - 1$. Always subtract the test set first: CV runs only on what is left.

      GATE DA 2026 · Q12 · MCQ · 1 mark

      Consider that you are training a classifier for a 10-class classification problem. Each input is represented as a 512-dimensional vector. There are 1000 samples, out of which first 100 will be used for testing. Let Leave-One-Out-Cross-Validation (LOOCV) be used for selection of the classifier model before testing. Which of the following options is the correct number of validation splits that will be generated?

      1. 10
      2. 512
      3. 900
      4. 1000

      1. Remove the test set: $1000 - 100 = 900$ samples remain for model selection.

        The test samples must not be touched during model selection, so cross-validation only sees the other 900.

      2. LOOCV is $k$-fold with $k = n$: each split leaves out exactly one of the $n = 900$ samples.

        One split per sample, each sample being the validation set once.

      3. Number of splits $= 900$: answer (C). Official key: C.

        The distractors use other numbers in the question: 10 is the number of classes, 512 the input dimension, 1000 includes the test set. None of them changes the count of samples.

      The Nagpur Neural Nets have 1200 labelled matches after setting the test set aside. They compare 4 values of λ with 6-fold CV. How large is each training and validation split, and how many models are trained in total, including the final refit?

      1. Fold size $= 1200/6 = 200$, so each round validates on 200 and trains on $1200 - 200 = 1000$.

        One fold is held out, the other five are used for training.

      2. Per λ: 6 models. For 4 values: $4 \times 6 = 24$.

        Each candidate needs its own full round of $k$ fits.

      3. Plus one refit of the winner on all 1200: 25 models.

        The CV models were only for choosing λ; the deployed model uses every training example.

      A 5-fold cross-validation gives validation errors 0.20, 0.25, 0.15, 0.30 and 0.10 on five equal-sized folds. What is the CV estimate of the error?

      Equal-sized folds, so a plain average.

      $(0.20 + 0.25 + 0.15 + 0.30 + 0.10)/5 = 1.00/5 = 0.20$.

      LOOCV is run on a training set of 50 matches. How many models are trained, and on how many points is each trained?

      Each split leaves out exactly one point.

      One model per left-out point: 50 models, each trained on $50 - 1 = 49$ points.
