      A data set of 200 overs has 40 overs with a wicket (positive) and 160 without. Stratified 5-fold CV is used. How many positives are in each validation fold, and how many in each training split?

      Stratification keeps the 20% positive rate in every fold of 40.

      Each fold has $200/5 = 40$ overs, 20% positive: $8$ positives. Each training split is the other four folds: $40 - 8 = 32$ positives (out of 160 overs).

      GATE DA 2024 sample paper · Q11 · MCQ · 1 mark

      A binary classification dataset contains only 5% of positive instances. Which one of the following experimental design and performance measures is most suited for measuring the generalizability of a classifier trained on this dataset?

      1. fixed training and test sets, accuracy
      2. fixed training and test sets, area under the ROC curve
      3. stratified cross-validation, accuracy
      4. stratified cross-validation, area under the ROC curve

      Two separate choices: a design that uses the data well and keeps the 5% in every fold, and a measure that a “always negative” classifier can’t game.

      Accuracy is misleading at 5% positives: always predicting negative gives 95%. AUC is unaffected by that. Stratified cross-validation uses all the data for evaluation and keeps the 5% rate in each fold, giving a more reliable estimate of generalisation than one fixed split. Answer (D). (Sample paper, no official key; this is our answer.)

      The “model” predicts every label as the mean of its training labels. Training labels: $y = (2, 4, 6, 8)$. Compute the LOOCV mean squared error. (Round off to two decimal places.)

      Leave out each point in turn, predict it by the mean of the other three, square the error, then average the four squared errors. Shortcut: for the mean predictor the left-out error is $\frac{n}{n-1}(y_i - \bar y)$.

      Leave out 2: mean of (4, 6, 8) is 6, error $(2 - 6)^2 = 16$.

      Leave out 4: mean of (2, 6, 8) is $16/3$, error $(4 - 16/3)^2 = 16/9$.

      Leave out 6: mean of (2, 4, 8) is $14/3$, error $(6 - 14/3)^2 = 16/9$.

      Leave out 8: mean of (2, 4, 6) is 4, error 16.

      Average: $\frac{16 + 16/9 + 16/9 + 16}{4} = \frac{320/9}{4} = \frac{80}{9} \approx$ 8.89.

      Check with the shortcut: $\bar y = 5$, residuals $-3, -1, 1, 3$, scaled by $\frac43$: $-4, -\frac43, \frac43, 4$, squares averaging $80/9$. The tempting wrong answer is the training MSE, $(9 + 1 + 1 + 9)/4 = 5$, which is smaller because each point helped compute its own prediction.

      The Hyderabad Hyperplanes have 300 matches and 5,000 candidate features. Which procedure gives an honest estimate of how their final model will do on next season’s matches?

      1. Use all 300 matches to pick the 20 features most correlated with the label, then run 10-fold CV on those 20 features and report the CV error.
      2. Set 60 matches aside as a test set. On the other 240, choose λ (and do any feature selection inside each training fold) by 10-fold CV, refit on all 240, and report the error on the 60.
      3. Split 240/60, try 50 values of λ, and report the lowest of the 50 test errors.
      4. Train on all 300 matches and report the training error, since it uses the most data.

      For each option, ask: did the number that gets reported ever influence a choice that was made?

      (B) keeps the 60 test matches completely unused until the single final evaluation, and does every data-driven choice inside the training folds. Answer (B).

      (A) is the classic trap: the features were chosen using the labels of every match, including the ones later used for validation, so the CV error is badly optimistic (with 5,000 features, some correlate with the label by pure chance). (C) picks λ by test error, so the reported minimum is biased downwards. (D) reports training error, which says nothing about overfitting.

      A data set of $n$ examples is used for cross-validation. Which statements are true? (Select all that apply.)

      (A) LOOCV trains $n$ models.
      (B) Repeating LOOCV on the same data gives exactly the same estimate.
      (C) In 10-fold CV, each model is trained on 90% of the data.
      (D) Increasing $k$ in $k$-fold CV makes each training set smaller.

      Each fold has $n/k$ points and the training set is everything else.

      (A) True: one model per left-out example.

      (B) True: there is only one way to leave out one point at a time, so there is no randomness in the splits (assuming a deterministic training algorithm).

      (C) True: one tenth is held out.

      (D) False: the training set has $n - n/k$ points, which grows with $k$. More folds means smaller validation folds and larger training sets.

      Answer: A, B, C.

      • Lock the test set away first; run CV only on the rest.
      • Do every data-driven step (scaling, feature selection, choosing λ) inside the training folds.
      • Stratify the folds and use a measure such as AUC, precision or recall when one class is rare.
      • Counting the test samples in the number of LOOCV splits.
      • Choosing a hyperparameter by its test error, then reporting that same test error.
      • Forgetting the final refit on all the training data after choosing the hyperparameter.
      1. Validation data (hold-out or k-fold) chooses hyperparameters; the test set is used once, at the end.
      2. k-fold: k models, each trained on (k−1)/k of the data, error averaged. LOOCV: k = n, so n splits of n − 1 training points each.
      3. For rare classes, use stratified folds and a measure such as AUC, not plain accuracy.

      An analyst tries 30 values of λ and keeps the one with the lowest error on the test set, then reports that error. The reported error is most likely

      an unbiased estimate of future error
      Ask whether the test set influenced a choice. If so, can it still be impartial?
      too optimistic
      The minimum of 30 noisy test errors is lower than the true error of the chosen model: the test set has leaked into model selection.
      too pessimistic
      Taking a minimum pushes the reported number down, not up.
      exactly equal to the training error
      The test set is separate from training; the issue is how it was used.

      5-fold CV on 500 examples trains each model on how many examples?

      100
      That is the size of each validation fold.
      500
      One fold is always held out.
      400
      $500 - 500/5 = 400$.
      499
      That would be leave-one-out.

      Why use stratified folds?

      To make the folds different sizes
      Folds stay (roughly) equal in size; something else is matched.
      To reduce the number of models trained
      Stratified k-fold still trains k models.
      To make sure the test set is never used
      That is good practice, but it isn’t what stratification does.
      So each fold keeps the class proportions of the whole data set
      Without it, a rare class can be missing from some folds entirely.

      Training MSE 5.8, test MSE 6.0, noise variance about 1. The model is most likely

      overfitting
      Overfitting shows a large gap between training and test error. Is there one here?
      underfitting (high bias)
      Both errors are similar and far above the noise floor: the model is too simple.
      just right
      Errors near 6 against a noise floor of 1 leave a lot of reducible error.
      impossible to judge without more data
      The two errors and the noise level are enough to diagnose it.

      Increasing λ in ridge regression

      decreases bias and increases variance
      That is the effect of making the model more flexible. Is a heavier penalty more or less flexible?
      sets weights exactly to zero
      That is a property of the L1 penalty.
      increases bias and decreases variance
      Stronger shrinkage makes the model stiffer.
      leaves the training error unchanged
      The penalty trades away training fit.

      Least squares fails to give a unique answer when $X^\top X$ is singular. Ridge fixes this because

      $X^\top X + \lambda I$ has all eigenvalues at least $\lambda \gt 0$, so it is invertible
      Adding $\lambda I$ shifts every eigenvalue up by λ.
      it removes the singular features
      Ridge keeps every feature; it changes the matrix being inverted.
      it uses gradient descent instead of an inverse
      Ridge has a closed form; the change is inside it.
      it adds λ to every entry of $X^\top X$
      Only the diagonal gets λ.

      Of 600 samples, 150 are reserved for testing and LOOCV is run on the rest. How many validation splits are there?

      600
      The test samples are never used in cross-validation.
      150
      That is the test set itself.
      449
      That is the size of each LOOCV training set.
      450
      $600 - 150 = 450$, one split per remaining sample.

      The right way to choose λ for ridge regression is to

      pick the λ with the lowest training error
      That always picks λ = 0, plain least squares.
      pick the λ with the lowest test error
      Then the test error is no longer an honest estimate.
      pick the λ with the lowest cross-validation error on the training data
      Then refit on all the training data and evaluate once on the test set.
      always use λ = 1
      The best λ depends on the data, its scale and the noise.

      So far the module has predicted numbers. This part predicts categories: win or loss, spam or not, red or green. You’ll meet the three classic ways to draw a line between classes: logistic regression (learn the probability of a class directly), naive Bayes (count how each class tends to look, then apply Bayes’ theorem) and Fisher’s linear discriminant (find the one direction that pulls the classes apart). Between them they account for a GATE DA question or two every year.

      You need: features, labels and accuracy from Chapter 1.1; the score $w^\top x + b$ from linear regression in Chapter 1.2; the L2 penalty from Chapter 2.2 (briefly); Bayes’ theorem from Probability; dot products and eigenvectors from Linear algebra.

      Logistic regression and the perceptron: drawing a line between classes

      Logistic regression turns a straight-line score $w^\top x + b$ into a probability between 0 and 1, and classifies by which side of a line (or plane) a point falls on.

      GATE DA asked about the perceptron update in 2025 Q22 and about “discriminative versus generative” models in 2024 Q18. The same score-and-sign idea returns in SVMs and neural networks later in this module.

      It’s like a selector’s rule of thumb: add up points for good form and fitness, subtract points for injury, and pick the player if the total is above zero. The rule is a weighted sum; the line where the total is exactly zero is where the decision flips.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      The perceptron update rule, the sigmoid and log-odds, and recognising logistic regression as a discriminative model.

      2025 Q22 · perceptron update2024 Q18 · generative or discriminative?2025 Q53, 2024 Q17 · linear classifiers (SVM, Part 4)
      Heat: most years, 1 mark each

      First, what is a classifier?

      A classifier is a rule that takes the features of an example and returns a class label from a fixed, small list. Recall from Chapter 1.1 that a feature is a measured input (runs scored, wickets in hand) and a label is the answer we want to predict. In regression the label is a number; in classification it is a category. Tiny example: given the toss result and the pitch type, predict “Win” or “Loss” for the Kalinga Kernels.

      When there are just two features, every example is a point in the plane. A classifier then colours the whole plane: every location gets a predicted label. The curve where the colour changes is the decision boundary. Points on one side are predicted one class, points on the other side the other class.

      The simplest boundary is a straight line. A linear classifier computes a score $z = w^\top x + b = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2 + \dots + b$ (exactly the formula from linear regression) and predicts one class when $z \gt 0$ and the other when $z \le 0$. The numbers $w$ (the weights) and $b$ (the bias) are the model’s parameters: the values learned from data.

      The boundary is the set where $z = 0$. In two dimensions that’s a line; in three, a plane; in $d$ dimensions it is called a hyperplane (a flat surface one dimension lower than the space). Recall from Linear algebra that $w^\top x = 0$ means "$x$ is perpendicular to $w$": so $w$ points straight across the boundary, towards the side predicted positive.

      A DPL story

      The Hyderabad Hyperplanes’ analyst records two numbers at the halfway point of each chase: $x_1$, how far the team is ahead of the required run rate, and $x_2$, a wickets-in-hand score. Each past chase is labelled 1 (won) or 0 (lost). They want more than a yes/no verdict: they want “we’re 80% likely to win from here”. That’s what logistic regression adds.

      The sigmoid (logistic) function squashes any real number into $(0, 1)$: $$\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}.$$ It has $\sigma(0) = 0.5$, $\sigma(z) \to 1$ as $z \to \infty$, $\sigma(z) \to 0$ as $z \to -\infty$, and $\sigma(-z) = 1 - \sigma(z)$.

      The odds of an event with probability $p$ are $\frac{p}{1-p}$ (probability 0.8 means odds of 4 to 1). The log-odds (or logit) is $\ln\frac{p}{1-p}$; it is the inverse of the sigmoid: if $p = \sigma(z)$ then $\ln\frac{p}{1-p} = z$.

      For features $x$ and a label $y \in \{0, 1\}$, logistic regression models $$P(y = 1\mid x) = \sigma(w^\top x + b), \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \ln\frac{P(y=1\mid x)}{P(y=0\mid x)} = w^\top x + b.$$ In words: the log-odds is a linear function of the features. It predicts class 1 when $P(y=1\mid x) \ge 0.5$, which happens exactly when $w^\top x + b \ge 0$. So the decision boundary is the hyperplane $w^\top x + b = 0$, and logistic regression is a linear classifier.

      Despite the name, logistic regression is a classification method; “regression” survives because it fits a linear function (to the log-odds).

      Why not just run ordinary linear regression on 0/1 labels? Its predictions are not probabilities (they can be −0.3 or 1.4), and a few far-away but obvious examples drag the line and move the boundary. The sigmoid fixes both: it saturates, so an obvious example far from the boundary has probability near 0 or 1 and little pull.

      How is it trained? Cross-entropy loss

      A loss measures how bad one prediction is; training picks the parameters with the smallest average loss (recall Chapter 1.1). For a probability prediction $p = \sigma(w^\top x + b)$ the natural loss asks: how much probability did the model give to what actually happened? If $y = 1$, that’s $p$; if $y = 0$, it’s $1 - p$. Taking minus the logarithm turns “high probability is good” into “low loss is good”.

      For one example, $$\ell = -\big[\,y\ln p + (1-y)\ln(1-p)\,\big], \qquad p = \sigma(w^\top x + b).$$ If $y = 1$ this is $-\ln p$; if $y = 0$ it is $-\ln(1-p)$. Training minimises the average of $\ell$ over the training set. This is the same as maximising the likelihood of the labels (the probability the model assigns to the observed data), because $P(y\mid x) = p^y(1-p)^{1-y}$.

      The loss is convex in $(w, b)$ and its gradient is strikingly simple: $\dfrac{\partial \ell}{\partial w} = (p - y)\,x$ and $\dfrac{\partial \ell}{\partial b} = p - y$ (“prediction minus truth, times input”). There is no closed-form solution like the normal equations, so it is trained by gradient descent (Chapter 5.2).

      Careful: a confident wrong answer is punished hard. Predicting $p = 0.99$ for a match that was lost costs $-\ln 0.01 \approx 4.6$, while $p = 0.6$ for a match that was won costs only $-\ln 0.6 \approx 0.51$.
      Go deeper: where $(p - y)x$ comes from

      Write $z = w^\top x + b$ and $p = \sigma(z)$. First, $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z)) = p(1-p)$. Then $\dfrac{\partial \ell}{\partial p} = -\dfrac{y}{p} + \dfrac{1-y}{1-p} = \dfrac{p - y}{p(1-p)}$. The chain rule gives $\dfrac{\partial \ell}{\partial z} = \dfrac{p-y}{p(1-p)}\cdot p(1-p) = p - y$, and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} = x$. With more than two classes the sigmoid becomes the softmax $P(y = k\mid x) = e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}$, one score $z_k = w_k^\top x + b_k$ per class, and the same “prediction minus truth” gradient appears.

      Try it

      Circles are chases the Hyperplanes won, squares are losses. Move the sliders to place the boundary (solid line); the arrow $w$ points to the “win” side and the shading shows the predicted probability. Then press Gradient step a few times and watch the loss fall. Notice two things: scaling up $w$ and $b$ together doesn’t move the line but makes the probabilities more extreme (the dashed $p = 0.1$ and $0.9$ lines close in), and the two mislabelled-looking points stop the loss from reaching zero. Tap a point to see its own loss.

      The perceptron: the original linear classifier

      Before logistic regression became standard, Rosenblatt’s perceptron (1958) learned a linear classifier with an even simpler rule. Labels are $y \in \{+1, -1\}$ and the prediction is $\operatorname{sign}(w^\top x + b)$. Go through the training points one at a time. If the current point is classified correctly, do nothing. If it’s wrong, nudge the weights towards it.

      1. Start with $w = 0$, $b = 0$.
      2. For each training example $(x_n, y_n)$ in turn: if $\operatorname{sign}(w^\top x_n + b) \ne y_n$ (a mistake), update $$w \leftarrow w + y_n x_n, \qquad b \leftarrow b + y_n.$$
      3. Repeat passes over the data until a full pass makes no mistake.

      Why it helps: after an update, the score on that same point changes by $y_n(\norm{x_n}^2 + 1)$, which has the sign of $y_n$. So a positive example’s score goes up and a negative example’s score goes down: the point moves towards the right side.

      Convergence theorem. If the data are linearly separable (some hyperplane puts every positive on one side and every negative on the other), the perceptron stops after finitely many updates. If they are not separable, it never settles.

      Try it

      Press Next point to let the perceptron look at one point at a time (numbers show the order). A green ring means it was classified correctly; a red ring means a mistake and an update, and the readout shows the score on that point jumping by $y(\norm{x}^2 + 1)$. Keep going until a full pass makes no mistakes. Notice that an update can fix one point and break another; it still gets there because the data are separable.

      GATE DA 2025 · Q22 · MCQ · 1 mark

      Consider designing a linear classifier $$y = \text{sign}(f(x; w, b)), \quad f(x; w, b) = w^\top x + b$$ on a dataset $D = \{(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \ldots, (x_N, y_N)\}$, $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d, y_i \in \{+1, -1\}$, $i = 1, 2, \ldots, N$. Recall that the sign function outputs +1 if the argument is positive, and $-1$ if the argument is non-positive. The parameters $w$ and $b$ are updated as per the following training algorithm: $$w_{new} = w_{old} + y_n x_n, \quad b_{new} = b_{old} + y_n$$ whenever $\text{sign}(f(x_n; w_{old}, b_{old})) \ne y_n$. In other words, whenever the classifier wrongly predicts a sample $(x_n, y_n)$ from the dataset, $w_{old}$ gets updated to $w_{new}$, and likewise $b_{old}$ gets updated to $b_{new}$. Consider the case $(x_n, +1)$, $f(x_n; w_{old}, b_{old}) \lt 0$. Then

      1. $f(x_n; w_{new}, b_{new}) \gt f(x_n; w_{old}, b_{old})$
      2. $f(x_n; w_{new}, b_{new}) \lt f(x_n; w_{old}, b_{old})$
      3. $f(x_n; w_{new}, b_{new}) = f(x_n; w_{old}, b_{old})$
      4. $y_n f(x_n; w_{old}, b_{old}) \gt 1$

      1. Recognise the rule: this is the perceptron. Here $y_n = +1$ and $f \lt 0$, so the prediction is $-1$: a mistake, and the update happens with $y_n = +1$: $w_{new} = w_{old} + x_n$, $b_{new} = b_{old} + 1$.

        The update only fires on a mistake, so first confirm one occurred.

      2. Evaluate the new score on the same point: $f(x_n; w_{new}, b_{new}) = (w_{old} + x_n)^\top x_n + b_{old} + 1 = f(x_n; w_{old}, b_{old}) + \norm{x_n}^2 + 1$.

        Expand the dot product: $(w + x)^\top x = w^\top x + x^\top x$, and $x^\top x = \norm{x}^2$.

      3. Since $\norm{x_n}^2 + 1 \ge 1 \gt 0$, the new score is strictly larger: (A). (B) and (C) contradict this; (D) is false because $y_n f(x_n; w_{old}, b_{old}) = f \lt 0$.

        The update always moves the score towards the correct sign, although one update need not make it positive. Official key: A.

      Generative or discriminative?

      There are two broad ways to build a probabilistic classifier, and GATE likes to ask which is which.

      A discriminative model learns $P(y\mid x)$ (or just the boundary) directly: “given these features, how likely is each class?”. Examples: logistic regression, the perceptron, SVMs, neural network classifiers.

      A generative model learns how each class produces its data, $P(x\mid y)$, together with the class frequencies $P(y)$, and then classifies with Bayes’ theorem: $P(y\mid x) \propto P(x\mid y)P(y)$. Because it models $x$ itself, it could in principle generate new fake examples. Examples: naive Bayes (Chapter 3.2), Gaussian discriminant analysis (the probabilistic view of LDA in Chapter 3.3), hidden Markov models.

      Neither is a classifier “type” like PCA, which is dimensionality reduction: it uses no labels at all (Chapter 6.3).

      A logistic regression model for the Hyderabad Hyperplanes has $w = (0.5, -1)$ and $b = 0.5$. For a chase with $x = (3, 1)$, what probability of winning does it give? (Round off to two decimal places.)

      Compute the score $z = w^\top x + b$ first, then $\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$.

      $z = 0.5\times3 + (-1)\times1 + 0.5 = 1$. Then $\sigma(1) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-1}} = \dfrac{1}{1.3679} \approx$ 0.73.

      A model predicts $p = P(y = 1\mid x) = 0.9$ for a match that was actually lost ($y = 0$). What is the cross-entropy loss for this example, using natural logarithms? (Round off to two decimal places.)

      With $y = 0$ only the $(1-y)\ln(1-p)$ term survives.

      $\ell = -\ln(1 - 0.9) = -\ln 0.1 = \ln 10 \approx$ 2.30. Compare $-\ln 0.9 \approx 0.105$ had the match been won: confident mistakes are expensive.

      A logistic model has $w = (1, 2)$, $b = -3$. A coach only wants to call a chase “safe” when $P(y = 1\mid x) \ge 0.8$. The set of safe points is bounded by a straight line. Where does that line cross the $x_1$-axis (where $x_2 = 0$)? (Round off to two decimal places.)

      $\sigma(z) \ge 0.8$ exactly when the log-odds $z \ge \ln\frac{0.8}{0.2}$.

      $\sigma(z) = 0.8 \iff z = \ln\frac{0.8}{0.2} = \ln 4 \approx 1.386$. The boundary is $x_1 + 2x_2 - 3 = \ln 4$. With $x_2 = 0$: $x_1 = 3 + \ln 4 \approx$ 4.39.

      Changing the threshold shifts the line parallel to the usual $p = 0.5$ boundary ($x_1 + 2x_2 = 3$); the boundary stays linear.

      GATE DA 2024 · Q18 · MCQ · 1 mark

      Match the items in Column 1 with the items in Column 2 in the following table:

      Column 1Column 2
      (p) Principal Component Analysis(i) Discriminative Model
      (q) Naïve Bayes Classification(ii) Dimensionality Reduction
      (r) Logistic Regression(iii) Generative Model
      1. (p) − (iii), (q) − (i), (r) − (ii)
      2. (p) − (ii), (q) − (i), (r) − (iii)
      3. (p) − (ii), (q) − (iii), (r) − (i)
      4. (p) − (iii), (q) − (ii), (r) − (i)

      Which of the three models $P(x\mid y)$, which models $P(y\mid x)$ directly, and which uses no labels?

      PCA finds directions of maximum variance without labels: dimensionality reduction, (ii). Naive Bayes models $P(x\mid y)P(y)$ and applies Bayes’ theorem: generative, (iii). Logistic regression models $P(y\mid x)$ directly: discriminative, (i). So (C). Official key: C.

      A perceptron with labels $y \in \{+1, -1\}$ predicts $\operatorname{sign}(w^\top x + b)$, where sign gives $+1$ for a positive argument and $-1$ otherwise (so $\operatorname{sign}(0) = -1$). It starts at $w = (0, 0)$, $b = 0$ and visits the points below in the order 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4, …, applying $w \leftarrow w + yx$, $b \leftarrow b + y$ after each mistake. It stops after a complete pass with no mistakes.

      Points: 1: $x = (1, 0)$, $y = +1$; 2: $x = (0, 1)$, $y = +1$; 3: $x = (-1, 1)$, $y = -1$; 4: $x = (1, -2)$, $y = -1$.

      How many updates does it make in total?

      Track $(w, b)$ in a small table, one row per visit. Pay attention to any score that is exactly 0.

      Pass 1. Point 1: $f = 0$, predicts $-1$, wrong: $w = (1, 0)$, $b = 1$. Point 2: $f = 0 + 0 + 1 = 1$, correct. Point 3: $f = -1 + 0 + 1 = 0$, predicts $-1$, correct. Point 4: $f = 1 + 0 + 1 = 2$, predicts $+1$, wrong: $w = (0, 2)$, $b = 0$.

      Pass 2. Point 1: $f = 0$, predicts $-1$, wrong: $w = (1, 2)$, $b = 1$. Point 2: $f = 3$, correct. Point 3: $f = -1 + 2 + 1 = 2$, wrong: $w = (2, 1)$, $b = 0$. Point 4: $f = 2 - 2 + 0 = 0$, predicts $-1$, correct.

      Pass 3. Scores: $2, 1, -1, 0$ give predictions $+1, +1, -1, -1$, all correct, so it stops. Total updates: 4, ending at $w = (2, 1)$, $b = 0$.

      The trap is $\operatorname{sign}(0)$. Treating a zero score as “correct” for the positive points would skip the update at point 1 in pass 2 and give a different count; the question fixes $\operatorname{sign}(0) = -1$, exactly as GATE 2025 Q22 did.

      A logistic regression model $P(y = 1\mid x) = \sigma(w^\top x + b)$ has been trained. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)

      1. The set of points with $P(y = 1\mid x) = 0.7$ is a hyperplane parallel to the decision boundary for threshold 0.5.
      2. Replacing $(w, b)$ by $(2w, 2b)$ moves the 0.5 decision boundary.
      3. Replacing $(w, b)$ by $(2w, 2b)$ leaves every predicted label unchanged but pushes every predicted probability further from 0.5.
      4. On a linearly separable training set, the unregularised cross-entropy loss is minimised at some finite $w$.

      $\sigma(z) = 0.7$ fixes the value of $z$. For (D), what happens to the loss on a correctly classified point as you scale $w$ and $b$ up?

      (A) True: $\sigma(z) = 0.7 \iff w^\top x + b = \ln\frac{0.7}{0.3}$, a hyperplane with the same normal $w$.

      (B) False: $2w^\top x + 2b = 0 \iff w^\top x + b = 0$, the same set.

      (C) True: the sign of every score is unchanged, but each $\lvert z\rvert$ doubles, so $\sigma(z)$ moves away from 0.5.

      (D) False: if some $(w, b)$ separates the data, scaling it by $c \to \infty$ sends every point’s loss to 0 without ever reaching it, so there is no finite minimiser. In practice an L2 penalty $\lambda\norm{w}^2$ (as in ridge regression, Chapter 2.2) is added to keep $w$ finite.

      Answer: A; C.

      Logistic regression starts at $w = (0, 0)$, $b = 0$. One step of gradient descent with learning rate $\eta = 0.5$ is taken on the cross-entropy loss of the single example $x = (2, 1)$, $y = 1$, updating both $w$ and $b$. What probability $P(y = 1\mid x)$ does the updated model give to this same $x$? (Round off to two decimal places.)

      Use the gradients $(p - y)x$ for $w$ and $p - y$ for $b$, evaluated at the starting point, where $p = \sigma(0)$. Gradient descent subtracts $\eta$ times the gradient.

      At the start $z = 0$, so $p = 0.5$ and $p - y = -0.5$.

      Gradients: $\nabla_w = -0.5\,(2, 1) = (-1, -0.5)$ and $\partial_b = -0.5$.

      Update: $w = (0, 0) - 0.5(-1, -0.5) = (0.5, 0.25)$ and $b = 0 - 0.5(-0.5) = 0.25$.

      New score: $z = 0.5\times2 + 0.25\times1 + 0.25 = 1.5$, so $p = \sigma(1.5) = \dfrac{1}{1 + e^{-1.5}} \approx$ 0.82.

      Tempting errors: forgetting to update $b$ gives $z = 1.25$ and 0.78; adding the gradient instead of subtracting it gives $z = -1.5$ and 0.18.

      • Read a linear classifier as “score, then sign”: $z = w^\top x + b$, boundary at $z = 0$, $w$ perpendicular to it.
      • Convert between probability, odds and log-odds fluently: $p = 0.8 \leftrightarrow$ odds 4 $\leftrightarrow$ log-odds $\ln 4$.
      • For a perceptron question, check the sign convention at 0 and trace updates in a table.
      • Thinking logistic regression predicts a number: it’s a classifier with a linear boundary.
      • Forgetting the bias update $b \leftarrow b + y$ in the perceptron.
      • Calling logistic regression generative: it models $P(y\mid x)$ directly, so it’s discriminative.
      1. A linear classifier predicts by the sign of w⊤x + b; its decision boundary w⊤x + b = 0 is a hyperplane with w perpendicular to it.
      2. Logistic regression: P(y = 1 | x) = σ(w⊤x + b), so the log-odds is linear; it is trained by minimising cross-entropy, whose gradient is (p − y)x.
      3. Perceptron: on a mistake, w ← w + yx, b ← b + y; the score on that point moves by y(‖x‖² + 1). Discriminative models learn P(y | x); generative ones learn P(x | y)P(y).

      Despite its name, logistic regression is mainly used to

      predict a number, such as runs scored
      That’s ordinary (linear) regression. Think about what the sigmoid’s output range $(0, 1)$ is used for.
      group unlabelled matches into clusters
      Logistic regression needs labels; clustering doesn’t use them.
      predict a class, together with a probability for it
      It outputs $P(y = 1\mid x)$ and classifies by thresholding it, usually at 0.5.
      reduce many features to a few
      That’s dimensionality reduction, such as PCA.

      A logistic regression model gives a match a score $w^\top x + b = 0$. Its predicted probability of a win is

      0.5
      $\sigma(0) = 1/(1 + 1) = 0.5$: the point lies exactly on the decision boundary.
      0
      A score of 0 is the log-odds, not the probability. Odds $e^0 = 1$ means even chances.
      1
      Only a very large positive score gives a probability near 1.
      $e^{-1}$
      Substitute $z = 0$ into $1/(1 + e^{-z})$.

      A perceptron misclassifies the point $(x, y = -1)$ and updates. On that same point, the score $w^\top x + b$

      increases by $\norm{x}^2 + 1$
      The update adds $y x$ with $y = -1$. Which way does that push the score?
      stays the same
      The weights changed, and the change is aligned with $x$.
      becomes exactly $-1$
      One update moves it by a fixed amount; it need not land on any particular value.
      decreases by $\norm{x}^2 + 1$
      New score $=$ old $+\,y(\norm{x}^2 + 1)$ with $y = -1$: it moves towards the correct, negative side.

      Naive Bayes: classify by counting

      Naive Bayes applies Bayes’ theorem to pick the most probable class, after assuming the features are independent of each other once the class is known.

      It has appeared in every GATE DA paper so far in some form: 2024 Q20 (counting its parameters), 2025 Q35 (misclassification probability) and the sample paper’s Q28; 2026 Q23 matched it to “classification”.

      It’s like a scout judging a new bowler from a checklist: “fast bowlers usually have a long run-up, usually are tall, usually bowl bouncers”. The scout scores each clue separately and multiplies the evidence, without worrying that tall bowlers also tend to have long run-ups.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      Counting parameters, computing a posterior or misclassification probability, and spotting it as a generative model.

      2024 Q20 · number of parameters2025 Q35 · misclassification probabilitySample Q28 · parameters, K classes2024 Q18 · generative model2026 Q23 · task matching
      Heat: every year, 1–2 marks

      The Kalinga Kernels’ analyst has a simple table of their last ten matches: did they win the toss, were they at home, was the pitch spin-friendly, and did they win. Tomorrow they’ve won the toss, are playing away, on a spin pitch. Should the analyst expect a win?

      Bayes’ theorem (recall Probability 2.2) says $$P(\text{Win}\mid x) = \frac{P(x\mid \text{Win})\,P(\text{Win})}{P(x)},$$ where $x$ is the whole feature vector (Won toss, Away, Spin). The prior $P(\text{Win})$ is easy: 6 wins out of 10. The trouble is the likelihood $P(x\mid\text{Win})$: the exact combination (Won, Away, Spin) appears among the wins only once, and with more features most combinations never appear at all. You can’t estimate a probability from zero or one example.

      The naive fix: pretend that, within each class, the features don’t influence each other. Then the probability of the whole combination is a product of one-feature probabilities, and each of those can be estimated from plenty of rows.

      Events $A$ and $B$ are conditionally independent given $C$ if $P(A \cap B\mid C) = P(A\mid C)\,P(B\mid C)$: once you know $C$, learning $B$ tells you nothing more about $A$.

      Tiny example: a player’s shoe size and reading score are related across all children (older children have both bigger feet and better reading), but given the child’s age they are roughly independent. Age “explains away” the link.

      Assume the features $x_1, \ldots, x_D$ are conditionally independent given the class $c$. Then $$P(x\mid c) = \prod_{j=1}^{D} P(x_j\mid c), \qquad\text{and the classifier predicts}\qquad \hat y = \argmax_c\; P(c)\prod_{j=1}^{D} P(x_j\mid c).$$ The denominator $P(x)$ is the same for every class, so it doesn’t affect which class wins; you only need it if you want the actual posterior probabilities, and then it’s the sum of the class scores (normalise so they add to 1).

      From training data the estimates are simple fractions: $P(c) = \frac{N_c}{N}$ and $P(x_j = v\mid c) = \frac{N_{c,v}}{N_c}$, where $N_c$ counts training rows of class $c$ and $N_{c,v}$ counts those rows whose feature $j$ equals $v$. These are the maximum-likelihood estimates.

      Careful: “naive” means features are independent given the class, not independent overall. Toss result and venue may well be correlated across all matches; naive Bayes only assumes the correlation disappears once you know whether the match was won.

      The zero-count problem and Laplace smoothing

      If a feature value never appears with a class in the training data, its estimate is $0/N_c = 0$, and that single zero wipes out the whole product, however strongly the other features point to that class. With small data, “never seen” usually means “rare”, not “impossible”.

      Add one imaginary example of every value to every class: $$\hat P(x_j = v\mid c) = \frac{N_{c,v} + 1}{N_c + V_j},$$ where $V_j$ is the number of possible values of feature $j$. The estimates still add to 1 over the $V_j$ values, and none is zero. (Priors are usually left as $N_c/N$.)

      Tiny example: 0 of 4 losses were on spin pitches, and pitch has 2 values, so the smoothed estimate is $\frac{0+1}{4+2} = \frac16$ instead of 0.

      Try it

      Choose tomorrow’s match conditions with the chips; the table shades every cell that agrees with the new match. The readout multiplies prior × three likelihoods for each class and normalises. Start with Won, Away, Spin: the Kernels have never lost on a spin pitch, so “Loss” scores exactly 0. Switch Laplace smoothing on and watch Loss get a small, sensible probability. Then try Lost, Away, Pace.

      Using the Kalinga Kernels table in the widget (10 matches: 6 wins, 4 losses), predict the result of a match with Toss = Won, Venue = Away, Pitch = Spin, first with raw counts and then with Laplace smoothing. Give $P(\text{Win}\mid x)$ in each case.

      1. Count. Among the 6 wins: Won toss 4, Away 2, Spin 3. Among the 4 losses: Won toss 2, Away 3, Spin 0. Priors: $P(\text{Win}) = \frac{6}{10}$, $P(\text{Loss}) = \frac{4}{10}$.

        Every estimate is a fraction of rows within one class, so count class by class.

      2. Raw scores. Win: $\frac{6}{10}\cdot\frac46\cdot\frac26\cdot\frac36 = \frac{1}{15} \approx 0.0667$. Loss: $\frac{4}{10}\cdot\frac24\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac04 = 0$. So $P(\text{Win}\mid x) = 1$.

        Naive Bayes multiplies one likelihood per feature. The single zero count for (Spin, Loss) forces a certainty the data can’t justify.

      3. Smoothed likelihoods (each feature has 2 values, so add 1 on top and 2 below). Win: $\frac{4+1}{6+2} = \frac58$, $\frac{2+1}{8} = \frac38$, $\frac{3+1}{8} = \frac12$. Loss: $\frac{2+1}{4+2} = \frac12$, $\frac{3+1}{6} = \frac23$, $\frac{0+1}{6} = \frac16$.

        Laplace smoothing uses $\frac{N_{c,v}+1}{N_c + V_j}$ with $V_j = 2$ here.

      4. Smoothed scores. Win: $0.6\cdot\frac58\cdot\frac38\cdot\frac12 = \frac{9}{128} \approx 0.0703$. Loss: $0.4\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdot\frac16 = \frac{1}{45} \approx 0.0222$.

        Same recipe: prior times the product of likelihoods.

      5. Normalise: $P(\text{Win}\mid x) = \frac{0.0703}{0.0703 + 0.0222} \approx$ 0.76. The prediction is still Win, but now with an honest 24% chance of a loss.

        The two scores are proportional to the posteriors; dividing by their sum is the $P(x)$ in Bayes’ theorem.

      A free parameter is a number the model must learn that isn’t forced by the others. A distribution over $V$ values has $V - 1$ free parameters, because they must add to 1.

      • Two classes, $K$ binary features (the 2024 Q20 setting): 1 for the prior $P(y = 1)$, plus one number $P(x_j = 1\mid y)$ for each feature and each class: $2K + 1$.
      • Without the naive assumption, each class needs a full table over all $2^K$ feature combinations: $2(2^K - 1) + 1 = 2^{K+1} - 1$, exponential in $K$. That’s the reason for the assumption.
      • $K$ classes, $D$ features with $V$ values each: free parameters $(K - 1) + K D (V - 1)$. If instead you count every table entry, ignoring the sum-to-1 constraints, you get $K + KDV$.

      Misclassification probability of the Bayes rule at a point $x$: compute both scores $P(c)P(x\mid c)$, normalise; the classifier picks the larger posterior and is wrong with probability equal to the smaller one, $1 - \max_c P(c\mid x)$.

      Parameter counts: decide first whether the options count free parameters or all table entries, then use the formulas above.

      Go deeper: naive Bayes is a linear classifier in disguise

      With binary features, take logs of the ratio of the two class scores: $\ln\frac{P(1)\prod_j P(x_j\mid 1)}{P(0)\prod_j P(x_j\mid 0)} = \ln\frac{P(1)}{P(0)} + \sum_j \ln\frac{P(x_j\mid 1)}{P(x_j\mid 0)}$. Each term is $a_j x_j + c_j$ for constants $a_j, c_j$ (because $x_j$ is 0 or 1), so the log-odds is linear in $x$: exactly the form logistic regression uses. The two models share a boundary shape but fit it differently: naive Bayes counts per class (generative), logistic regression tunes $w$ to the labels directly (discriminative). In practice, products of many small probabilities underflow, so implementations add logarithms instead of multiplying. For continuous features, Gaussian naive Bayes uses a normal density per feature and class.

      The Haryana Heuristics lost 20 matches last season and none of them was on a “flat” pitch. Pitch type takes 3 values (spin, pace, flat). With Laplace smoothing, what is the estimate of $P(\text{flat}\mid\text{Loss})$? (Round off to three decimal places.)

      Add 1 to the count and the number of possible values to the class total.

      $\dfrac{0 + 1}{20 + 3} = \dfrac{1}{23} \approx$ 0.043.

      GATE DA 2025 · Q35 · NAT · 1 mark

      The naive Bayes classifier is used to solve a two-class classification problem with class-labels $y_1, y_2$. Suppose the prior probabilities are $P(y_1) = \frac13$ and $P(y_2) = \frac23$. Assuming a discrete feature space with $$P(x\mid y_1) = \frac34 \quad\text{and}\quad P(x\mid y_2) = \frac14$$ for a specific feature vector $x$. The probability of misclassifying $x$ is ______ (Round off to two decimal places)

      Compute prior × likelihood for each class and normalise. The classifier picks the larger posterior.

      Scores: $\frac13\cdot\frac34 = \frac14$ and $\frac23\cdot\frac14 = \frac16$. Sum $= \frac{5}{12}$. Posteriors: $P(y_1\mid x) = \frac{1/4}{5/12} = 0.6$ and $P(y_2\mid x) = 0.4$.

      The classifier picks $y_1$, and is wrong whenever the true class is $y_2$: probability 0.4. Official key: 0.39 to 0.41.

      GATE DA 2024 · Q20 · MCQ · 1 mark

      Given a dataset with $K$ binary-valued attributes (where $K \gt 2$) for a two-class classification task, the number of parameters to be estimated for learning a naïve Bayes classifier is

      1. $2^K + 1$
      2. $2K + 1$
      3. $2^{K+1} + 1$
      4. $K^2 + 1$

      How many numbers describe one binary feature within one class? How many describe the two-class prior?

      Each binary attribute needs one number per class, $P(x_j = 1\mid y)$ (its complement is forced), giving $2K$. The prior needs one number, $P(y = 1)$. Total $2K + 1$: (B). Official key: B.

      The exponential options describe a model without the naive assumption, which needs a table over all $2^K$ combinations per class.

      GATE DA 2024 sample paper · Q28 · MCQ · 2 marks

      Given a $K$-class dataset containing $N$ points, where sample points are described using $D$ discrete features with each feature capable of taking $V$ values, how many parameters need to be estimated for Naïve Bayes Classifier?

      1. $V^D K$
      2. $K^{V^D}$
      3. $VDK + K$
      4. $K(V + D)$

      Here $K$ is the number of classes, not features. For each class, how many numbers describe each feature? How many numbers describe the prior?

      For each of the $K$ classes and each of the $D$ features, naive Bayes stores a distribution over $V$ values: $VDK$ numbers. The class prior adds $K$ numbers. Total $VDK + K$: (C). (Sample paper, no official key; this is our answer.)

      This option counts every table entry. Counting only free parameters would give $(K-1) + KD(V-1)$, which is not offered, so the intended answer is (C). (A) is the size of a full joint table per class, which is what naive Bayes avoids.

      #WeatherTossResult
      1DryWonWin
      2HumidWonWin

      A naive Bayes classifier with Laplace smoothing on the likelihoods (priors unsmoothed) is used for a match with Weather = Rainy and Toss = Won. What is $P(\text{Win}\mid\text{Rainy}, \text{Won})$? (Round off to two decimal places.)

      Weather has 3 possible values and Toss has 2, so the denominators get $+3$ and $+2$ respectively. Without smoothing, check what happens to both classes.

      Counts: 5 wins (Rainy 0, Won 3) and 3 losses (Rainy 1, Won 0). Priors $\frac58$ and $\frac38$.

      Win: $\frac58\cdot\frac{0+1}{5+3}\cdot\frac{3+1}{5+2} = \frac58\cdot\frac18\cdot\frac47 = \frac{5}{112} \approx 0.0446$.

      Loss: $\frac38\cdot\frac{1+1}{3+3}\cdot\frac{0+1}{3+2} = \frac38\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac15 = \frac{1}{40} = 0.025$.

      $P(\text{Win}\mid x) = \dfrac{5/112}{5/112 + 1/40} = \dfrac{25}{39} \approx$ 0.64.

      Without smoothing both scores are 0 (no rainy wins, no toss-won losses), so the posterior is undefined: a vivid case for smoothing. Using $+2$ for Weather as if it were binary gives about 0.63, a common slip.

      Which statements about naive Bayes classifiers are correct? (Select all that apply.)

      1. It assumes the features are independent of each other across the whole dataset.
      2. If one feature is accidentally included twice (an exact copy), its evidence is counted twice, and this can change the predicted class.
      3. With Laplace smoothing, no estimated likelihood $P(x_j = v\mid c)$ is zero.
      4. With $D$ binary features and 2 classes, the number of free parameters grows exponentially in $D$.

      Re-read the assumption carefully: independent given what? For (B), what does the product look like when the same factor appears twice?

      (A) False: the assumption is conditional independence given the class.

      (B) True: a duplicated feature contributes its likelihood ratio squared. If, say, the duplicated feature favours class 1 by a factor of 2 and the others favour class 2 by a factor of 3, one copy gives class 2 and two copies ($2^2 = 4 \gt 3$) give class 1.

      (C) True: the numerator is at least 1.

      (D) False: it is $2D + 1$, linear in $D$. Exponential growth is what the naive assumption avoids.

      Answer: B; C.

      A naive Bayes classifier predicts which of 3 DPL teams will top the table. Each example has 4 binary features and 2 further features that each take 5 values. Counting free parameters (every probability distribution must sum to 1), how many parameters must be estimated?

      1. 36
      2. 38
      3. 57
      4. 1199

      Per class: a binary feature needs 1 number, a 5-valued feature needs 4. Then add the prior over 3 classes.

      Per class: $4\times1 + 2\times4 = 12$ free numbers. Three classes: 36. Prior over 3 classes: $3 - 1 = 2$. Total 38: (B).

      (A) forgets the prior. (C) counts every table entry: $3\times(4\times2 + 2\times5) + 3 = 57$. (D) is the full joint model without the naive assumption: $3\times(2^4\times5^2 - 1) + 2 = 1199$.

      • Count class by class: for each class, the prior and then one likelihood per feature.
      • Normalise only at the end, and only if a probability (not just a label) is asked for.
      • Use $V_j$, the number of values of that feature, in the Laplace denominator.
      • Forgetting the prior and comparing likelihoods alone (it can flip the decision).
      • Letting one zero count decide the answer; smooth it.
      • Mixing “free parameters” and “all table entries” when counting; read the options first.
      1. Naive Bayes predicts argmax over c of P(c) ∏ P(xⱼ | c), assuming features are conditionally independent given the class.
      2. Estimates are class-wise fractions; Laplace smoothing (count + 1)/(N_c + V) stops a single zero from wiping out a class.
      3. Parameters grow linearly: 2K + 1 free parameters for K binary features and two classes, against 2^(K+1) − 1 without the naive assumption.

      Naive Bayes is called “naive” because it assumes

      every class is equally likely
      Naive Bayes uses the class priors $P(c)$; they need not be equal.
      every feature follows a normal distribution
      That’s one variant (Gaussian naive Bayes), not the defining assumption.
      the classes can be separated by a straight line
      That’s linear separability, a different idea.
      the features are independent of each other once the class is known
      Conditional independence given the class lets $P(x\mid c)$ be a product of one-feature terms.

      The word “cashback” never appeared in any spam email in the training set. Without smoothing, a naive Bayes filter gives a new email containing “cashback” a spam probability of

      a small but positive number
      That’s what smoothing would give. Look at what one zero factor does to a product.
      exactly 0
      $P(\text{cashback}\mid\text{spam}) = 0$ makes the whole spam score 0, whatever else the email says.
      0.5
      Nothing in the model makes it fall back to even chances.
      the prior $P(\text{spam})$
      The prior is multiplied by the likelihoods, including the zero one.

      A naive Bayes classifier has 10 binary features and 2 classes. How many free parameters does it estimate?

      20
      That’s the likelihoods. The class prior also needs a number.
      2047
      That’s $2^{11} - 1$, the count without the naive assumption.
      21
      $2K + 1$ with $K = 10$: one number per feature per class, plus the prior.
      11
      Each class has its own likelihood for each feature.

      Linear discriminant analysis: the direction that separates classes best

      Fisher’s linear discriminant finds the direction $u$ such that, after projecting every point onto it, the two class means are as far apart as possible relative to the spread within each class.

      GATE DA 2024 Q22 asked for the eigenvalue equation $S_W^{-1}S_Bu = \lambda u$ that the best direction satisfies, and 2025 Q55 asked why the nearest-mean classifier is linear. 2026 Q23 listed LDA among classification and feature-extraction tools.

      It’s like photographing two flocks of birds from the side so that they look as separate as possible: you choose the camera angle where the flocks’ shadows overlap least, not just where their centres look farthest apart.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      The Fisher criterion and its eigen-equation, the two-class solution, and the nearest-mean classifier.

      2024 Q22 · $S_W^{-1}S_Bu^* = \lambda u^*$2025 Q55 · nearest-mean classifier is linear2026 Q23 · LDA for classification
      Heat: most years, 1–2 marks

      The Nagpur Neural Nets’ analyst has two numbers for each match (say, a batting index $x_1$ and a bowling index $x_2$) and wants to compress them into one score that best tells wins from losses. The simplest one-number summary of a point $x$ is its projection onto a direction $u$: $z = u^\top x$ (recall from Linear algebra that this is the length of $x$’s shadow on the line through $u$, when $\norm{u} = 1$).

      Which direction? A first guess is the line joining the two class means: that pushes the projected means furthest apart. But if each class is a long, tilted cloud, that direction can smear both clouds across each other. Fisher’s idea: reward a large gap between projected means, and penalise a large spread of each class along the line.

      Notation
      $m_1, m_2$
      the mean (average point) of class 1 and of class 2
      $S_W$
      within-class scatter: $\sum_{x \in C_1}(x - m_1)(x - m_1)^\top + \sum_{x \in C_2}(x - m_2)(x - m_2)^\top$, a $d \times d$ matrix measuring how spread each class is around its own mean
      $S_B$
      between-class scatter: $(m_2 - m_1)(m_2 - m_1)^\top$, measuring how far apart the means are

      For a direction $u$, the projected class means are $u^\top m_1$ and $u^\top m_2$, so their squared gap is $(u^\top(m_2 - m_1))^2 = u^\top S_B u$. The total squared spread of the projected points around their own class means is $u^\top S_W u$. Fisher’s linear discriminant chooses $u$ to maximise $$J(u) = \frac{u^\top S_B u}{u^\top S_W u} = \frac{\text{(gap between projected means)}^2}{\text{spread within classes along } u}.$$ Scaling $u$ by any non-zero number leaves $J$ unchanged, so only the direction matters.

      Try it

      Turn the purple line with the slider. Each point casts a dotted shadow onto the line; the strip underneath shows the shadows as a number line (squares are losses, dots are wins, tall ticks are the projected means). Press Mean difference: the means are far apart but both clouds smear across each other. Now press Fisher direction: the gap is smaller but the clouds are much tighter, and $J$ more than triples.

      GATE DA 2024 · Q22 · MCQ · 1 mark

      For any binary classification dataset, let $S_B \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ and $S_W \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ be the between-class and within-class scatter (covariance) matrices, respectively. The Fisher linear discriminant is defined by $u^* \in \mathbb{R}^d$, that maximizes $$J(u) = \frac{u^T S_B u}{u^T S_W u}$$ If $\lambda = J(u^*)$, $S_W$ is non-singular and $S_B \ne 0$, then $(u^*, \lambda)$ must satisfy which ONE of the following equations?

      Note: $\mathbb{R}$ denotes the set of real numbers.

      1. $S_W^{-1} S_B u^* = \lambda u^*$
      2. $S_W u^* = \lambda S_B u^*$
      3. $S_B S_W u^* = \lambda u^*$
      4. ${u^*}^T u^* = \lambda^2$

      1. At a maximum, the gradient of $J$ is zero. Write $J = N/D$ with $N = u^\top S_B u$ and $D = u^\top S_W u$. For a symmetric matrix $A$, the gradient of $u^\top A u$ is $2Au$.

        Both scatter matrices are symmetric (sums of $vv^\top$ terms), so the standard quadratic-form gradient applies (recall Calculus).

      2. Quotient rule: $\nabla J = \dfrac{2S_Bu\,D - 2S_Wu\,N}{D^2} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; S_B u = \dfrac{N}{D}\,S_W u = J(u)\,S_W u$.

        Setting the numerator to zero and dividing by $D \gt 0$.

      3. At $u^*$, $J(u^*) = \lambda$, so $S_B u^* = \lambda S_W u^*$. Multiply on the left by $S_W^{-1}$ (it exists): $S_W^{-1} S_B u^* = \lambda u^*$. That’s (A).

        This is a generalised eigenvalue problem: $u^*$ is an eigenvector of $S_W^{-1}S_B$, and the maximum value of $J$ is its largest eigenvalue.

      4. Check the others. (B) has $S_W$ and $S_B$ swapped: it would hold with $1/\lambda$, not $\lambda$. (C) multiplies the matrices in the wrong order and without the inverse. (D) is a normalisation, and $J$ doesn’t depend on the length of $u$ at all. Official key: A.

        A quick dimension or scaling check eliminates distractors like (D).

      With two classes, $S_B u = (m_2 - m_1)\big[(m_2 - m_1)^\top u\big]$ is always a multiple of $m_2 - m_1$. So $S_B u^* = \lambda S_W u^*$ forces $$u^* \propto S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1), \qquad J_{\max} = \lambda = (m_2 - m_1)^\top S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1).$$ $S_B$ has rank 1, so $S_W^{-1}S_B$ has exactly one non-zero eigenvalue. With $K$ classes, $S_B$ has rank at most $K - 1$, so LDA gives at most $K - 1$ useful directions; this is how LDA is used for feature extraction (supervised dimensionality reduction).

      To classify, project a new point onto $u^*$ and compare with a threshold, typically the midpoint of the two projected means. The boundary $u^{*\top}x = t$ is a hyperplane: LDA is a linear classifier.

      Wins of the Nagpur Neural Nets: $(1, 1), (2, 3), (3, 2)$. Losses: $(4, 5), (5, 7), (6, 6)$. Find the Fisher direction, the maximum value of $J$, and a classification rule.

      1. Means: $m_1 = (2, 2)$, $m_2 = (5, 6)$, so $m_2 - m_1 = (3, 4)$.

        Average each coordinate within the class.

      2. Deviations from the mean are $(-1, -1), (0, 1), (1, 0)$ in both classes. Each class contributes $\begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, so $S_W = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 2\\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.

        Sum the outer products $vv^\top$: $(-1,-1)$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$, $(0,1)$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, $(1,0)$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$.

      3. $S_W^{-1} = \frac{1}{12}\begin{pmatrix}4 & -2\\ -2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$, so $u^* \propto \begin{pmatrix}4 & -2\\ -2 & 4\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}3\\4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}4\\10\end{pmatrix} \propto (2, 5)$.

        The 2×2 inverse: swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant $16 - 4 = 12$. The constant $\frac{1}{12}$ only rescales $u$.

      4. $J_{\max} = (3, 4)\cdot\frac{1}{12}(4, 10) = \frac{12 + 40}{12} = \frac{13}{3} \approx 4.33$. For comparison, the mean-difference direction $(3, 4)$ gives $J = \frac{25^2}{148} \approx 4.22$.

        Fisher’s direction tilts from $(3, 4)$ towards the axis along which the clouds are thin.

      5. Projected means: $(2, 5)\cdot(2, 2) = 14$ and $(2, 5)\cdot(5, 6) = 40$. Rule: predict Loss if $2x_1 + 5x_2 \gt 27$, Win otherwise.

        The midpoint $\frac{14 + 40}{2} = 27$ is the natural threshold when the classes are equally common.

      The nearest-mean classifier is linear too

      An even simpler rule: assign a point to whichever class mean it is closer to. It sounds like it should give a curved boundary, because distances are squared. It doesn’t. Expand $f(x) = \norm{\mu_r - x}^2 - \norm{\mu_g - x}^2$: $$f(x) = \norm{\mu_r}^2 - 2\mu_r^\top x + \norm{x}^2 - \norm{\mu_g}^2 + 2\mu_g^\top x - \norm{x}^2 = 2(\mu_g - \mu_r)^\top x + \norm{\mu_r}^2 - \norm{\mu_g}^2.$$ The $\norm{x}^2$ terms cancel, leaving $w^\top x + b$ with $w = 2(\mu_g - \mu_r)$ and $b = \norm{\mu_r}^2 - \norm{\mu_g}^2$. The boundary $f = 0$ is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two means.

      The link to LDA: if each class is a Gaussian with the same covariance $\Sigma$ and the classes are equally likely, the Bayes-optimal rule has a linear boundary with normal $\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_2 - \mu_1)$, the same direction as Fisher’s. When $\Sigma$ is a multiple of $I$ (round clouds), that’s exactly the nearest-mean rule. If the classes have different covariances, the boundary becomes quadratic (QDA).

      For the worked example above ($m_2 - m_1 = (3, 4)$, $S_W = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 2\\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$), compute the Fisher score $J(u)$ for $u = (1, 0)$, that is, using only the first feature.

      $u^\top S_B u = (u^\top(m_2 - m_1))^2$ and $u^\top S_W u$ is the top-left entry of $S_W$ when $u = (1, 0)$.

      Numerator $(1\cdot3 + 0\cdot4)^2 = 9$. Denominator $= 4$. $J = 9/4 =$ 2.25, well below the best possible $13/3 \approx 4.33$.

      Two classes have $m_2 - m_1 = (2, 4)$ and within-class scatter $S_W = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 0\\ 0 & 8\end{pmatrix}$. If the Fisher direction is scaled so that its first component is 1, what is its second component?

      $u^* \propto S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1)$; a diagonal matrix is inverted entry by entry.

      $S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1) = (2/2,\; 4/8) = (1, 0.5)$. Second component 0.5. The second feature is noisier (spread 8), so Fisher trusts it less than the mean difference alone would suggest.

      A nearest-mean classifier has class means $\mu_A = (0, 0)$ and $\mu_B = (4, 2)$ and computes $f(x) = \norm{\mu_A - x}^2 - \norm{\mu_B - x}^2$, assigning class A when $f(x) \lt 0$. Find $f(x)$ at $x = (3, 0)$.

      Either compute both squared distances directly, or use $f(x) = 2(\mu_B - \mu_A)^\top x + \norm{\mu_A}^2 - \norm{\mu_B}^2$.

      $\norm{\mu_A - x}^2 = 9$ and $\norm{\mu_B - x}^2 = 1 + 4 = 5$, so $f = $ 4, and $x$ goes to class B. Check with the linear form: $2(4, 2)\cdot(3, 0) + 0 - 20 = 24 - 20 = 4$.

      GATE DA 2025 · Q55 · MSQ · 2 marks

      Consider a two-class problem in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with class labels red and green. Let $\mu_{red}$ and $\mu_{green}$ be the means of the two classes. Given test sample $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$, a classifier calculates the squared Euclidean distance (denoted by $\norm{\cdot}^2$) between $x$ and the means of the two classes and assigns the class label that the sample $x$ is closest to. That is, the classifier computes $$f(x) = \norm{\mu_{red} - x}^2 - \norm{\mu_{green} - x}^2$$ and assigns the label red to $x$ if $f(x) \lt 0$, and green otherwise. Which of the following statements is/are correct?

      1. The sample $x = 0$ is assigned the label green if $\norm{\mu_{red}} \lt \norm{\mu_{green}}$
      2. $f$ is a linear function of $x$
      3. $f(x) = w^\top x + b$, where $w$ and $b$ are functions of $\mu_{red}$ and $\mu_{green}$
      4. $f$ is a quadratic polynomial in $x$

      Expand both squared norms. What happens to the $\norm{x}^2$ terms? Then evaluate at $x = 0$.

      Expanding, $f(x) = 2(\mu_{green} - \mu_{red})^\top x + \norm{\mu_{red}}^2 - \norm{\mu_{green}}^2$: the $\norm{x}^2$ terms cancel. So (C) holds with $w = 2(\mu_{green} - \mu_{red})$, $b = \norm{\mu_{red}}^2 - \norm{\mu_{green}}^2$, and (B) holds in the sense used here (a linear function plus a constant). (D) fails: there is no $x^2$ term left.

      (A): $f(0) = \norm{\mu_{red}}^2 - \norm{\mu_{green}}^2 \lt 0$ when $\norm{\mu_{red}} \lt \norm{\mu_{green}}$, so $x = 0$ is labelled red, not green. False.

      Answer: B; C. Official key: B; C.

      Two classes have $m_2 - m_1 = (3, 0)$ and within-class scatter $S_W = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1\\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. What is the largest possible value of the Fisher criterion $J(u) = \dfrac{u^\top S_B u}{u^\top S_W u}$?

      For two classes, $J_{\max} = (m_2 - m_1)^\top S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1)$. Invert the 2×2 matrix.

      $S_W^{-1} = \frac13\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1\\ -1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, so $S_W^{-1}(3, 0) = (2, -1)$. That is the Fisher direction.

      $J_{\max} = (3, 0)\cdot(2, -1) = $ 6.

      The tempting answer 4.5 comes from using the mean-difference direction $u = (3, 0)$: $J = \frac{9^2}{(3,0)S_W(3,0)^\top} = \frac{81}{18} = 4.5$. The optimum tilts away from $m_2 - m_1$ because the clouds are elongated along $(1, 1)$.

      Which statements about Fisher’s linear discriminant are correct? (Select all that apply.)

      1. $J(cu) = J(u)$ for every non-zero real number $c$.
      2. For two classes, the between-class scatter matrix $S_B$ has rank 1.
      3. The Fisher direction is always parallel to $m_2 - m_1$.
      4. With $K$ classes, LDA yields at most $K - 1$ directions with a non-zero eigenvalue.

      (A): $c$ appears squared in numerator and denominator. (C): look at the hard question above.

      (A) True: both quadratic forms pick up $c^2$, which cancels.

      (B) True: $S_B = vv^\top$ with $v = m_2 - m_1 \ne 0$.

      (C) False: $u^* \propto S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1)$, which is parallel to $m_2 - m_1$ only in special cases, such as $S_W$ a multiple of $I$.

      (D) True: $S_B$ is a sum of $K$ rank-one terms whose vectors $m_k - m$ satisfy one linear relation (their weighted sum is 0), so its rank is at most $K - 1$.

      Answer: A; B; D.

      A nearest-mean classifier has $\mu_{red} = (1, 2)$ and $\mu_{green} = (5, 4)$. Its decision boundary is a straight line. At what value of $x_1$ does that line cross the $x_1$-axis?

      Write $f(x) = 2(\mu_{green} - \mu_{red})^\top x + \norm{\mu_{red}}^2 - \norm{\mu_{green}}^2$ and solve $f = 0$ with $x_2 = 0$.

      $w = 2(4, 2) = (8, 4)$ and $b = (1 + 4) - (25 + 16) = -36$. The boundary is $8x_1 + 4x_2 = 36$, that is $2x_1 + x_2 = 9$.

      At $x_2 = 0$: $x_1 = $ 4.5.

      Check: the boundary is the perpendicular bisector of the segment between the means. Its midpoint $(3, 3)$ satisfies $2\cdot3 + 3 = 9$, and the line’s normal $(2, 1)$ is parallel to $\mu_{green} - \mu_{red} = (4, 2)$. A common slip is to forget the $b$ term and answer 0, or to use the midpoint’s $x_1 = 3$.

      • Remember the recipe: means, then $S_W$, then $u^* \propto S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1)$.
      • Use the “gap squared over spread” reading of $J$ to sanity-check answers.
      • Expand squared distances to show a nearest-mean boundary is linear.
      • Writing $S_B^{-1}S_W$ or $S_BS_W$ instead of $S_W^{-1}S_B$.
      • Assuming the best direction is the line joining the means.
      • Calling the nearest-mean rule quadratic because of the squares: the $\norm{x}^2$ terms cancel.
      1. Fisher’s LDA maximises J(u) = u⊤S_B u / u⊤S_W u: projected means far apart, each class tight.
      2. The optimum solves S_W⁻¹S_B u = λu with λ = J(u); for two classes u ∝ S_W⁻¹(m₂ − m₁).
      3. The nearest-mean classifier is linear: f(x) = 2(μ_g − μ_r)⊤x + ‖μ_r‖² − ‖μ_g‖², the perpendicular bisector of the means.

      You must squash two-dimensional data from two classes onto a single line and still tell the classes apart. The best line is the one where

      the overall spread of all the points is largest
      That’s what PCA looks for, and it ignores the labels; the spread could be within a class.
      the projected class means are far apart and each class stays tightly packed
      That’s Fisher’s criterion: gap squared divided by within-class spread.
      the projected class means are as far apart as possible, whatever the spread
      Large overlapping spreads can make far-apart means useless. Try the widget’s mean-difference button.
      the line passes through both class means
      That’s the mean-difference direction; it ignores the shape of the clouds.

      For two classes, the Fisher direction is proportional to

      $m_2 - m_1$
      Only when $S_W$ is a multiple of the identity. In general the within-class scatter tilts it.
      the top eigenvector of $S_W$
      That direction is where the classes are most spread out: the worst choice.
      $S_W^{-1}(m_2 - m_1)$
      From $S_Bu = \lambda S_Wu$, with $S_Bu$ always a multiple of $m_2 - m_1$.
      $S_B^{-1}(m_2 - m_1)$
      $S_B$ has rank 1 and is not invertible when $d \ge 2$.

      The decision boundary of a nearest-mean classifier with two classes is

      a circle around one of the means
      Expand the squared distances: the $\norm{x}^2$ terms cancel.
      the line through the two means
      Points on that line can be closer to either mean. Where are points equally close to both?
      a parabola
      No squared terms in $x$ survive.
      the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the means
      The set of points equidistant from two points is their perpendicular bisector, a hyperplane.

      Which of these models is discriminative?

      Naive Bayes
      It models $P(x\mid y)P(y)$, then uses Bayes’ theorem: generative.
      Logistic regression
      It models $P(y\mid x)$ directly.
      Gaussian discriminant analysis
      It models each class as a Gaussian, $P(x\mid y)$: generative, despite “discriminant” in the name.
      PCA
      PCA isn’t a classifier at all; it uses no labels.

      A naive Bayes classifier computes prior × likelihood scores of 0.03 for Win and 0.01 for Loss. $P(\text{Win}\mid x)$ is

      0.03
      That’s the unnormalised score. Divide by the total.
      0.3
      Recompute: the total of the two scores is 0.04.
      0.75
      $0.03 / (0.03 + 0.01)$.
      0.97
      Normalise by the sum of the class scores, not by 1.

      If $u$ maximises the Fisher criterion $J(u)$, then so does

      only $u/\norm{u}$
      Any non-zero multiple works, not only the unit vector.
      $-3u$
      $J(cu) = J(u)$ for every $c \ne 0$: the factor $c^2$ cancels.
      $S_W u$
      Multiplying by a matrix changes the direction in general.
      $u + (m_2 - m_1)$
      Adding a vector changes the direction.

      A logistic regression model labels a match “Win” when $P(\text{Win}\mid x) \ge t$. Raising the threshold $t$ from 0.5 to 0.9 typically makes the “Win” predictions

      higher in both precision and recall
      Fewer matches are called “Win” at all. What does that do to the share of actual wins you catch?
      lower in precision, higher in recall
      That’s what lowering the threshold tends to do.
      higher in precision, lower in recall
      Only very confident cases are called “Win”, so they’re more often right (precision up) but more real wins are missed (recall down).
      unchanged, because the boundary is still linear
      The boundary stays linear but shifts parallel, so the predictions change.

      Logistic regression is trained on linearly separable data. Adding an L2 penalty $\lambda\norm{w}^2$ to the cross-entropy loss (as in ridge regression)

      keeps the weights finite instead of letting them grow without bound
      Without the penalty, scaling a separating $w$ up always lowers the loss; the penalty stops that.
      makes the decision boundary curved
      The model is still $\sigma(w^\top x + b)$, so the boundary is still a hyperplane.
      sets some weights exactly to zero
      That’s typical of an L1 penalty (lasso), not L2.
      has no effect, because the data are separable
      Separable data is exactly when the unpenalised weights blow up.

      Three classifiers that think in pictures. k-nearest neighbours copies the label of the most similar past examples. A support vector machine draws the line with the widest empty street around it. A decision tree asks a short chain of yes/no questions. Between them they have produced a question in every GATE DA paper: support vectors, the margin, the smallest k that flips a prediction, an information gain.

      You need: features, labels and training sets from Part 1; the bias–variance trade-off and cross-validation from Part 2; linear classifiers and decision boundaries from Part 3; dot products and lengths of vectors from the vectors refresher; logarithms base 2.

      k-nearest neighbours: ask the most similar examples

      k-nearest neighbours (kNN) labels a new point by finding the $k$ training points closest to it and taking a majority vote of their labels.

      GATE DA 2024 Q63 (2 marks) gave five points on a grid and asked for the smallest odd $k$ that flips a prediction; kNN also turns up in options about overfitting and scaling.

      It’s like guessing a new neighbour’s favourite team by asking the three nearest houses on the street and going with the majority.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      A small grid of labelled points, a query point, and “what does kNN predict for this k?”

      2024 Q63 · smallest odd k for “square”
      Heat: 1 question in 3 papers, 2 marks; quick marks once distances are listed
      DPL story

      The Haryana Heuristics have signed a new batter and want to know what kind of player they are: an anchor (bats long, scores steadily) or a hitter (scores fast, gets out more). The scouts have scored every batter in the league on two numbers from 0 to 10: consistency and power. The new batter scores 4.9 and 4.9.

      The scouts’ rule of thumb: find the three existing batters whose two numbers are closest to the new one’s, and go with what most of them are. That rule is the whole algorithm.

      Some words from Part 1, in this setting. Each batter is a data point. The two numbers describing them are features (here $x_1$ = consistency, $x_2$ = power), so each batter is a point $\x = (x_1, x_2)$ on a plane. The answer we want to predict, anchor or hitter, is the label. The batters whose labels we already know form the training set. The new batter is the query.

      kNN has no formula to fit. It stores the training set and does all its work when a query arrives. Because it postpones the work, it is called a lazy learner.

      For points $\x = (x_1, \ldots, x_d)$ and $\z = (z_1, \ldots, z_d)$ with $d$ features:

      Euclidean distance (the straight-line, ruler distance): $$\norm{\x - \z} = \sqrt{(x_1 - z_1)^2 + \cdots + (x_d - z_d)^2}.$$ Manhattan distance (walking along a city grid): $$|x_1 - z_1| + \cdots + |x_d - z_d|.$$ Example: from $(1, 2)$ to $(4, 6)$ the Euclidean distance is $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$ and the Manhattan distance is $3 + 4 = 7$.

      Given a training set $(\x_1, y_1), \ldots, (\x_n, y_n)$, a number $k$ and a query $\x$:

      1. Compute the distance from $\x$ to every training point.
      2. Keep the $k$ training points with the smallest distances: the $k$ nearest neighbours.
      3. Classification: predict the label that occurs most often among them (majority vote). Regression (a number to predict): predict the average of their values.

      There is no training step. Predicting one query costs $n$ distance computations, each over $d$ features.

      Try it

      Drag the diamond (the new batter). The dashed circle passes through the $k$-th nearest neighbour, so everything inside it gets a vote. Set $k = 1$ and watch the shaded regions become jagged islands around single points; raise $k$ towards 15 and they smooth out until the larger class takes over. Try an even $k$ near the border to see a tied vote, and switch to Manhattan distance to see the circle turn into a diamond.

      Choosing k

      Small $k$ (say 1) follows every training point, including odd ones. With $k = 1$ each training point is its own nearest neighbour, so the training error is zero (as long as no two identical points carry different labels). The boundary is jagged and the model reacts to noise: low bias, high variance, in the language of Part 2.

      Large $k$ averages over many points, so the boundary is smooth. Push it to $k = n$ and every query gets the same answer: the majority class of the whole training set. That is high bias.

      So $k$ is a hyperparameter: a setting you choose rather than learn from the data. The usual way to choose it is cross-validation. With two classes, pick an odd $k$ so the vote cannot tie.

      Two kinds of tie

      A vote tie (two hitters, two anchors with $k = 4$) is avoided by odd $k$. A distance tie happens when the $k$-th and $(k+1)$-th neighbours are equally far. Exam questions are set so that it doesn’t matter, but check: list the distances in order and see whether the cut-off falls in the middle of a tie.

      Scaling the features

      Distance adds up differences across features, so a feature measured in big units swamps the others. If one feature is an auction price in lakh rupees (from 20 to 1500) and the other is age in years (18 to 40), the price difference decides almost every distance. The fix is to put features on a common scale first, for example min–max scaling $x \mapsto \frac{x - \min}{\max - \min}$ (everything between 0 and 1) or standardising $x \mapsto \frac{x - \bar x}{s}$ (mean 0, standard deviation 1).

      Careful: multiplying every feature by the same positive number never changes a kNN prediction (all distances scale together, so their order stays the same). Rescaling one feature can change it completely.
      Go deeper: the shape of the 1-NN boundary, and many features

      With $k = 1$ the plane splits into one cell per training point: the region closer to that point than to any other (a Voronoi cell). Between two neighbouring points the boundary is their perpendicular bisector, so the 1-NN decision boundary is made of straight pieces of bisectors between points of different classes.

      With many features, distances behave strangely: in 100 dimensions the nearest and farthest training points from a query are often almost equally far, so “nearest” loses its meaning. This is the curse of dimensionality, and it is why kNN works best with a modest number of well-scaled features.

      GATE DA 2024 · Q63 · NAT · 2 marks

      Given the two-dimensional dataset consisting of 5 data points from two classes (circles and squares) and assume that the Euclidean distance is used to measure the distance between two points. The minimum odd value of $k$ in $k$-nearest neighbor algorithm for which the diamond (⋄) shaped data point is assigned the label square is ______.

      (Figure redrawn from the paper.)

      1. Read the points: circles at $(1,1)$ and $(1,2)$; squares at $(2,3)$, $(3,3)$ and $(3,2)$; the diamond (the query) at $(2,1)$.

        Writing coordinates down first stops you misreading a point mid-calculation.

      2. Distances from $(2,1)$: to $(1,1)$ it is $1$; to $(1,2)$ it is $\sqrt{1+1} = \sqrt2 \approx 1.41$; to $(3,2)$ also $\sqrt2$; to $(2,3)$ it is $2$; to $(3,3)$ it is $\sqrt{1+4} = \sqrt5 \approx 2.24$.

        Euclidean distance: square the differences in each coordinate, add, take the square root.

      3. Sorted: circle (1), circle ($\sqrt2$), square ($\sqrt2$), square (2), square ($\sqrt5$).

        kNN only cares about the order of the distances.

      4. $k = 1$: one circle, so circle. $k = 3$: two circles and one square, so circle. (The 2nd and 3rd are tied at $\sqrt2$, but $k = 3$ takes both, so the tie does not matter.)

        The question asks for odd $k$, so even values are skipped.

      5. $k = 5$: two circles and three squares, so square. The answer is 5.

        The two circles are the closest points, so the squares can only outvote them once all five points vote. Official key: 5.

      List every training point with its squared distance (no square roots needed: squaring keeps the order). Sort once. Then read off the vote for each $k$ by counting labels from the top of the list.

      Find the Euclidean and the Manhattan distance between the batters $(1, 2)$ and $(4, 6)$.

      The differences are 3 and 4. Euclidean: square, add, square root. Manhattan: add the absolute differences.

      Euclidean: $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = \sqrt{25} = 5$. Manhattan: $3 + 4 = 7$. Manhattan is never smaller than Euclidean, because walking along the grid is never shorter than the straight line.

      Training points: $(1,1)$ class A, $(2,2)$ class A, $(4,3)$ class B, $(5,2)$ class B, $(3,5)$ class B. Using Euclidean distance, what does kNN predict for the query $(3,2)$ with $k = 1$, and then with $k = 3$?

      Squared distances from $(3,2)$: 5, 1, 2, 4, 9.

      Distances: $(2,2)$ A: 1; $(4,3)$ B: $\sqrt2$; $(5,2)$ B: 2; $(1,1)$ A: $\sqrt5$; $(3,5)$ B: 3.

      $k = 1$: the nearest is $(2,2)$, class A. $k = 3$: A, B, B, so B. Answer: A then B. A single close point can win at $k = 1$ and be outvoted as soon as more neighbours join.

      A kNN model describes DPL players by auction price (in lakh rupees, between 20 and 1500) and age (in years, between 18 and 40), with no scaling. Which feature mostly decides who counts as a “nearest” neighbour?

      Compare a typical difference in price with a typical difference in age.

      Price. Two players can differ by hundreds of lakhs but by at most 22 years, and the squared differences are added, so price dominates. Min–max scaling or standardising both features first gives them equal say.

      kNN can also predict numbers. Past matches at one ground had grass length (mm) and first-innings score: (2, 160), (4, 172), (5, 180), (7, 150), (9, 140). Predict the score for grass length 5.4 by averaging the scores of the 3 nearest matches. (Round to two decimal places.)

      Distances from 5.4: 3.4, 1.4, 0.4, 1.6, 3.6.

      The three nearest are 5 (0.4 away), 4 (1.4) and 7 (1.6), with scores 180, 172 and 150. Average: $\frac{180 + 172 + 150}{3} = \frac{502}{3} \approx$ 167.33.

      Seven players are described by one feature with labels: 1.0 (A), 2.0 (A), 3.5 (B), 4.2 (A), 6.1 (B), 7.1 (B), 9.0 (A). In leave-one-out evaluation each point in turn is removed, classified by kNN using the other six, and counted as an error if the prediction is wrong. How many errors does 1-NN make, and how many does 3-NN make?

      For each point, list its distances to the other six (never to itself). For 3-NN, take a majority of the three closest.

      1-NN. 1.0 → 2.0 (A) right; 2.0 → 1.0 (A) right; 3.5 → 4.2 (A) wrong; 4.2 → 3.5 (B) wrong; 6.1 → 7.1 (B) right; 7.1 → 6.1 (B) right; 9.0 → 7.1 (B) wrong. Errors: 3.

      3-NN. 1.0: 2.0 A, 3.5 B, 4.2 A → A, right. 2.0: 1.0 A, 3.5 B, 4.2 A → A, right. 3.5: 4.2 A, 2.0 A, 1.0 A (2.5) → A, wrong. 4.2: 3.5 B, 6.1 B, 2.0 A → B, wrong. 6.1: 7.1 B, 4.2 A, 3.5 B → B, right. 7.1: 6.1 B, 9.0 A, 4.2 A → A, wrong. 9.0: 7.1 B, 6.1 B, 4.2 A → B, wrong. Errors: 4.

      A larger $k$ is not automatically better: here the lone A at 9.0 still loses, and 7.1 now gets outvoted. The tempting slip is to include the point itself among its neighbours, which makes 1-NN look perfect.

      Two known players: P = (40 runs, 1 wicket per match), a batter; Q = (30 runs, 4 wickets), an all-rounder. A new player has (36 runs, 3.5 wickets). Runs range from 0 to 100 and wickets from 0 to 5. What does 1-NN with Euclidean distance predict on the raw features, and after min–max scaling each feature by its range?

      1. batter, then batter
      2. batter, then all-rounder
      3. all-rounder, then batter
      4. all-rounder, then all-rounder

      Scaling here means dividing runs by 100 and wickets by 5. Compute both distances in both versions.

      Raw: to P, $\sqrt{4^2 + 2.5^2} = \sqrt{22.25} \approx 4.72$; to Q, $\sqrt{6^2 + 0.5^2} = \sqrt{36.25} \approx 6.02$. Nearest is P: batter.

      Scaled: P = (0.40, 0.20), Q = (0.30, 0.80), new = (0.36, 0.70). To P, $\sqrt{0.04^2 + 0.5^2} \approx 0.502$; to Q, $\sqrt{0.06^2 + 0.1^2} \approx 0.117$. Nearest is Q: all-rounder. Answer (B).

      On raw numbers the 10-run gap looks large and the 3-wicket gap small, yet 3 wickets is most of the wicket range. (A) is what you get if you forget to scale; (C) and (D) come from mixing up which point is closer.

      Which statements about kNN classification (unweighted majority vote) are true? Assume no two training points are identical.

      1. With $k = 1$, the error on the training set itself is zero.
      2. With $k = n$ (the whole training set), every query gets the training set’s majority class.
      3. Increasing $k$ always lowers the error on new data.
      4. Multiplying every feature by 10 can change some predictions.

      For (D), think about what happens to the order of the distances.

      (A) True: each training point is at distance 0 from itself, so it predicts its own label. (B) True: all $n$ points vote whatever the query, so the answer never changes.
