(C) False: too large a $k$ underfits (Ch. 4.1 hard question 1 shows a larger $k$ doing worse). (D) False: every distance is multiplied by 10, so the order and the neighbours are unchanged. Only scaling features differently can change predictions. Answer: A; B.

      • Write all distances in a sorted list before voting; use squared distances to skip square roots.
      • Scale features to comparable ranges before using distances.
      • Choose odd $k$ for two classes, and pick $k$ by cross-validation.
      • Counting the query itself as one of its neighbours when it is a training point (leave-one-out).
      • Assuming larger $k$ is always better: very large $k$ just predicts the majority class.
      • Forgetting that an even $k$ can tie, and that the $k$-th distance can tie with the next.
      1. kNN stores the training data and, for a query, takes a majority vote of the k closest points (an average for regression).
      2. Small k: jagged boundary, low bias, high variance (k = 1 has zero training error). Large k: smooth boundary, high bias; k = n predicts the majority class.
      3. Distances depend on units: scale features first; prefer odd k for two classes.

      A new batter’s nearest neighbour is an anchor at distance 0.5. The next two are hitters at distances 0.9 and 1.0. What does 3-NN predict?

      Anchor, because it is the closest
      Closeness only decides who gets a vote. Once inside the top 3, each neighbour’s vote counts the same.
      Hitter
      The three nearest are one anchor and two hitters, and the majority wins.
      A tie
      With three voters and two classes, one class always has at least two votes.
      It can’t be decided without the other points
      For 3-NN only the three nearest points matter, and you know all of them.

      Why do people choose an odd $k$ for a two-class kNN problem?

      Odd $k$ makes the boundary linear
      The boundary’s shape doesn’t depend on whether $k$ is odd. Think about the vote count.
      Odd $k$ gives zero training error
      Only $k = 1$ guarantees that.
      So the majority vote can never be tied
      With two classes and an odd number of votes, one class always has more.
      Odd $k$ removes the need to scale features
      Scaling is about the units of the features, not about $k$.

      A training set has 60 hitters and 40 anchors. kNN is run with $k = 100$ (all of them). What does it predict for a new batter who is extremely close to one anchor?

      Anchor
      Every one of the 100 points gets a vote, wherever the query is.
      Hitter
      With $k = n$, all 100 points vote every time: 60 to 40 for hitter, whatever the query.
      It depends on the distance measure
      With all points voting, distances no longer matter.
      A tie
      60 against 40 is not a tie.

      Support vector machines: the widest street between two classes

      A support vector machine (SVM) separates two classes with the straight line (or flat plane) that stays as far as possible from the nearest points of both classes.

      SVMs have appeared in every GATE DA paper so far: 2024 Q17 (which points are support vectors), 2024 Q53 (which datasets are linearly separable), 2025 Q53 (find $w$, $b$ and the margin) and the sample paper’s Q29 (what happens if you delete a point).

      It’s like painting a road between two villages: you want the widest road that touches no house, and only the houses at the very edge of the road decide where it goes.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      Small 2-D datasets: find the separator, the support vectors or the margin, or decide whether a line can separate the classes at all.

      2024 Q17 · possible support vectors2025 Q53 · w, b, margin √22024 Q53 · linearly separable?Sample Q29 · remove a non-support vector
      Heat: every year, 1 to 2 questions, 1–2 marks each
      DPL story

      The Hyderabad Hyperplanes’ analyst plots last season’s matches on two numbers: run rate in the first six overs ($x_1$) and run rate at the death ($x_2$). Wins and losses fall into two clouds, and many straight lines separate them. Which line should they trust for next season? A line that grazes a past win will misjudge the next similar match. The safest line keeps the biggest gap to both clouds.

      Recall from Part 3 that a linear classifier computes a score $\w\cdot\x + b$ and predicts by its sign: $f(\x) = \text{sign}(\w\cdot\x + b)$, which is $+1$ on one side and $-1$ on the other. Here $\w$ is a vector of weights (one per feature) and $b$ is a number called the bias. Labels are written $y = +1$ and $y = -1$.

      The decision boundary is where the score is zero: $\w\cdot\x + b = 0$. In two dimensions this is a straight line; in three, a flat plane; in general it is called a hyperplane, meaning a flat boundary with one dimension fewer than the space. Example: $\w = (1, 1)$, $b = -1$ gives the line $x_1 + x_2 = 1$.

      How far is a point from the line?

      Two facts from the vectors refresher do all the work. First, $\w$ points straight across the boundary (it is perpendicular to it): if $\x$ and $\x'$ are both on the boundary, $\w\cdot\x + b = \w\cdot\x' + b = 0$, so $\w\cdot(\x - \x') = 0$. Second, if you step a distance $t$ along the unit vector $\w/\norm{\w}$, the score changes by exactly $t\,\norm{\w}$. So a point whose score is $s$ is $|s|/\norm{\w}$ away from the place where the score is zero.

      The distance from a point $\x_0$ to the hyperplane $\w\cdot\x + b = 0$ is $$\text{dist} = \frac{|\w\cdot\x_0 + b|}{\norm{\w}}.$$ Example: from $(3, 4)$ to $3x_1 + 4x_2 - 5 = 0$ the distance is $\frac{|9 + 16 - 5|}{\sqrt{9 + 16}} = \frac{20}{5} = 4$.

      The margin and the support vectors

      Multiplying $\w$ and $b$ by the same positive number gives the same line, so we are free to fix the scale. The SVM convention: scale them so that the training points closest to the line have score exactly $+1$ (on the positive side) or $-1$ (on the negative side). Every training point then satisfies $y_i(\w\cdot\x_i + b) \ge 1$.

      With that scale, the closest points are $1/\norm{\w}$ from the boundary, and the empty “street” between the lines $\w\cdot\x + b = +1$ and $\w\cdot\x + b = -1$ is $2/\norm{\w}$ wide. That width is the margin. The training points lying exactly on the two edges of the street are the support vectors: they “support” the street the way pillars hold up a roof.

      For training data $(\x_i, y_i)$ with $y_i \in \{+1, -1\}$, the hard-margin SVM solves $$\min_{\w,\,b}\ \tfrac12\norm{\w}^2 \quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i(\w\cdot\x_i + b) \ge 1 \text{ for every } i.$$ Making $\norm{\w}$ small makes the margin $2/\norm{\w}$ large. The constraints say every point is on its correct side, at least on the edge of the street. The support vectors are the points with $y_i(\w\cdot\x_i + b) = 1$.

      Careful with the word “margin”: some books use it for the distance from the boundary to the nearest point, $1/\norm{\w}$. GATE DA 2025 Q53 uses the full street width $2/\norm{\w}$. If both appear in the options, read the question’s wording; if only one fits, that tells you the convention.

      The solution can be written $\w = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i \x_i$ with weights $\alpha_i \ge 0$, and $\alpha_i \gt 0$ only for support vectors. Moving or deleting a point that is not a support vector (while it stays outside the street) leaves $\w$, $b$ and the margin unchanged.

      Try it

      Choose “Your direction” and turn the slider: for each direction of $\w$ the widget draws the widest street that direction allows. Find the angle with the widest street, then switch to “Maximum margin” to compare. Drag a point that is not ringed: nothing moves until it enters the street. Drag one into the other cloud and the data stops being separable. Finally load “2025 Q53” and “2024 Q17” and read off $\w$, $b$, the margin and the points on the margin lines.

      GATE DA 2025 · Q53 · MSQ · 2 marks

      Consider designing a linear binary classifier $f(x) = \text{sign}(w^\top x + b)$, $x \in \R^2$ on the following training data:

      Class-1: $\left\{\begin{pmatrix}2\\0\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}0\\2\end{pmatrix}, \begin{pmatrix}2\\2\end{pmatrix}\right\}$, Class-2: $\left\{\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}\right\}$

      Hard-margin support vector machine (SVM) formulation is solved to obtain $w$ and $b$. Which of the following options is/are correct?

      1. $w = \begin{pmatrix}4\\4\end{pmatrix}$ and $b = 1$
      2. The number of support vectors is 3
      3. The margin is $\sqrt2$
      4. Training accuracy is 98%

      1. Picture it. Class-1 is $(2,0)$, $(0,2)$, $(2,2)$; Class-2 is the origin. Take Class-1 as $y = +1$. The Class-1 points nearest the origin are $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$, both on the line $x_1 + x_2 = 2$; $(2,2)$ is farther out, on $x_1 + x_2 = 4$.

        The support vectors are the points closest to the other class, so find those first.

      2. The widest street runs between the origin (on $x_1 + x_2 = 0$) and the line $x_1 + x_2 = 2$. So $\w$ points along $(1, 1)$ and the boundary is halfway: $x_1 + x_2 = 1$.

        No street can be wider: the origin is $\sqrt2$ from the point $(1,1)$, the midpoint of $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$, and any separating street must fit between them.

      3. Fix the scale: $\w = c(1,1)$ with score $-1$ at $(0,0)$ and $+1$ at $(2,0)$: $b = -1$ and $2c - 1 = 1$, so $c = 1$. Hence $\w = (1, 1)$, $b = -1$.

        The SVM scale puts the nearest points of each class at scores $\pm1$.

      4. Scores: $(2,0)$ and $(0,2)$ give $+1$, $(0,0)$ gives $-1$, $(2,2)$ gives $+3$. Three points on the margin lines, so three support vectors: (B) is true.

        A support vector is a point with $y_i(\w\cdot\x_i + b) = 1$ exactly.

      5. Margin $= 2/\norm{\w} = 2/\sqrt2 = \sqrt2$: (C) is true. Check with the distance formula: $(0,0)$ is $|0 + 0 - 1|/\sqrt2 = 1/\sqrt2$ from the boundary, and the street is twice that.

        This question calls the full street width the margin.

      6. (A) is false: with $\w = (4,4)$, $b = 1$, the origin scores $+1$, the same sign as Class-1, so it is misclassified (and the scale is wrong too). (D) is false: the data are separable and a hard-margin SVM classifies every training point correctly, so training accuracy is 100%.

        Hard margin means no training point may be on the wrong side. Official key: B; C.

      When no line works: soft margins and kernels

      A dataset is linearly separable if some hyperplane has every positive point on one side and every negative point on the other. The hard-margin SVM only has a solution for separable data.

      A quick test for “not separable”: if a point of one class is an average of points of the other class (it sits inside their convex hull, the region you get by stretching a rubber band around them), no line can separate them. The score $\w\cdot\x + b$ of an average is the average of the scores, so it cannot have the opposite sign to all of them.

      Allow each point a slack $\xi_i \ge 0$ (how far it is allowed to violate the street) and pay for it: $$\min_{\w,\,b,\,\xi}\ \tfrac12\norm{\w}^2 + C\sum_i \xi_i \quad\text{subject to}\quad y_i(\w\cdot\x_i + b) \ge 1 - \xi_i,\ \ \xi_i \ge 0.$$ $\xi_i = 0$: on the correct side, outside the street. $0 \lt \xi_i \le 1$: inside the street but still correct. $\xi_i \gt 1$: misclassified.

      The hyperparameter $C$ sets the price of violations. Large $C$: violations are expensive, so the street narrows to avoid them (as $C \to \infty$ on separable data you get the hard margin). Small $C$: a wider street that tolerates more violations, usually less overfitting.

      The other way out is to add features. A kernel lets the SVM work as if each point $\x$ had been mapped to a longer feature vector $\phi(\x)$, without ever building that vector: the SVM only ever needs dot products between points, and a kernel function $k(\x, \z) = \phi(\x)\cdot\phi(\z)$ supplies them directly. A straight boundary in the new features is a curved boundary in the original ones.

      Linear: $k(\x, \z) = \x\cdot\z$ (the plain SVM). Polynomial: $k(\x, \z) = (\x\cdot\z + c)^p$. RBF (Gaussian): $k(\x, \z) = \exp(-\gamma\norm{\x - \z}^2)$. Example: in two dimensions $(\x\cdot\z)^2 = \phi(\x)\cdot\phi(\z)$ with $\phi(\x) = (x_1^2,\ \sqrt2\,x_1x_2,\ x_2^2)$, so the kernel computes a dot product in three dimensions while only touching two.

      Go deeper: the dual problem and the hinge loss

      The hard-margin problem has an equivalent “dual” form in the weights $\alpha_i$: maximise $\sum_i \alpha_i - \tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j y_i y_j\,\x_i\cdot\x_j$ subject to $\alpha_i \ge 0$ and $\sum_i \alpha_i y_i = 0$. The data enter only through dot products $\x_i\cdot\x_j$, which is exactly why kernels can be swapped in. Points with $\alpha_i \gt 0$ are the support vectors. When several points lie on the margin lines (2024 Q17 has four), a solver may give positive weight to only some of them; all of them are on the margin and are usually called support vectors.

      The soft-margin problem is the same as minimising $\tfrac12\norm{\w}^2 + C\sum_i \max(0,\ 1 - y_i(\w\cdot\x_i + b))$. The term $\max(0, 1 - y\,s)$ is the hinge loss: zero for points safely outside the street, growing linearly with the violation.

      An SVM has $\w = (3, 4)$ and $b = -5$, already scaled so that the support vectors have scores $\pm1$. Find the distance of the point $(3, 4)$ from the boundary, and the margin $2/\norm{\w}$.

      $\norm{\w} = 5$. The score of $(3,4)$ is $9 + 16 - 5$.

      Distance $= |3\cdot3 + 4\cdot4 - 5|/5 = 20/5 = 4$. Margin $= 2/5 = 0.4$. A bigger $\norm{\w}$ always means a narrower street.

      GATE DA 2024 · Q17 · MCQ · 1 mark

      Consider the dataset with six datapoints: $\{(\x_1, \y_1), (\x_2, \y_2), \ldots, (\x_6, \y_6)\}$, where $\x_1 = \begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}$, $\x_2 = \begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}$, $\x_3 = \begin{bmatrix}0\\-1\end{bmatrix}$, $\x_4 = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\0\end{bmatrix}$, $\x_5 = \begin{bmatrix}2\\2\end{bmatrix}$, $\x_6 = \begin{bmatrix}-2\\-2\end{bmatrix}$ and the labels are given by $\y_1 = \y_2 = \y_5 = 1$, and $\y_3 = \y_4 = \y_6 = -1$. A hard margin linear support vector machine is trained on the above dataset.

      Which ONE of the following sets is a possible set of support vectors?

      1. $\{\x_1, \x_2, \x_5\}$
      2. $\{\x_3, \x_4, \x_5\}$
      3. $\{\x_4, \x_5\}$
      4. $\{\x_1, \x_2, \x_3, \x_4\}$

      Plot the six points. The positive points nearest the negatives are $\x_1$ and $\x_2$, on the line $x_1 + x_2 = 1$. Where are the nearest negative points?

      The positives $\x_1, \x_2$ lie on $x_1 + x_2 = 1$ and the negatives $\x_3, \x_4$ on $x_1 + x_2 = -1$; $\x_5$ and $\x_6$ are far out, on $x_1 + x_2 = \pm4$. The widest street is between those two lines: $\w = (1, 1)$, $b = 0$, and the scores are $\x_1, \x_2: +1$; $\x_3, \x_4: -1$; $\x_5: +4$; $\x_6: -4$. The margin is $2/\sqrt2 = \sqrt2$.

      The points on the margin lines are $\x_1, \x_2, \x_3, \x_4$, so (D). Every other option contains $\x_5$, which is $4/\sqrt2 \approx 2.83$ from the boundary, well outside the street; a point that far away cannot be a support vector. Official key: D.

      GATE DA 2024 · Q53 · MSQ · 2 marks

      Consider the following figures representing datasets consisting of two-dimensional features with two classes denoted by circles and squares.

      Which of the following is/are TRUE?

      1. (i) is linearly separable.
      2. (ii) is linearly separable.
      3. (iii) is linearly separable.
      4. (iv) is linearly separable.

      (Figure redrawn from the paper; positions read from the printed grids.)

      Try to draw a line for each picture. For the ones where you can’t, look for a point of one class that is an average of points of the other class.

      (i) The line $x_2 = x_1 - 0.5$ has all three circles above it and all three squares below it: separable.

      (ii) The circle $(2,2)$ is the midpoint of the squares $(1,2)$ and $(3,2)$. Any linear score at $(2,2)$ is the average of the scores at those two squares, so it has their sign: not separable.

      (iii) This is the XOR pattern. $(2,2)$ is the midpoint of the two circles and also of the two squares, so its score would have to be both positive and negative: not separable.

      (iv) The same line $x_2 = x_1 - 0.5$ has the three squares above and the three circles below: separable.

      Answer: A; D. Official key: A; D.

      GATE DA 2024 sample paper · Q29 · MCQ · 2 marks

      A maximum margin linear SVM (SVM1) is learned for a binary classification task. Another maximum margin linear SVM (SVM2) is trained for the same task using the same training set but with one of the non-support vectors of SVM1 removed. Which one of the following statements is TRUE?

      1. Margin of SVM1 > Margin of SVM2
      2. Margin of SVM2 > Margin of SVM1
      3. Margin of SVM1 = Margin of SVM2
      4. No conclusion can be drawn between the margins of SVM1 and SVM2

      Which training points does the SVM solution actually depend on?

      The SVM solution depends only on the support vectors: solving the problem with just their constraints gives the same street, and every other point was strictly outside it. SVM2 still has all of SVM1’s support vectors, and its street is still valid for the reduced data. So SVM2 finds the same $\w$, $b$ and margin: (C). (Sample paper, no official key; this is our answer.)

      (A) and (B) would need the solution to depend on a point with $\alpha_i = 0$. (D) is the guess for when you don’t remember that only support vectors matter.

      Positive class: $(4,1)$, $(3,3)$, $(5,4)$. Negative class: $(0,0)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,0)$. A hard-margin linear SVM is trained. Find the margin $2/\norm{\w}$ (round to two decimal places) and the number of training points that lie exactly on the margin lines.

      Try the direction $\w \propto (2, 1)$ and compute $2x_1 + x_2$ for every point. For an upper bound on any margin, find the distance between the midpoint of two negative points and the midpoint of two positive points.

      Scores $2x_1 + x_2$: negatives $0, 4, 4$; positives $9, 9, 14$. In the unit direction $(2,1)/\sqrt5$ the classes are separated by a gap of $(9 - 4)/\sqrt5 = \sqrt5$.

      No street can be wider. The midpoint of the negatives $(1,2)$ and $(2,0)$ is $(1.5, 1)$; the midpoint of the positives $(4,1)$ and $(3,3)$ is $(3.5, 2)$. Any separating street must fit between these two points, which are $\sqrt{2^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt5$ apart.

      Scaling: $\w = c(2,1)$ with $4c + b = -1$ and $9c + b = 1$ gives $c = 0.4$, $b = -2.6$, so $\w = (0.8, 0.4)$ and $2/\norm{\w} = 2/\sqrt{0.8} = \sqrt5 \approx$ 2.24.

      Points with score exactly $\pm1$: $(1,2)$, $(2,0)$, $(4,1)$, $(3,3)$, so 4. The tempting slips: using $1/\norm{\w} \approx 1.12$ (half the street), or taking the closest pair of opposite points, $(2,0)$ and $(4,1)$, also $\sqrt5$ apart, and stopping at 2 support vectors without checking the other scores.

      For a soft-margin linear SVM with penalty $C$ and slacks $\xi_i$, which statements are true?

      1. On linearly separable data, as $C \to \infty$ the solution approaches the hard-margin SVM.
      2. Increasing $C$ typically makes the margin wider.
      3. A training point with $\xi_i \gt 1$ is misclassified.
      4. A point strictly outside the street on its correct side has $\xi_i = 0$, and moving it a little (staying outside) does not change $\w$.

      $C$ is the price per unit of violation. What does the optimiser do when violations become very expensive?

      (A) True: infinitely expensive slack forces every $\xi_i = 0$, which is the hard-margin problem. (B) False: larger $C$ punishes violations more, so the street usually narrows to avoid them; small $C$ gives the wider street. (C) True: $y_i(\w\cdot\x_i + b) \ge 1 - \xi_i$ with the smallest allowed slack means the score has the wrong sign when $\xi_i \gt 1$. (D) True: such a point has $\alpha_i = 0$, so it does not appear in $\w = \sum\alpha_i y_i \x_i$. Answer: A; C; D.

      The XOR data: circles at $(1,1)$ and $(3,3)$, squares at $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$. You add one new feature $z$ and train a linear SVM on $(x_1, x_2, z)$. Which choice of $z$ makes the data linearly separable?

      1. $z = x_1 + x_2$
      2. $z = (x_1 - 2)(x_2 - 2)$
      3. $z = x_1 - x_2$
      4. $z = x_1^2$

      A feature that is a linear combination of $x_1$ and $x_2$ adds nothing a line couldn’t already do. For the others, compute $z$ at all four points.

      (B): $z = (-1)(-1) = 1$ at $(1,1)$ and $1\cdot1 = 1$ at $(3,3)$, but $z = -1$ at $(1,3)$ and $(3,1)$. The plane $z = 0$ separates them.

      (A) and (C) are linear in $x_1, x_2$, so any linear rule in $(x_1, x_2, z)$ is still a linear rule in $(x_1, x_2)$, and XOR is not linearly separable. (D) fails too: a rule $a x_1 + c x_2 + e x_1^2 + d$ at $x_1 = 1$ needs $c \lt 0$ (circle at $x_2 = 1$ above, square at $x_2 = 3$ below), while at $x_1 = 3$ it needs $c \gt 0$. Answer (B). A degree-2 polynomial kernel contains exactly this product $x_1x_2$.

      • Sketch the points; the support vectors are the ones nearest the other class.
      • Fix the scale so the support vectors score exactly $\pm1$, then use $2/\norm{\w}$.
      • Check every point’s score at the end: all positives $\ge 1$, all negatives $\le -1$.
      • Reporting $1/\norm{\w}$ when the question means the full street width (or the reverse).
      • Believing a far-away point can be a support vector, or that deleting it changes the margin.
      • Saying "large $C$ means a wider margin": it is the other way round.
      1. Distance from x₀ to the hyperplane w·x + b = 0 is |w·x₀ + b| / ‖w‖.
      2. The SVM scales w, b so the nearest points score ±1 and minimises ½‖w‖²; the margin is 2/‖w‖ and the points on the margin lines are the support vectors, the only points that matter.
      3. Not separable? A soft margin (penalty C: large C, narrow street) or a kernel (a linear boundary in new features) handles it.

      Many straight lines separate two clouds of points. Which one does a hard-margin SVM pick?

      The one through the midpoint of the two class means
      That uses every point equally. The SVM’s line depends only on the points nearest the other class.
      The one with the fewest misclassified points
      All separating lines make zero mistakes, so that doesn’t pick one out.
      The one farthest from the nearest points of both classes
      It maximises the margin, the width of the empty street around the line.
      The one that passes closest to the most points
      The SVM wants to stay as far from the points as possible.

      An SVM has $\w = (6, 8)$, scaled so the support vectors score $\pm1$. Its margin $2/\norm{\w}$ is

      0.1
      That is $1/\norm{\w}$, the distance to one edge only.
      2
      Divide by the length of $\w$.
      10
      That is $\norm{\w}$ itself.
      0.2
      $\norm{\w} = \sqrt{36 + 64} = 10$, so $2/10 = 0.2$.

      What does the kernel trick let an SVM do?

      Use dot products in a richer feature space without building those features
      The SVM only needs $\phi(\x)\cdot\phi(\z)$, and the kernel computes it directly.
      Skip the optimisation and pick the support vectors directly
      The optimisation still has to be solved; only the dot products change.
      Remove the need for labels
      An SVM is still a supervised method.
      Guarantee zero test error
      A flexible kernel can make it easier to overfit.

      Decision trees: twenty questions, learned from data

      A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about the features, each answer sending you down one branch until you reach a leaf that holds the prediction.

      GATE DA 2024 Q62 (2 marks) asked for the information gain of one attribute in a ten-row cricket table: entropy, a weighted average and a subtraction. Expect that kind of calculation, plus questions on overfitting.

      It’s like a doctor’s checklist: “Fever? Yes. Rash? No. Cough? Yes. Then probably flu.” Each question is chosen to rule out as much as possible.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      Entropy and information gain from a small table; sometimes Gini, overfitting or what a tree can guarantee.

      2024 Q62 · InformationGain(C, Pitch)
      Heat: 1 numerical question in 3 papers, 2 marks; pure arithmetic once the formula is fixed
      DPL story

      The Kalinga Kernels’ coach wants a rule for predicting their own matches. From last season they write a flowchart: “Did we lose more than 2 wickets in the powerplay? If no, we usually win. If yes, were the powerplay runs above 50? …” Each question splits the past matches into two groups, and a good question makes each group as one-sided as possible, nearly all wins or nearly all losses.

      Vocabulary: each question is a node (the first one is the root); each answer is a branch; a node with no more questions is a leaf and predicts the majority label of the training examples that reach it. The number of questions on the longest path is the tree’s depth.

      The learning problem is choosing the questions. We need a number for “how mixed is this group?”, called impurity, and then we pick the question that reduces it most.

      For a group $S$ in which a fraction $p_k$ of the examples has class $k$:

      Entropy (in bits): $$H(S) = -\sum_k p_k \log_2 p_k \qquad (\text{with } 0\log_2 0 = 0).$$ Gini impurity: $$G(S) = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2.$$ Both are 0 for a pure group (one class only) and largest for an even mix. With two classes: $H$ ranges from 0 to 1, $G$ from 0 to 0.5. Example: 3 wins and 1 loss gives $H = -\tfrac34\log_2\tfrac34 - \tfrac14\log_2\tfrac14 \approx 0.811$ and $G = 1 - \tfrac{9}{16} - \tfrac{1}{16} = 0.375$.

      Splitting $S$ on attribute $A$ creates subgroups $S_v$, one for each value $v$ of $A$. The information gain is the drop in entropy: $$\text{IG}(S, A) = H(S) - \sum_v \frac{|S_v|}{|S|}\,H(S_v).$$ The children’s entropies are weighted by their sizes, so a tiny pure child doesn’t count for much. With Gini instead of entropy, the same difference is the Gini decrease.

      1. If all examples at the node have the same label (or no attributes remain, or a size or depth limit is reached), make a leaf with the majority label.
      2. Otherwise compute the information gain of every attribute (for a numeric feature, of every threshold between consecutive sorted values) and split on the best.
      3. Repeat on each child with the examples that reach it.

      This is greedy: at each node it takes the best split right now and never revisits it, so the final tree is not guaranteed to be the best possible tree.

      Try it

      Sixteen Kernels matches (circles won, squares lost). Slide the threshold and watch the counts on each side, their impurities and the gain; the lower chart shows the gain for every threshold at once. Compare “Split on runs” with “Split on wickets” and press “Jump to the best split” for each: the root question is the one with the higher peak. Switch to Gini and check that the best split stays the same here.

      $H$ of a two-class group with minority share: $\tfrac12 \to 1$; $\tfrac25 \to 0.971$; $\tfrac13 \to 0.918$; $\tfrac14 \to 0.811$; $\tfrac15 \to 0.722$; $\tfrac18 \to 0.544$; $0 \to 0$. Most exam tables use these fractions, which saves several logarithms.

      GATE DA 2024 · Q62 · NAT · 2 marks

      Details of ten international cricket games between two teams “Green” and “Blue” are given in Table C. This table consists of matches played on different pitches, across formats along with their winners. The attribute Pitch can take one of two values: spin-friendly (represented as $S$) or pace-friendly (represented as $F$). The attribute Format can take one of two values: one-day match (represented as $O$) or test match (represented as $T$).

      A cricket organization would like to use the information given in Table C to develop a decision-tree model to predict outcomes of future games between these two teams.

      To develop such a model, the computed InformationGain(C, Pitch) with respect to the Target is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).

      Table C
      Match NumberPitchFormatWinner (Target)
      1$S$$T$Green
      2$S$$T$Blue
      3$F$$O$Blue
      4$S$$O$Blue
      5$F$$T$Green
      6$F$$O$Blue
      7$S$$O$Green
      8$F$$T$Blue
      9$F$$O$Blue
      10$S$$O$Green

      1. Whole table: Green won matches 1, 5, 7, 10 (4 wins) and Blue the other 6. $H(C) = -0.4\log_2 0.4 - 0.6\log_2 0.6 \approx 0.971$.

        Information gain starts from the entropy before any split.

      2. Pitch $= S$: matches 1, 2, 4, 7, 10, winners Green, Blue, Blue, Green, Green: 3 Green, 2 Blue. $H = 0.971$ (minority share $\tfrac25$).

        Filter the rows by the attribute value, then count the target.

      3. Pitch $= F$: matches 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, winners Blue, Green, Blue, Blue, Blue: 1 Green, 4 Blue. $H = -0.2\log_2 0.2 - 0.8\log_2 0.8 \approx 0.722$.

        Minority share $\tfrac15$, one of the values in the shortcut box.

      4. Weighted entropy after the split: $\tfrac{5}{10}(0.971) + \tfrac{5}{10}(0.722) \approx 0.846$.

        Each child is weighted by its share of the rows: 5 of 10 each.

      5. $\text{IG}(C, \text{Pitch}) = 0.971 - 0.846 \approx$ 0.12 (more precisely 0.1245).

        Official key: 0.12 to 0.13. For comparison, Format gives only $0.971 - (0.4\cdot1 + 0.6\cdot0.918) \approx 0.02$, so a tree would ask about Pitch first.

      When trees go wrong: overfitting and pruning

      Keep splitting and every leaf eventually holds one example, so the tree is 100% right on the training data (unless two identical rows disagree). But the deep questions are fitting accidents of last season, not patterns: high variance, in the language of Part 2. Typical symptom: training accuracy near 100%, test accuracy much lower.

      Two remedies. Pre-pruning stops early: a maximum depth, a minimum number of examples per leaf, or a minimum gain for a split. Post-pruning grows the full tree and then removes subtrees whose removal does not hurt accuracy on held-out data (choose the amount by cross-validation).

      Information gain also has a blind spot: it favours attributes with many values. Splitting Table C on “Match Number” gives ten pure leaves, so its gain is the full 0.971, yet it says nothing about future matches. The gain ratio divides the gain by the entropy of the split itself to penalise this.

      With numeric features each question is “feature ≤ threshold?”, so a tree cuts the plane into rectangles with sides parallel to the axes. A diagonal boundary needs many small steps.

      A leaf holds 3 wins and 1 loss. What is its entropy in bits? (Round to two decimal places.)

      $p = \tfrac34$ and $\tfrac14$. $\log_2\tfrac14 = -2$ and $\log_2\tfrac34 \approx -0.415$.

      $H = -\tfrac34(-0.415) - \tfrac14(-2) = 0.311 + 0.5 \approx$ 0.81.

      A node holds 6 wins and 2 losses. What is its Gini impurity?

      $1 - (\tfrac68)^2 - (\tfrac28)^2$.

      $1 - 0.5625 - 0.0625 = $ 0.375. A pure node would give 0; a 4–4 node, 0.5.

      A node has 8 wins and 8 losses. Split A gives children (6 wins, 2 losses) and (2 wins, 6 losses). Split B gives children (8 wins, 4 losses) and (0 wins, 4 losses). Which split has the higher information gain?

      Parent entropy is 1. Use $H(\tfrac14) = 0.811$ and $H(\tfrac13) = 0.918$, and weight by child size.

      A: $1 - \tfrac12(0.811) - \tfrac12(0.811) = 0.189$. B: $1 - \tfrac{12}{16}(0.918) - \tfrac{4}{16}(0) = 1 - 0.689 = 0.311$. Split B wins: a completely pure child is worth a lot. (Gini agrees: decreases 0.125 and 0.167.)

      A fully grown tree is 100% accurate on the training matches but only 68% accurate on new matches. Which change is most likely to help?

      What does the gap between training and test accuracy tell you?

      The gap signals overfitting, so make the tree simpler: limit the depth or prune the tree. Growing deeper makes it worse; entropy and Gini usually choose nearly the same splits; and the test set is how you noticed the problem.

      Using Table C from the worked example, the root splits on Pitch. Within the Pitch $= F$ branch only, what is the information gain of splitting on Format? (Round to two decimal places.)

      The $F$ rows are matches 3, 5, 6, 8, 9. Split them by Format and count winners in each part.

      The $F$ branch has 1 Green and 4 Blue, so $H = 0.722$.

      Format $T$: matches 5 (Green) and 8 (Blue), $H = 1$. Format $O$: matches 3, 6, 9, all Blue, $H = 0$.

      $\text{IG} = 0.722 - \left(\tfrac25\cdot1 + \tfrac35\cdot0\right) = 0.722 - 0.4 \approx$ 0.32.

      Two slips to avoid: using the whole table’s entropy 0.971 as the parent (that gives 0.57), and forgetting the weights $\tfrac25$, $\tfrac35$. Note that Format looked useless at the root (gain 0.02) but is useful inside this branch, which is why trees recompute gains at every node.

      Eight matches, by powerplay runs, with results: 10 L, 20 L, 30 W, 40 L, 50 L, 60 W, 70 W, 80 W. Candidate thresholds are midpoints between consecutive values, and the rule is “runs ≤ t”. Which threshold gives the lowest weighted Gini impurity of the two children, and what is that weighted Gini?

      Check $t = 25$, $45$ and $55$ carefully. The parent Gini is 0.5.

      $t = 25$: left (0 W, 2 L) has $G = 0$; right (4 W, 2 L) has $G = 1 - \tfrac49 - \tfrac19 = \tfrac49$. Weighted: $\tfrac68\cdot\tfrac49 \approx 0.333$.

      $t = 45$: (1 W, 3 L) and (3 W, 1 L), each $G = 0.375$. Weighted 0.375.

      $t = 55$: left (1 W, 4 L) has $G = 1 - 0.04 - 0.64 = 0.32$; right (3 W, 0 L) is pure. Weighted: $\tfrac58\cdot0.32 =$ 0.2, the lowest of all seven thresholds (the others give 0.429, 0.467, 0.333, 0.429). Best threshold 55.

      The tempting answer is 25 because its left child is pure, but that child holds only 2 of 8 matches; at 55 the pure side holds 3 and the other side is nearly pure.

      Which statements are true?

      1. A node whose examples are spread equally over $m$ classes has entropy $\log_2 m$ bits.
      2. The information gain of a split is never negative.
      3. Splitting on an attribute that is unique to every row (such as a match ID) gives the maximum possible information gain, yet is useless for prediction.
      4. The Gini impurity of a two-class node can exceed 0.5.

      For (D), find the largest value of $1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2$.

      (A) True: each $p_k = 1/m$, so $H = -m\cdot\tfrac1m\log_2\tfrac1m = \log_2 m$ (3 classes: 1.585 bits). (B) True: the weighted average of the children’s entropies never exceeds the parent’s (entropy is concave), so the gain is at least 0. (C) True: every child is pure, so the gain equals $H(S)$, the most possible; but a new match has a new ID that no branch covers. (D) False: $1 - p^2 - (1-p)^2 = 2p(1-p)$, at most 0.5 at $p = \tfrac12$. Answer: A; B; C.

      • Count the target in each child carefully: tabulate (value, wins, losses) before any logarithms.
      • Weight each child’s entropy by its share of the rows.
      • Recompute gains inside each branch; an attribute weak at the root can be strong lower down.
      • Forgetting to subtract from the parent entropy (reporting the weighted entropy as the gain).
      • Using natural logs when the question means bits ($\log_2$).
      • Trusting a deep tree because its training accuracy is 100%.
      1. Entropy H = −Σ p log₂ p and Gini 1 − Σ p² measure how mixed a node is: 0 when pure, largest when evenly mixed (1 and 0.5 for two classes).
      2. Information gain = parent entropy − size-weighted child entropies; a tree greedily splits on the attribute with the largest gain.
      3. Fully grown trees overfit; limit depth or prune, and beware attributes with many values.

      Which group of matches is the most “impure” (hardest to predict with one label)?

      10 wins, 0 losses
      One label fits every match: that’s a pure group.
      9 wins, 1 loss
      Predicting “win” is right 90% of the time. Look for the most even mix.
      5 wins, 5 losses
      An even split is the most uncertain: entropy 1 bit, Gini 0.5.
      7 wins, 3 losses
      Mixed, but still leaning to wins. One option is more balanced.

      The entropy (base 2) of a node with 4 wins and 4 losses is

      0
      That’s for a pure node.
      0.5
      That’s its Gini impurity, not its entropy.
      1
      $-\tfrac12\log_2\tfrac12 - \tfrac12\log_2\tfrac12 = 1$ bit.
      2
      With two classes, entropy is at most 1 bit.

      A tree scores 100% on its training data and 68% on new data. Pruning it will most likely

      raise the training accuracy
      It’s already 100%; a smaller tree can only match or lower it.
      lower the training accuracy a little and raise the test accuracy
      Pruning removes branches that fit noise: a little worse on training data, better on new data.
      leave both unchanged
      Removing branches changes some predictions.
      lower both
      That happens only if you prune far too much. The gap here signals overfitting.

      All training points are distinct. A 1-NN classifier is evaluated on its own training set. Its error is

      about 50%
      Each training point has a neighbour at distance 0.
      0
      Each point’s nearest neighbour is itself, with its own label.
      the same as its test error
      Training error is usually much lower than test error for 1-NN.
      impossible to say without k-fold cross-validation
      Think about which training point is nearest to a training point.

      An SVM has boundary $x_1 + x_2 - 1 = 0$ with $\w = (1, 1)$, $b = -1$. How far is the point $(2, 2)$ from the boundary?

      3
      That’s the score $\w\cdot\x + b$. Divide by $\norm{\w}$.
      $\sqrt2$
      That’s the margin $2/\norm{\w}$, not this point’s distance.
      $3/\sqrt2 \approx 2.12$
      $|2 + 2 - 1|/\sqrt{1 + 1} = 3/\sqrt2$.
      $2\sqrt2$
      That’s the distance from the origin to $(2, 2)$.

      Which training points determine a hard-margin SVM’s boundary?

      All of them, equally
      Points far from the boundary can move without changing it.
      The points farthest from the boundary
      Those are the ones that matter least.
      The class means
      That describes a nearest-mean classifier, not an SVM.
      Only the support vectors on the margin lines
      $\w = \sum\alpha_i y_i\x_i$ with $\alpha_i \gt 0$ only for support vectors.

      A parent node has entropy 1. A split creates two equal-sized children with entropies 0.5 and 0.3. The information gain is

      0.2
      Subtract the weighted average of the children, not their difference.
      0.6
      $1 - (0.5\cdot0.5 + 0.5\cdot0.3) = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6$.
      0.4
      That’s the weighted child entropy. The gain is what’s left after subtracting it from the parent.
      0.2 or 0.6 depending on the class labels
      The formula only needs the entropies and the sizes.

      Which classifier’s decision boundary is always a single hyperplane (a straight line in two dimensions)?

      1-nearest neighbour
      Its boundary is made of many pieces of bisectors.
      A decision tree of depth 3
      It makes axis-parallel staircases.
      Logistic regression on the raw features
      It predicts by the sign of $\w\cdot\x + b$, like a linear SVM.
      An SVM with an RBF kernel
      The kernel makes the boundary curved in the original features.

      A neural network is many small logistic-regression-like units wired in layers. This part builds one from a single neuron, shows why the activation function is what makes depth worth having, counts a network’s parameters the way GATE asks, and then trains it: gradient descent, its stochastic version, and backpropagation, which is the chain rule applied carefully.

      You need: loss functions and linear regression (Part 1), logistic regression and the perceptron update (Part 3), the dot product (refreshers) and the chain rule (refreshers: derivatives).

      Neurons and feed-forward networks: stacking simple units

      A neural network passes its input through layers of neurons; each neuron takes a weighted sum of what it receives, adds a bias, and applies a simple non-linear function.

      GATE DA asks about the structure more than the training: 2024 Q43 asked when a ReLU network equals a single neuron, and 2026 Q56 and sample Q43 asked you to count a network’s learnable parameters. Each of these is 2 marks and takes a minute once you see the pattern.

      It’s like a selection committee: each selector scores the players on a few weighted criteria, the chair combines the selectors’ verdicts, and the final decision depends on the whole chain, not on any one person.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      Network structure: forward passes through ReLU layers, equivalent networks, and counting weights and biases.

      2024 Q43 · equivalent ReLU networks2026 Q56 · parameters, no biasesSample Q43 · parameters with biases
      Heat: every paper, usually one 2-mark question

      The Nagpur Neural Nets’ analyst wants to predict, partway through a chase, whether the team will win. Two numbers seem to matter: $x_1$, the wickets still in hand, and $x_2$, the runs still needed per over. Each of these is a feature (an input measurement), and “won” or “lost” is the label (the answer we want to predict), as in Part 1.

      Recall logistic regression from Part 3: weight each feature, add a constant, and squash the total into a probability. Suppose the weights are $0.8$ for wickets and $-0.5$ for the required rate, and the constant is $1$. With 6 wickets in hand and 9 runs an over needed, the total is $0.8\times6 - 0.5\times9 + 1 = 1.3$, and the squashing function turns 1.3 into about $0.79$: a 79% chance of winning.

      That single calculation is one neuron. A neural network is nothing more than many of them, with the outputs of some becoming the inputs of others.

      A neuron with inputs $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ computes $$z = w_1x_1 + \cdots + w_nx_n + b = \mathbf{w}\T\x + b, \qquad a = g(z).$$ The numbers $w_i$ are its weights (how much each input counts), $b$ is its bias (a constant that shifts the threshold), $z$ is the pre-activation and $g$ is the activation function. The output $a$ is called the activation. Weights and biases are the parameters: the numbers training adjusts.

      Step (the perceptron of Part 3): $g(z) = 1$ if $z \ge 0$, else $0$.
      Sigmoid: $\sigma(z) = \dfrac{1}{1+e^{-z}}$, output strictly between 0 and 1, $\sigma(0) = 0.5$. Logistic regression is one sigmoid neuron.
      ReLU (rectified linear unit): $\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = \max(0, z)$. It passes positive values unchanged and replaces negative ones by 0. Example: $\mathrm{ReLU}(3) = 3$, $\mathrm{ReLU}(-2) = 0$.
      Identity (no activation): $g(z) = z$.

      Why one neuron is not enough

      A single neuron with a step or sigmoid activation decides by the sign of $\mathbf{w}\T\x + b$. The boundary $\mathbf{w}\T\x + b = 0$ is a straight line in two dimensions (a hyperplane in general: a flat cut through the feature space). Some patterns cannot be split by one straight line.

      The classic example is XOR (“exclusive or”): the output is 1 when exactly one of two yes/no inputs is 1. Put the four points (0,0), (1,0), (0,1), (1,1) on a grid: the two 1s sit on one diagonal and the two 0s on the other. No single line separates them, so no single perceptron learns XOR.

      The fix is to add a hidden layer: neurons between the inputs and the output whose values nobody labels. Each hidden neuron draws its own line; the output neuron combines them.

      Neurons are arranged in layers. The input layer just holds the features (it has no parameters); then come one or more hidden layers; the last is the output layer. In a fully connected layer every neuron receives every activation of the layer before. Information flows one way, input to output, with no loops: that’s what feed-forward means. A multi-layer perceptron (MLP) is such a network.

      The forward pass computes, layer by layer, with $\a^{(0)} = \x$: $$\z^{(l)} = W^{(l)}\a^{(l-1)} + \b^{(l)}, \qquad \a^{(l)} = g\big(\z^{(l)}\big),$$ where $W^{(l)}$ has one row per neuron in layer $l$ and one column per neuron in layer $l-1$, and $g$ is applied to each entry.

      Try it

      This 2-2-1 network has hidden neurons $h_1 = \mathrm{ReLU}(x_1 + x_2)$ and $h_2 = \mathrm{ReLU}(x_1 + x_2 - 1)$, and outputs class 1 when $h_1 + v\,h_2 \gt 0.5$. With the default $v = -2$ it gets all four XOR points right. Drag the probe to follow the forward pass. Then switch to “No activation”: the shaded region becomes a half-plane and at least one XOR point is always wrong, whatever $v$ you choose.

      If every activation is the identity, a network with weight matrices $W^{(1)}, W^{(2)}, \ldots, W^{(L)}$ (and zero biases) computes $$W^{(L)}\cdots W^{(2)}W^{(1)}\x = M\x,$$ one matrix times $\x$: a single linear layer. With biases it is still one affine map $M\x + \mathbf{c}$. So the non-linear activation is what lets extra layers represent new shapes.

      Corollary for ReLU: if every pre-activation in the network is positive, every ReLU acts as the identity, and the network again collapses to $M\x$. With non-negative weights, zero biases and positive inputs, this always happens.

      When every ReLU stays active, the coefficient of input $x_i$ in the collapsed network is the sum, over every path from $x_i$ to the output, of the product of the weights on that path. If all weights in a layer are equal, this is (number of paths) × (product of one weight per layer).

      Counting parameters

      A fully connected layer from $m$ neurons to $n$ neurons has one weight per pair, so $m\times n$ weights, plus one bias per receiving neuron, so $n$ biases. Add this up over the layers. The sizes of the layers are hyperparameters (choices you make before training), not parameters.

      For layer sizes $n_0$ (inputs), $n_1, \ldots, n_L$ (output), $$\#\text{parameters} = \sum_{l=1}^{L} n_{l-1}\,n_l \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{l=1}^{L} n_l}_{\text{only if biases are used}} = \sum_{l=1}^{L} (n_{l-1}+1)\,n_l \text{ with biases}.$$ The input layer contributes no biases of its own.

      Try it

      Set the four layer sizes and switch biases on or off. The readout shows each layer’s weights and biases. Check the rule: with biases, each layer costs (inputs to it + 1) × (its neurons). Set a second hidden layer to 0 to remove it, and notice how the count changes.

      GATE DA 2024 · Q43 · MCQ · 2 marks

      Consider the two neural networks (NNs) shown in Figures 1 and 2, with $ReLU$ activation ($ReLU(z) = \max\{0, z\}, \forall z \in \mathbb{R}$). $\mathbb{R}$ denotes the set of real numbers. The connections and their corresponding weights are shown in the Figures. The biases at every neuron are set to 0. For what values of $p, q, r$ in Figure 2 are the two NNs equivalent, when $x_1, x_2, x_3$ are positive?

      Figure 1

      Figure 2

      1. $p = 36, q = 24, r = 24$
      2. $p = 24, q = 24, r = 36$
      3. $p = 18, q = 36, r = 24$
      4. $p = 36, q = 36, r = 36$

      1. Every weight is positive, every bias is 0 and every input is positive, so every pre-activation is positive and every ReLU acts as the identity.

        This is the corollary above: with nothing negative anywhere, $\max\{0, z\} = z$ at every neuron, so the network is linear on this region.

      2. First hidden layer: top $= x_1 + x_2$, middle $= x_1 + x_3$, bottom $= x_1 + x_2 + x_3$.

        Read the edges into each neuron: $x_1$ feeds all three, $x_2$ feeds top and bottom, $x_3$ feeds middle and bottom, all with weight 1.

      3. Each second-hidden neuron receives $2\times$(sum of the three) $= 2(3x_1 + 2x_2 + 2x_3)$.

        Every first-hidden neuron feeds both second-hidden neurons with weight 2, and the three sums add to $3x_1 + 2x_2 + 2x_3$.

      4. Output $= 3\cdot 2(3x_1 + 2x_2 + 2x_3) + 3\cdot 2(3x_1 + 2x_2 + 2x_3) = 36x_1 + 24x_2 + 24x_3$.

        Path check: $x_1$ reaches the output by $3\times2 = 6$ paths, each with weight product $1\cdot2\cdot3 = 6$, giving 36; $x_2$ and $x_3$ each have $2\times2 = 4$ paths, giving 24.

      5. Figure 2 outputs $\mathrm{ReLU}(px_1 + qx_2 + rx_3) = px_1 + qx_2 + rx_3$ for positive inputs and weights, so $p = 36$, $q = 24$, $r = 24$: (A).

        (B) swaps $x_1$ and $x_3$; (C) halves $x_1$’s coefficient; (D) treats all three inputs as if each fed three neurons. Official key: A.

      A network has inputs $\x = (2, -1)$, one hidden layer of two ReLU neurons with $$W^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 3\\ 3 & 1\end{pmatrix},\qquad \b^{(1)} = \begin{pmatrix}-1\\ -2\end{pmatrix},$$ and a linear output neuron $y = 2h_1 + 1\cdot h_2 + 0.5$. Find $y$.

      Compute $\z = W^{(1)}\x + \b^{(1)}$ first, then apply ReLU to each entry before the output layer.

      $z_1 = 1\cdot2 + 3\cdot(-1) - 1 = -2$, so $h_1 = \mathrm{ReLU}(-2) = 0$.

      $z_2 = 3\cdot2 + 1\cdot(-1) - 2 = 3$, so $h_2 = 3$.

      $y = 2\cdot0 + 3 + 0.5 = $ 3.5. Forgetting the ReLU would give $2(-2) + 3 + 0.5 = -0.5$.

      Which statements about activation functions are true? (Select all that apply.)

      (A) $\mathrm{ReLU}(z)$ is never negative.   (B) The sigmoid’s output lies strictly between 0 and 1.   (C) The derivative of ReLU at $z = -2$ is 1.   (D) $\sigma(0) = 0$.

      Sketch both functions. ReLU is flat on the negative side; the sigmoid crosses the vertical axis halfway between its two limits.

      (A) True: $\max(0, z) \ge 0$. (B) True: $e^{-z} \gt 0$ makes the denominator exceed 1, and it is finite. (C) False: for $z \lt 0$ ReLU is the constant 0, so its slope is 0. (D) False: $\sigma(0) = \tfrac{1}{1+1} = 0.5$.

      GATE DA 2026 · Q56 · NAT · 2 marks

      Consider a fully-connected feed-forward multi-layer perceptron. It has 30 neurons in the input layer, followed by two hidden layers and an output layer. The first hidden layer has 4 neurons and the second hidden layer has 3 neurons. The output layer has only one neuron. Assume that no bias parameters are used.

      The number of learnable parameters in the multi-layer perceptron is ______ . (Answer in integer)

      No biases, so only weights: multiply the sizes of each pair of consecutive layers and add.

      $30\times4 + 4\times3 + 3\times1 = 120 + 12 + 3 = $ 135. The input “neurons” hold the features and have no parameters of their own. Official key: 135.

      GATE DA 2024 sample paper · Q43 · NAT · 2 marks

      Consider a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) model with one hidden layer and one output layer. The hidden layer has 10 neurons, and the output layer has 3 neurons. The input to the MLP is a 5-dimensional vector. Each neuron is connected to every neuron in the previous layer, and a bias term is included for each neuron. The activation function used is the sigmoid function. The total number of trainable parameters in this MLP model is ______.

      Each layer costs (inputs to it + 1) × (its neurons). The activation function has no parameters.

      Hidden layer: $(5 + 1)\times10 = 60$. Output layer: $(10 + 1)\times3 = 33$. Total 93. Without the biases it would be 80; the sigmoid adds nothing. (Sample paper, no official key; this is our answer.)

      A fully connected network takes 12 input features, has one hidden layer of $H$ neurons and 4 output neurons, and every neuron has a bias. It has 344 learnable parameters. The Hyderabad Hyperplanes’ analyst replaces the single hidden layer by two hidden layers of 10 neurons each (biases everywhere, still fully connected). How many fewer learnable parameters does the new network have?

      Write the count of the first network as a function of $H$ and solve for $H$. Then count the new network layer by layer.

      First network: $(12 + 1)H + (H + 1)\times4 = 17H + 4 = 344$, so $H = 20$.

      New network: $(12+1)\times10 + (10+1)\times10 + (10+1)\times4 = 130 + 110 + 44 = 284$.

      Difference: $344 - 284 = $ 60. Two narrower layers can be cheaper than one wide one. Dropping the biases from the new network gives $120 + 100 + 40 = 260$ and a wrong difference of 84.

      A network with zero biases has three ReLU hidden neurons $h_A = \mathrm{ReLU}(2x_1 + x_2)$, $h_B = \mathrm{ReLU}(-x_1 - x_2)$, $h_C = \mathrm{ReLU}(x_1 + 3x_2)$, and a ReLU output $y = \mathrm{ReLU}(h_A + 5h_B + 2h_C)$. For all positive $x_1, x_2$, the network is equivalent to

      1. $y = 4x_1 + 7x_2$
      2. $y = -x_1 + 2x_2$
      3. $y = 3x_1 + 4x_2$
      4. no single linear neuron, because $h_B$ has negative weights

      For positive inputs, decide which hidden neurons are switched on. A ReLU that is always switched off contributes nothing, whatever its outgoing weight.

      For $x_1, x_2 \gt 0$: $2x_1 + x_2 \gt 0$ and $x_1 + 3x_2 \gt 0$, so $h_A$ and $h_C$ pass their inputs unchanged; $-x_1 - x_2 \lt 0$, so $h_B = 0$ always.

      Output pre-activation: $(2x_1 + x_2) + 5\cdot0 + 2(x_1 + 3x_2) = 4x_1 + 7x_2 \gt 0$, so the output ReLU is also the identity: (A).

      (B) ignores the ReLU on $h_B$ and multiplies its negative pre-activation by 5. (C) drops the output weight 2 on $h_C$. (D) is wrong because a switched-off neuron simply disappears on this region; the network is linear there.

      Which statements are true? (Select all that apply.)

      (A) A network with any number of layers but identity activations everywhere can represent only affine functions $M\x + \mathbf{c}$ of its input.
      (B) A single neuron with a step activation can classify all four XOR points correctly if its weights are chosen well.
      (C) A network whose hidden activations are all ReLU (and whose output is linear) computes a continuous, piecewise-linear function of its input.
      (D) With ReLU activations, zero biases, non-negative weights and positive inputs, the network equals a single linear neuron.

      Composing affine maps gives an affine map. ReLU is itself continuous and piecewise linear. For (B), think about what boundary one neuron draws.

      (A) True: $W_2(W_1\x + \b_1) + \b_2 = (W_2W_1)\x + (W_2\b_1 + \b_2)$, and so on for more layers.

      (B) False: one neuron’s boundary is a single line, and XOR’s two classes sit on opposite diagonals, so no line separates them.

      (C) True: sums, scalings and compositions of continuous piecewise-linear functions stay continuous and piecewise linear.

      (D) True: every pre-activation is non-negative, so each ReLU is the identity and the network collapses to a product of weight matrices (this is 2024 Q43). Answer A, C, D.

      • Before simplifying a ReLU network, check the sign of every pre-activation for the inputs in question.
      • Count parameters layer by layer: (inputs + 1) × neurons with biases, inputs × neurons without.
      • Read the figure carefully: list, for each neuron, exactly which inputs feed it.
      • Counting the input layer’s “neurons” as having weights or biases.
      • Adding parameters for the activation function: sigmoid, ReLU and step have none.
      • Believing more layers always means more power: without a non-linear activation they collapse to one layer.
      1. A neuron computes a = g(wᵀx + b); a network feeds the activations of one layer into the next.
      2. Without a non-linear activation, any stack of layers is one linear map; ReLU networks are linear wherever no neuron changes on/off state.
      3. Parameters = Σ nₗ₋₁·nₗ weights, plus Σ nₗ biases if biases are used.

      A network has two hidden layers but no activation functions at all: each neuron just outputs its weighted sum. Compared with a single linear neuron per output, what can it represent?

      Much more complicated, curved decision boundaries
      Try multiplying the weight matrices together: what kind of map do you get?
      Exactly the same family of linear (affine) functions
      A product of matrices is a matrix, so the whole network is one linear layer. The non-linear activation is what makes depth useful.
      Only constant functions
      The output still depends on the input; think about what kind of dependence.
      XOR, but nothing more complex
      XOR needs a non-linear boundary. Can a composition of linear maps produce one?

      A fully connected 3-4-2 network (3 inputs, 4 hidden, 2 outputs) uses biases. How many learnable parameters does it have?

      20
      That counts only the weights. Every hidden and output neuron also has a bias.
      9
      That’s the number of neurons, counting the inputs. Parameters live on the connections and in the biases.
      26
      $(3+1)\times4 + (4+1)\times2 = 16 + 10 = 26$.
      29
      The input layer has no biases. Use (inputs + 1) × neurons for each layer.

      In neural-network terms, logistic regression from Part 3 is

      a network with no hidden layer and one sigmoid output neuron
      Weighted sum plus bias, then the sigmoid: exactly one neuron.
      a network with one hidden ReLU layer
      Logistic regression has no hidden layer: its boundary is a single hyperplane.
      a single neuron with a step activation
      That’s the perceptron. Logistic regression outputs a probability, not a hard 0/1.
      a network with identity activations everywhere
      That would be linear regression. Which function turns a score into a probability?

      Training a network: gradient descent and backpropagation

      Training means adjusting the weights so the loss gets smaller: gradient descent says which way to move each weight, and backpropagation computes those directions efficiently with the chain rule.

      GATE DA 2025 Q42 asked for two gradients through a small ReLU network, and 2026 Q29 asked for one stochastic gradient descent step. Both are quick if you know where gradients stop: at a switched-off ReLU.

      It’s like walking down a foggy hillside: you can’t see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet, so you take a step downhill and feel again.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      One-step gradient updates, and gradients of the output with respect to individual weights.

      2025 Q42 · ∂y/∂a and ∂y/∂f through ReLUs2026 Q29 · one SGD step
      Heat: 2025 and 2026, 1–2 marks

      The Bengaluru Backprops’ network has a few thousand weights. Before training they are random, and its predictions are poor. Recall from Part 1 that a loss measures how wrong the predictions are on the training set (the examples whose labels we know): for example the mean squared error $\frac1N\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2$, or for classification the cross-entropy of Part 3.

      The loss is a function of the weights. Picture it as a landscape: each point is one setting of all the weights, and the height is the loss. Training is a search for a low point.

      The gradient $\grad L$ is the vector of partial derivatives $\partial L/\partial w$, one per weight (see refreshers: gradients). It points in the direction in which the loss rises fastest. So step the other way.

      Starting from some weights $\mathbf{w}_0$, repeat $$\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,\grad L(\mathbf{w}).$$ The step size $\eta \gt 0$ is the learning rate, a hyperparameter. Each weight moves against its own partial derivative: if $\partial L/\partial w \gt 0$, increasing $w$ would raise the loss, so $w$ decreases.

      A tiny example. Let $L(w) = (w-4)^2 + 1$, start at $w = 1$, and use $\eta = 0.1$. The derivative is $L'(w) = 2(w-4)$.

      • Step 1: $L'(1) = -6$, so $w = 1 - 0.1\times(-6) = 1.6$.
      • Step 2: $L'(1.6) = -4.8$, so $w = 1.6 + 0.48 = 2.08$.

      Each step closes 20% of the remaining gap to the minimum at $w = 4$: the gap goes $3 \to 2.4 \to 1.92$.

      The training loss is an average over examples: $L(\mathbf{w}) = \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \ell_i(\mathbf{w})$, where $\ell_i$ is the loss on example $i$.

      (Full-)batch gradient descent uses the gradient of the whole average at every step.
      Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) uses the gradient of one example’s loss $\ell_i$ (chosen at random, or in shuffled order) per step: $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\,\grad\ell_i(\mathbf{w})$.
      Mini-batch SGD averages over a small random batch, say 32 examples.

      One iteration is one update; one epoch is one pass through all $N$ examples. SGD’s steps are cheap and noisy; on average they point the same way as the full gradient.

      Try it

      The model $\hat y = w x$ is fitted to three points by gradient descent on the mean squared error. Press Step a few times at the default learning rate and watch $w$ slide to the green minimum. Then raise $\eta$ above 0.214 and reset: each step overshoots further and the loss grows. Finally switch to SGD: it uses one point per step, so the path zig-zags and keeps jittering near the minimum instead of settling exactly.

      Careful: too small a learning rate is slow; too large a learning rate diverges. For a quadratic loss $L(w) = \frac{k}{2}(w - w^\ast)^2$ one step multiplies the gap $w - w^\ast$ by $(1 - \eta k)$, so gradient descent converges exactly when $0 \lt \eta \lt 2/k$, and it oscillates (overshoots back and forth) when $1/k \lt \eta \lt 2/k$.

      Backpropagation: the chain rule, organised

      To run gradient descent on a network we need $\partial L/\partial w$ for every weight. Each weight affects the loss only through a chain of intermediate values: its neuron’s pre-activation, that neuron’s activation, the next layer, and so on. The chain rule (from refreshers) multiplies the local derivatives along that chain.

      Backpropagation does this for all weights at once. The forward pass computes and stores every $z$ and $a$. The backward pass starts at the loss and moves towards the input, computing $\partial L/\partial z$ for each neuron from the layer after it. Each weight’s gradient is then one multiplication.

      For $z = w\,x$: $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial w} = x$ and $\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = w$.
      ReLU: $\dfrac{d}{dz}\mathrm{ReLU}(z) = 1$ if $z \gt 0$, and $0$ if $z \lt 0$ (at $z = 0$ take 0).
      Sigmoid: $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)\big(1 - \sigma(z)\big)$, at most $0.25$ (at $z = 0$).

      Write $\delta_j = \partial L/\partial z_j$ for neuron $j$ ("the error signal arriving at $j$"). For the weight $w_{ji}$ on the edge from activation $a_i$ into neuron $j$: $$\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{ji}} = \delta_j\,a_i, \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial b_j} = \delta_j,$$ and the signals are passed backwards by $$\delta_j = g'(z_j)\sum_{k} w_{kj}\,\delta_k,$$ summing over the neurons $k$ that $j$ feeds.

      (signal arriving at the neuron’s $z$) × (the value that travelled along that edge in the forward pass). A ReLU that was switched off in the forward pass ($z \lt 0$) passes back 0, so every weight feeding it, and every weight that only reaches the output through it, gets gradient 0 for this example.

      Try it

      The network from 2025 Q42 with weights $a = b = c = 1$, $e = 4$ and adjustable $u$, $v$, $d$, $f$. Coral numbers above each neuron are the forward pass; blue numbers below are the backward signals $\partial y/\partial z$. With the defaults the bottom neuron is switched off (grey): see that $\partial y/\partial c$, $\partial y/\partial d$ and $\partial y/\partial f$ are all 0. Now raise $d$ until the bottom neuron switches on, and watch those gradients appear.

      GATE DA 2025 · Q42 · MCQ · 2 marks

      Consider the neural network shown in the figure with

      inputs: $u, v$
      weights: $a, b, c, d, e, f$
      output: $y$
      $R$ denotes the ReLU function, $R(x) = \max(0, x)$.

      Given $u = 2, v = 3$,
      $a = 1, b = 1, c = 1, d = -1, e = 4, f = -1$,
      which one of the following is correct?

      1. $\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial a} = 8, \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial f} = 0$
      2. $\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial a} = 1, \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial f} = 0$
      3. $\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial a} = 1, \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial f} = -1$
      4. $\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial a} = 2, \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial f} = -1$

      1. Forward pass, top neuron: $z_1 = au + bv = 2 + 3 = 5$, $h_1 = R(5) = 5$.

        Read from the figure: $u$ reaches the top neuron through $a$, $v$ through $b$.

      2. Bottom neuron: $z_2 = cu + dv = 2 - 3 = -1$, $h_2 = R(-1) = 0$. It is switched off.

        $u$ reaches the bottom neuron through $c$, $v$ through $d = -1$.

      3. Output: $z_o = e h_1 + f h_2 = 4\times5 + (-1)\times0 = 20$, $y = R(20) = 20$. The output ReLU is on, so $\partial y/\partial z_o = 1$.

        Store every $z$ and $h$: the backward pass needs them to know which ReLUs pass gradient.

      4. $\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial f} = \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z_o}\cdot h_2 = 1\times0 = 0$.

        The gradient of a weight is the signal at its neuron times the value that travelled along its edge, and $h_2 = 0$ travelled along $f$.

      5. $\dfrac{\partial y}{\partial a} = \dfrac{\partial y}{\partial z_o}\cdot e\cdot R'(z_1)\cdot u = 1\times4\times1\times2 = 8$. Answer (A).

        Chain rule from $y$ back to $a$: through the output ReLU (1), weight $e$ (4), the top ReLU, which is on (1), and finally $\partial z_1/\partial a = u = 2$. Option (D)'s $\partial y/\partial a = 2$ stops at $u$, and (C)'s $-1$ uses $f$’s own value instead of $h_2$. Official key: A.

      Gradient descent with learning rate $\eta = 0.25$ minimises $L(w) = (w - 2)^2$ starting from $w_0 = 5$. What is $w$ after two steps?

      $L'(w) = 2(w-2)$. Apply $w \leftarrow w - \eta L'(w)$ twice.

      Step 1: $L'(5) = 6$, $w_1 = 5 - 0.25\times6 = 3.5$.

      Step 2: $L'(3.5) = 3$, $w_2 = 3.5 - 0.75 = $ 2.75. Each step halves the gap to 2 (here $k = 2$ and $1 - \eta k = 0.5$).

      A single sigmoid neuron outputs $\hat y = \sigma(wx)$ and is trained with loss $L = \tfrac12(\hat y - y)^2$. For the example $x = 2$, $y = 1$, at the current weight $w = 0$, find $\partial L/\partial w$.

      Chain rule: $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w} = (\hat y - y)\cdot\sigma'(z)\cdot x$ with $z = wx$, and $\sigma'(z) = \sigma(z)(1 - \sigma(z))$.

      $z = 0$, so $\hat y = \sigma(0) = 0.5$ and $\sigma'(0) = 0.5\times0.5 = 0.25$.

      $\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial w} = (0.5 - 1)\times0.25\times2 = $ −0.25. It is negative, so gradient descent increases $w$, pushing $\hat y$ towards the label 1.

      A training set has 10,000 examples. Which statement about stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with one example per update is correct?

      1. Each update uses the gradient of the average loss over all 10,000 examples.
      2. One epoch consists of exactly one update.
      3. One epoch consists of 10,000 updates, each using the gradient of a single example’s loss.
      4. SGD needs no learning rate because the noise sets the step size.

      An epoch is one pass through every example. How many examples does each SGD step look at?

      SGD updates after every single example, so one pass through 10,000 examples is 10,000 updates: (C). (A) and (B) describe full-batch gradient descent; (D) is false, since every SGD step is $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow \mathbf{w} - \eta\grad\ell_i$.

      GATE DA 2026 · Q29 · NAT · 1 mark

      Consider that for a supervised learning task, the objective function being minimized is $f_w(x) = wx$, where $x \in \mathbb{R}$ is the input and $w \in \mathbb{R}$ is the parameter. Stochastic Gradient Descent with learning rate of 0.10 is used for parameter updates.

      Suppose that at the end of iteration $i$, the value of $w$ becomes 10.00.

      Let $x = 10.00$ be the input for iteration $(i + 1)$.

      The value of $w$ at the end of iteration $(i + 1)$ is ______ . (Rounded off to two decimal places)

      Differentiate the objective with respect to the parameter $w$, not the input: $\partial(wx)/\partial w = x$.

      The gradient of $f_w(x) = wx$ with respect to $w$ is $x = 10$.

      One SGD step: $w \leftarrow 10 - 0.10\times10 = $ 9.00. Adding the gradient instead of subtracting it gives 11.00, the common slip. Official key: 8.90 to 9.10.

      A logistic-regression neuron (Part 3) has $\mathbf{w} = (0.5, -1)$, $b = 0$ and is trained with the cross-entropy loss, for which $\dfrac{\partial\ell}{\partial\mathbf{w}} = (\sigma(z) - y)\,\x$ and $\dfrac{\partial\ell}{\partial b} = \sigma(z) - y$, where $z = \mathbf{w}\T\x + b$. One SGD step with $\eta = 0.5$ is taken on the example $\x = (2, 1)$, $y = 1$. What is the new value of $z$ for that same example?

      Three stages: compute $z$ and $\sigma(z)$ at the current weights, update both $\mathbf{w}$ and $b$, then recompute $z$ with the new values.

      Current: $z = 0.5\times2 - 1\times1 + 0 = 0$, $\sigma(0) = 0.5$, so $\sigma(z) - y = -0.5$.

      Update: $\mathbf{w} \leftarrow (0.5, -1) - 0.5\times(-0.5)(2, 1) = (0.5, -1) + (0.5, 0.25) = (1, -0.75)$; $b \leftarrow 0 - 0.5\times(-0.5) = 0.25$.

      New $z = 1\times2 - 0.75\times1 + 0.25 = $ 1.5, so the predicted probability rises from 0.5 to $\sigma(1.5) \approx 0.82$.

      Getting the sign of the step wrong gives $-1.5$; forgetting to update $b$ gives $1.25$.

      A network has input $\x = (x_1, x_2) = (1, 2)$, two ReLU hidden neurons $h_1 = \mathrm{ReLU}(w_{11}x_1 + w_{12}x_2)$ and $h_2 = \mathrm{ReLU}(w_{21}x_1 + w_{22}x_2)$ with $w_{11} = 1$, $w_{12} = -1$, $w_{21} = 2$, $w_{22} = 1$, and a linear output $\hat y = v_1h_1 + v_2h_2$ with $v_1 = 3$, $v_2 = 0.5$. The loss is $L = \tfrac12(\hat y - y)^2$ with label $y = 5$. Which statements are true? (Select all that apply.)

      (A) $\partial L/\partial v_2 = -12$   (B) $\partial L/\partial w_{11} = -9$   (C) $\partial L/\partial w_{22} = -3$   (D) One gradient descent step with $\eta = 0.1$ changes $v_1$.

      Forward pass first: find both pre-activations, both $h$’s, $\hat y$ and $\hat y - y$. Then each gradient is a chain of local derivatives; watch for a switched-off ReLU.

      Forward: $z_1 = 1 - 2 = -1$, $h_1 = 0$ (off); $z_2 = 2 + 2 = 4$, $h_2 = 4$. $\hat y = 3\cdot0 + 0.5\cdot4 = 2$, so $\partial L/\partial\hat y = \hat y - y = -3$.

      (A) $\partial L/\partial v_2 = -3\times h_2 = -12$. True.

      (B) $\partial L/\partial w_{11} = -3\times v_1\times\mathrm{ReLU}'(z_1)\times x_1 = -3\times3\times0\times1 = 0$, not $-9$. False ($-9$ is what you get by ignoring that $h_1$ is off).

      (C) $\partial L/\partial w_{22} = -3\times v_2\times1\times x_2 = -3\times0.5\times2 = -3$. True.

      (D) $\partial L/\partial v_1 = -3\times h_1 = 0$, so $v_1$ does not move. False. Answer A, C.

      Gradient descent with learning rate $\eta$ is run on $L(w) = 2(w - 3)^2$ starting from $w_0 = 5$. Which option gives both $w_2$ (the value after two steps when $\eta = 0.4$) and the full set of learning rates for which the iterates converge to 3 from every start?

      1. $w_2 = 3.72$; converges exactly when $0 \lt \eta \lt 0.5$
      2. $w_2 = 3.72$; converges exactly when $0 \lt \eta \lt 0.25$
      3. $w_2 = 2.28$; converges exactly when $0 \lt \eta \lt 0.5$
      4. $w_2 = 1.8$; converges exactly when $0 \lt \eta \lt 1$

      $L'(w) = 4(w-3)$, so one step maps the gap $w - 3$ to $(1 - 4\eta)(w - 3)$. When does repeatedly multiplying by $(1 - 4\eta)$ shrink the gap to 0?

      One step: $w - 3 \mapsto (1 - 4\eta)(w - 3)$. With $\eta = 0.4$ the factor is $-0.6$: the gap goes $2 \to -1.2 \to 0.72$, so $w_1 = 1.8$ and $w_2 = 3.72$.

      Convergence needs $|1 - 4\eta| \lt 1$, i.e. $0 \lt \eta \lt 0.5$. Answer (A).

      (B) is the condition for no overshoot ($1 - 4\eta \ge 0$, i.e. $\eta \le 0.25$), which is stricter than convergence. (C) drops the sign flip of the oscillation. (D) gives $w_1$, not $w_2$.

      • Do the forward pass first and write down every $z$: the signs decide which ReLUs pass gradient.
      • Move against the gradient: $w - \eta\,\partial L/\partial w$.
      • Differentiate with respect to the parameter, treating the input as a fixed number.
      • Adding the gradient instead of subtracting it.
      • Giving a non-zero gradient to weights that feed a switched-off ReLU.
      • Confusing an epoch (a pass through the data) with an iteration (one update).
      1. Gradient descent: w ← w − η∇L; too large an η overshoots and can diverge.
      2. SGD uses one example’s gradient per update (mini-batch: a few); one epoch is one pass through the data.
      3. Backprop: ∂L/∂w = (signal δ at the neuron) × (input on that edge); a ReLU with z < 0 passes back 0.

      At the current weight $w = 3$, the loss has slope $dL/dw = +4$. To reduce the loss, gradient descent will

      increase $w$
      A positive slope means the loss rises as $w$ increases. Which way is downhill?
      decrease $w$
      $w \leftarrow 3 - 4\eta$: it steps against the slope.
      leave $w$ unchanged until the slope is zero
      A non-zero slope is exactly what tells it to move.
      set $w$ to 0
      The step is small and proportional to the slope; it doesn’t jump to a fixed value.

      During training the loss bounces up and down and then grows without limit. The most likely cause is

      the learning rate is too small
      A tiny learning rate makes training slow, not explosive.
      the network has too few layers
      Depth affects what the network can represent, not whether the updates blow up.
      the training set is too large
      More data makes each gradient more reliable, not larger.
      the learning rate is too large
      Each step overshoots the minimum by more than it corrects, so the error grows.

      In the forward pass, a ReLU neuron had pre-activation $z = -1.5$. In the backward pass, the gradient of the loss with respect to each of its incoming weights is

      0
      $\mathrm{ReLU}'(-1.5) = 0$, so the chain is multiplied by 0.
      $-1.5$ times the input
      The pre-activation’s value isn’t the local derivative. What is the slope of ReLU for negative $z$?
      the input on that edge
      That would be right only if the neuron were on and the arriving signal were 1.
      undefined
      ReLU is only non-differentiable at exactly $z = 0$.

      Which activation function’s output can be read as a probability between 0 and 1?

      ReLU
      ReLU’s output is unbounded above.
      Sigmoid
      $\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})$ lies strictly between 0 and 1.
      Identity
      The identity can output any real number.
      Step
      The step outputs only 0 or 1, a hard decision rather than a probability.

      One gradient descent step on $L(w) = (w - 1)^2$ from $w = 3$ with $\eta = 0.5$ gives

      2
      Recompute the derivative: $L'(3) = 2(3 - 1)$.
      5
      Gradient descent subtracts the gradient.
      1
      $L'(3) = 4$, so $w = 3 - 0.5\times4 = 1$, the minimum.
      −1
      Check the size of the step: $\eta\times L'(3)$.

      A fully connected 2-3-1 network without biases is trained by backpropagation. How many partial derivatives $\partial L/\partial w$ does each backward pass produce?

      6
      That’s only the first layer. Count the output layer’s weights too.
      3
      That’s the number of hidden neurons.
      13
      That would include biases, which this network doesn’t have.
      9
      One per weight: $2\times3 + 3\times1 = 9$.

      Why can no single perceptron (Part 3) learn XOR?

      Its decision boundary is one straight line, and XOR’s classes sit on opposite diagonals
      One hyperplane cannot separate them; a hidden layer can.
      The perceptron update rule has no learning rate
      The update rule isn’t the obstacle: no choice of weights works at all.
      XOR has too few training points
      Four points are plenty; the problem is their arrangement.
      The step activation is not differentiable
      That matters for gradient descent, but a perceptron can’t represent XOR with any weights.

      For one example, the squared error of the model $\hat y = wx$ is $(y - wx)^2$. Its derivative with respect to $w$ is

      $2(y - wx)$
      The chain rule also multiplies by the derivative of $y - wx$ with respect to $w$.
      $-2w(y - wx)$
      Differentiate with respect to $w$: the inner derivative is $-x$, not $-w$.
      $-2x(y - wx)$
      Outer derivative $2(y - wx)$ times inner derivative $-x$.
      $x^2$
      That’s not the derivative; use the chain rule on the square.

      Everything so far in this module learned from labelled examples: each player came with the answer (a role, a score, a win or a loss). Unsupervised learning works with no answers at all. It looks for structure in the data itself: groups of similar players (clustering, with k-means and hierarchical clustering) and a few directions that capture most of the variation (principal component analysis). Each of these three topics has been asked in GATE DA, usually as a quick 1- or 2-mark question you can do by hand.

      You need: Chapter 1.1 (features, labels, supervised versus unsupervised); distances between points; for PCA, eigenvalues and eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix (Linear algebra 3.2) and covariance (Statistics 1.2).

      k-means and k-medoids: finding groups without labels

      k-means splits data into $k$ groups by repeating two moves: send every point to its nearest centre, then move every centre to the middle of its group.

      GATE DA has asked about it from several sides: which point must share a cluster (2024 Q19), one iteration by hand (sample paper Q42) and matching k-medoid to clustering (2026 Q23).

      It’s like placing three water coolers in a training ground: each player walks to the nearest cooler, then you move each cooler to the middle of the crowd using it, and repeat until nobody switches.

      Where it shows up in GATE DA

      Short conceptual MCQs and a by-hand iteration, 1–2 marks.

      2024 Q19 · which point must be in cluster 3Sample Q42 · one k-means iteration2026 Q23 · k-medoid is for clustering
      Heat: every year, 1–2 marks

      Learning without answers

      Recall from Chapter 1.1 that a feature is a measured property of an example (a player’s batting score) and a label is the answer we want to predict (the player’s role). In supervised learning every training example comes with its label, and the model learns to predict labels for new examples.

      In unsupervised learning there are no labels. You have only the features, and the goal is to find structure in them: groups of similar examples, unusual examples, or a smaller set of numbers that describes each example well.

      Why would anyone want that? Three everyday reasons:

      • Labels are expensive. The DPL’s scouts have statistics for every player in every league, but nobody has sat down and tagged each one as “batter”, “bowler” or “all-rounder”. Clustering can suggest those groups for free.
      • You may not know the groups yet. A franchise might discover that its fans fall into four buying patterns nobody had named before.
      • It helps other methods. Squeezing 20 statistics down to 2 (with PCA, Chapter 6.3) makes data easier to plot, faster to train on and less noisy.

      The clustering problem

      A cluster is a group of examples that are close to each other and far from the other groups. “Close” needs a distance; in this chapter it’s the ordinary straight-line (Euclidean) distance $\norm{\x - \y}$.

      Picture 19 DPL players plotted by a batting score and a bowling score. Your eye sees batters in one corner, bowlers in another and all-rounders in the middle. k-means is a recipe that finds such groups when there are too many points, or too many features, to see.
